01

The 25 facts most likely to be tested

Dark-topped cards are Aguirre's case material, where the exam questions come from. Blue-topped cards are Neira's frameworks.
If you only have an hour: read this list twice, then do the practice exam at the bottom.
  1. AguirreInvestment grade is BBB- and above on the S&P scale; below is speculative grade. Use the local-currency, long-term rating. Germany AAA, Spain AA-, India and State Bank of India BBB, Société Générale A. S&P rated Lehman AAA shortly before it failed. S&P is free to use.
  2. AguirreFactoring sells your whole receivables book for liquidity up to 90 percent of invoice value. Discounting is bill by bill and always with recourse. Without recourse: the factor takes default risk and receivables leave the balance sheet. With recourse: unpaid invoices come back, so it is a loan. Cost about 1 to 2 percent. Only works with high-quality debtors. Plamar sold to PDVSA.
  3. AguirrePlamar needed about USD 300,000 for a plant making 300,000 handles and 300,000 seals a month. Balance sheet 31 Dec 2002: cash VEB 97.7m, receivables 211.5m, total assets 621.6m. At the deck's rate that is USD 70,361 cash, 152,313 receivables, 447,526 assets. Receivables are one third of assets. Ask the currency and the year before reading any balance sheet.
  4. AguirreWhy Guatemala: free trade agreement with Mexico and so NAFTA access to the US, low cost, close to Venezuela, stable currency, inflation about 2 percent, GDP per capita USD 3,646. Brazil dismissed: Lula just elected, too big for USD 240,000. Dominican Republic: devalued peso, inflation 8.6 percent. Plamar today operates in Guatemala, the Dominican Republic, Brazil and Costa Rica.
  5. AguirreAsian crisis response: raise interest rates and defend dollar pegs. Both backfired. Korea's interbank rate hit 30 percent; the Thai market fell 75 percent. Do not raise rates when the debt burden is already large.
  6. AguirreMalaysia was the only country in IMF history (since 1944) to reject IMF aid, in 1997. It used capital controls and spending cuts, helped by oil. Mahathir fired Anwar on 2 Sept 1998, a day after imposing the controls.
  7. AguirreOriginal sin: developing countries borrow in USD or EUR, not their own currency. A stronger dollar or higher US rates grow the debt automatically.
  8. AguirreTrigger of the Asian crisis was loss of confidence. First sign: 5 Feb 1997, Somprasong Land missed a USD 3.1m interest payment. Thailand floated the baht on 2 July 1997; it fell 15 percent at once.
  9. AguirreIMF packages: Thailand USD 16bn (Aug 1997, 17bn with China), Indonesia 23bn rising to 40bn (Oct 1997), Korea 55bn rising to 58bn (Dec 1997). The IMF lends, it does not donate, at rates below private banks but with austerity conditions.
  10. AguirreSociété Générale lost EUR 4.9bn on Kerviel's unauthorized trades, announced 24 Jan 2008, plus about 2bn on subprime. About EUR 50bn of positions unwound in three days; EUR 5.5bn capital increase. 74 alerts closed procedurally. He took 4 days of holiday in 2007. He came from the middle office and knew when controls ran.
  11. AguirreOther rogue traders: Nick Leeson, Barings 1995, GBP 827m (USD 1.3bn), a bank founded in 1762. Kweku Adoboli, UBS 2011, USD 2bn.
  12. AguirreThe exporter's lesson from SocGen: never speculate on currency. Close or hedge every open position with a forward. Too many controllers means nobody controls.
  13. AguirreForward formula: swap points = (SONIA minus EURIBOR) x days x spot / (36,000 + EURIBOR x days); forward = spot + swap points. Class example: spot EUR/GBP 0.8479, EURIBOR 3.013 percent, SONIA 3.732 percent, 180 days, forward about 0.8509. Equal rates give forward equal to spot. Banks earn the bid-ask spread.
  14. AguirreConvertible currency (UN, any one of): unlimited purchase of foreign currency by residents and non-residents; no central bank authorization; traded internationally and widely used. Hard: USD, EUR, GBP, JPY, CHF, CAD, AUD, NZD, SEK, DKK, NOK. Not fully convertible: CNY, INR, RUB, TRY. Non-convertible pairs route through USD, doubling fees and risk.
  15. AguirreTurkish lira: 1 USD = 9 TRY in 1966, 1,650,000 in 2001, six zeros dropped in 2005, 18.30 in Sept 2022, 41.82 in Oct 2025, 49.22 on 8 Oct 2026.
  16. AguirreICC contract, 8 points: parties, object, transport, terms of payment, guarantees of payment, courts, legislation, risks. Three transaction risks: transport, currency, credit. Term of payment is not a guarantee of payment. Letters of credit cover about 44 percent of international trade.
  17. AguirreBasel capital ratio 8 percent of risk-weighted assets (Basel I, 1988). Basel II (June 2001) kept 8 percent, tied weights to borrower quality, three pillars: minimum capital, supervisory review, disclosure. Basel III added liquidity buffers; Basel IV is current. Schröder: "not acceptable for Germany" (Oct 2001). July 2002 fix: loans under EUR 1m as retail, EUR 1 to 50m turnover lower weights, no long-term surcharge up to EUR 500m, deadline Jan 2007.
  18. AguirreMittelstand: up to 499 employees and EUR 50m revenue (EU SME definition is 250). 3.6m firms, 68 percent of workers, 80 percent of apprentices. Equity below 20 percent for small firms, the Achilles' heel. Hausbank relationship banking versus Anglo-Saxon capital-market banking.
  19. AguirreGerman banking pillars (case): three. Public (Landesbanken and Sparkassen), cooperatives, private commercial. Aguirre counted four. Loan margins about 1 percent versus 2 to 3.5 in Europe and 4 in the US. State guarantees phased out after 2005.
  20. AguirreNegative working capital is normal for a supermarket and a red flag for a carmaker like Porsche. Main reason firms default. Creditor order in liquidation: government, banks, employees, suppliers.
  21. NeiraCAGE (Ghemawat): Cultural, Administrative, Geographic, Economic. Frankel and Rose: language +200 percent, trading bloc +330, currency +340, colony-colonizer +900, border +80, ocean access +50; 1 percent more distance cuts trade 1.1 percent. Star TV lost about USD 500m. Tricon's Mexico moved from 16th to 2nd.
  22. NeiraMarket selection funnel: PESTEL, then CAGE, then Porter plus detailed market analysis, then the competitive advantage equation (company resources and capabilities matched with country specifics and industry success factors; all three must align). Goals must be SMART.
  23. NeiraReadiness is three home-country analyses: external (five forces), internal (generic strategies, Ansoff), resources (RBV, VRIO). Internationalization is Ansoff's market development. Expect 6 to 18 months of ramp-up.
  24. NeiraEntry ladder, low to high commitment: indirect export, direct export, contractual agreements, FDI. Franchising is the fastest. Alliances fail about 60 percent of the time, mainly through poor partner choice and lack of trust. Sogo shoshas handle 50 percent of Japan's exports and 75 percent of imports.
  25. NeiraZara: 10 to 15 days sketch to shipment, about 12,000 designs a year, stores order twice a week, replenishment 2.8 percent, 17 visits a year versus 4.1, advertising 0.3 percent versus 3.5, prices 15 percent lower, over 60 percent made near Spain, gross margin 57.4 versus 38.3, FY2017 revenue EUR 25.3bn, 7,475 stores, 96 markets, 70.1 percent of Inditex EBIT.
02

Neira's half: the strategy of going abroad

A five-step arc: global trends, benefits and reasons, are we ready, where, how. The decks are numbered S6 "Ready" and S7 "Where", but he taught Where on 28 Sep before Ready on 2 Oct.

Global trends Sessions 1-2, 5-6

  • About half of today's Fortune 500 will be gone in 7 years; almost 90 percent of the 1955 list is gone.
  • Three drivers of disruption: technology (enabler), demographics (silent force), globalization (amplifier). Combinatory technology stacks open tools (Amazon Go). Tesla analyzes about 15 percent of the data it captures.
  • Cities generate 80 to 85 percent of GDP; Asia has over half of the 32 megacities; 41 by 2030.
  • Price drives 60 percent of international purchasing decisions (McKinsey); Chinese car brands took about 15 percent of Spain's market in 5 years.
  • Asset-light platforms expand faster: Alibaba owns no warehouses, Airbnb no hotels, Uber no taxis.
  • Distance still matters online: only 12 percent of internet users buy cross-border; e-commerce cross-border use is 11 to 15 percent versus about 50 percent for Facebook.
  • Growth is shifting to Southeast Asia, Africa, China and India. Incumbents fail through cultural resistance, not missing data (Kodak, Blockbuster, Nokia).

Benefits and reasons to internationalize Session 5

Five drivers on the deck plus one shared bucket. The exam question is usually "which of these is a home-market reason" or "which example goes with which reason".

BucketReasonsExamples used in class
Foreign market pullGrowth; resource seeking (supply, sourcing flexibility, technology, quality, cheaper factors, strategic assets, talent); a specific opportunity; partnerships and trust; serving global customers; learning; getting inside entry barriers; demand pullPM Guatemala port; Metrocompost Vietnam; General Kinematics JV; Netflix's Paris office; IKEA Japan "toughest competition"; auditors following clients
Home market pushSmall market; slow growth; saturation; seasonality; excess capacity; excessive regulation; recession; diversificationSingapore; Zara in Spain; IDE snowmaking (Switzerland and South Africa); ham and cava at Christmas; steel wire rod at 85 percent utilization; URBAR; Spanish firms to Argentina after 2008
Both marketsRegulation changes; tax; government incentivesUber Spain; Northern Ireland tax; ICEX
ProductExtend the life cycle abroad; exploit an exclusive product or technologyFull-fat milk, cereals, Coke
CompetitionIntense at home; weaker abroad; first-mover advantage; follower move; "offense as defense"Zara entered India 2010, H&M followed 2017 (deck); enter the rival's home market to tie up its resources
Scale and scopeScale lowers unit cost and earns ROI on big projects. Scope shares tangible (labs, distribution) and intangible (brand, reputation) resources, or transfers management capabilitiesNational Geographic licensing its brand to merchandise and stores

From the slide images (session 5)

  • Saturated market (slide 17): demand has been fully satisfied. The only ways to sell more are substitution or replacement of the existing product, taking share from competitors, or innovating to move to an unsaturated market or create a new target market.
  • Product life cycle (slide 22): introduction, growth, maturity, decline, drawn as sales against time. Internationalization extends the cycle of products already at maturity at home (full-fat milk, cereals, Coke).
  • Picture examples: MetroCompost's composting plant in Hai Duong, Vietnam (2011, 29,500 tonnes a year) for a specific opportunity; Celsa Group / Global Steel Wire for filling capacity; Singapore for a small home market; the Ford S-Max supplier map, the Big Four and global banks, and the top ten advertising agencies for serving global customers; Starbucks for knowledge integration; the October 2019 US tariffs on Spanish cava, cheese and olive oil for changing entry barriers; Kodak vs Fujifilm and Michelin vs Goodyear for "offense as defense"; a port terminal for strategic assets.

Ready to internationalize? Session 6

Strategy is not a goal ("be number 1"), not a single action ("merge"), and not vision or values. It is how you compete and what advantage you base it on. Readiness is three analyses done at home.

1. External: Porter's five forces

Identify the industry, identify the players, analyze each force in order, and ask of each whether it is strong enough to erase industry profit. Entry barriers: capital (Boeing and Airbus), scale (the A380 needed about 400 units to break even), absolute cost advantage (Aramco, Intel), differentiation (cosmetics high, low-cost airlines low), distribution access (Mercadona shelves), legal barriers (traffic rights), retaliation. Buyer power rises with concentration, information (Booking, Kayak) and vertical integration (Zara makes its own clothes). Class addition: define industry boundaries first; disruption is an extra angle.

Determinants on the summary slide (slide 14): threat of entry = capital requirements, economies of scale, absolute cost advantages, product differentiation, access to distribution, legal barriers, retaliation. Rivalry = concentration, diversity of competitors, product differentiation, excess capacity and exit barriers, cost conditions. Substitutes = buyers' propensity to substitute, relative prices and performance. Buyer power = price sensitivity (cost of the product relative to total cost, differentiation, competition between buyers) plus bargaining power (size and concentration, switching costs, information, ability to backward integrate). Supplier power mirrors buyer power. Substitution examples (slide 15): high for newspapers, travel agencies, urban transport, Audi Q5 vs Land Rover, pizza vs burger, Amazon vs El Corte Inglés; low for gasoline, cigarettes, high-speed train vs bus, orange juice vs cola, cement in Madrid vs Paris. The deck letters the forces a substitutes, b entrants, c rivalry, d buyers, e suppliers.

2. Internal: generic strategies and Ansoff

Two competitive advantages (slide 21): cost advantage means a similar product at lower cost; differentiation advantage means a price premium from a unique product. Generic strategies (slides 22 to 25) cross competitive advantage (costs or differentiation) with market scope (entire market or a segment). On the deck: cost leadership, "be the most competitive company in cost in the entire market", example Amazon; differentiation, "be a distinctive company recognized for its uniqueness, quality or personality", Apple; cost focus, "be very competitive in cost in a particular product or niche", Lidl; differentiation focus, "have a differentiated product or market niche", Ferrari. In class Neira also named Walmart, Aldi, Porsche and Tesla. Ansoff has two levers only, what is sold and to whom.

Existing product
New product
Existing market
Market penetrationOnly in a growing market. New locations, organic growth, lowest risk. Pictures: Aldi, Domino's.
Product developmentUsually on a trusted brand. Pictures: Coca-Cola variants, McDonald's McSalad.
New market
Market developmentNew segments, new channels, new geographies. This is internationalization. Pictures: Starbucks and Kellogg's in China; in class, Uber adapting to Spain's VTC licences.
DiversificationHighest risk, justified by economies of scope. Picture: the iPod; footer note Alphabet, Samsung.

3. Resources and capabilities: RBV and VRIO

Look inside for advantage. Tangible assets can be bought, so they confer little. Intangible assets (brand, know-how, culture) are heterogeneous and immobile, so they sustain advantage. Test each with VRIO (Barney):

Not valuableCompetitive disadvantage
Valuable, not rareCompetitive parity
Valuable and rare, but easy to imitateTemporary advantage
Valuable, rare, costly to imitate, not organized to capture valueTemporary or unexploited
All fourSustained competitive advantage

Costly to imitate comes from time, causal ambiguity and social complexity. Organization means systems, processes, structure and culture. Class addition on funding realism: plan 6 to 18 months of ramp-up before profit and hold cash for capex and working capital. "Spreadsheets can say anything, reality cannot."

Where? International market selection Session 7

Process: strategic analysis, set main goals (SMART and a little flexible), select potential markets, set country-specific goals, entry strategy, implementation. Ghemawat's warning opens the deck: companies routinely exaggerate the attractiveness of foreign markets. Górecka: selecting foreign markets is one of the most critical decisions in entry strategy.

Earliest screening · start from the company itself (the deck shows URBAR's own website and history)
Preliminary screening · macro view with PESTEL · about 200 countries down to 8 to 12
Second screening · the distance approach, CAGE · can we replicate the business there?
In-depth screening · Porter's five forces in 2 to 3 countries plus detailed market analysis (size, product acceptance, pricing, distribution, promotion)
Final selection · the competitive advantage equation: company resources and capabilities matched with country specifics and industry success factors. All three must align; one strength cannot cover a weakness.

Cost of entry, resource constraints and the main goals are weighed at every stage. The slide groups earliest, preliminary and second screening as "country macro specifics" and in-depth screening as "country industry specifics"; in-depth screening splits into industry attractiveness and barriers (Porter) and detailed market analysis of the product. The deck's CAGE boxes read Cultural, Administrative and political, Geographic, Economic/wealth.

CCultural: language, religion, ethnicity, social norms.Most affects TV and media, food, consumer durables (Japan's small cars), wine.
AAdministrative: colonial ties, shared currency or bloc, hostility, policy, corruption, weak institutions.Most affects telecoms, aerospace, electricity, drugs, farming, oil and mining, infrastructure.
GGeographic: remoteness, borders, sea access, size, infrastructure, climate, time zones.Most affects cement and steel, fruit and glass, financial services, services needing local supervision.
EEconomic: consumer income, cost and quality of resources, inputs, infrastructure, knowledge.Most affects cars, mobile phones, garments, insurance. Replicators want similar economies; arbitrageurs want different ones.

Data sources shown on the slides

  • Corruption Perceptions Index 2020, 180 countries, score 0 to 100 with higher meaning cleaner: Denmark and New Zealand 88; Finland, Singapore, Sweden and Switzerland 85; Germany 80; UK 77; US 67; Spain 62; China 42; India 40; Brazil 38; Mexico 31; Russia 30; Guatemala 25; Venezuela 15; Somalia and South Sudan 12.
  • Coface Country Risk Assessment Map, January 2018, 160 countries. Business defaulting risk scale: A1 very low, A2 low, A3 satisfactory, A4 reasonable, B fairly high, C high, D very high, E extreme. That month's upgrades: Brazil B, Greece B, Netherlands A1, Singapore A2, South Korea A2, Ukraine C. Downgrade: Saudi Arabia C, for oil dependence and political tension.
  • Ghemawat's industry sensitivity table (Mallick and Ghemawat, 70 industries): most sensitive to cultural (linguistic) distance are meat, cereals, edible products, tobacco and office machines; least are optical goods and watches, road vehicles, cork and wood, metalworking machinery and electricity. Electricity is highly sensitive to administrative and geographic distance but not at all to cultural. Economic distance reduces trade in metals, fertilizers and steel but increases it in coffee, animal oils and office machines.
  • Country portfolio analysis chart key: Japan 1, Canada 18, Germany 15 are the big bubbles before adjustment; after adjusting for distance Canada is largest and Mexico (19) second, with Japan and Germany shrinking below Mexico.

Country portfolio analysis is flawed. It plots per-capita income against penetration with bubbles for market size, so it counts only potential sales and ignores the cost of distance. Tricon (Pizza Hut, Taco Bell, KFC) ranked Mexico 16th of 20 on CPA; adjusting for distance from Dallas, a shared border and a trade agreement moved it to 2nd. Star TV assumed Asian elites wanted English programming and that satellite beat geography; it lost about USD 500m and triggered a Chinese ban after Murdoch called satellite TV a threat to totalitarian regimes. A survey of multinationals in China: 54 percent did worse than planned, 62 percent had overestimated market potential.

How? Country entry alternatives Session 9

Four levels, chosen by resource commitment, risk, return and the speed you need.

Low commitment, risk, returnHigh
Level 1Indirect exportImporter or export management company (acts as your export department, may use your name, low cost). Agent or representative (commission, does not buy, customers stay yours, may carry rivals). Distributor (buys and resells, wants territory exclusivity, owns the customer). Trading company (full service, no loyalty, Japan's sogo shoshas). Do due diligence: expertise, finances, prompt payment, conflicts, references.
Level 2Direct exportInternet orders leading to localized sites; wholesalers and purchasing groups; branded manufacturers selling through foreign retail chains (Lee, Wrangler); an export department for B2B high-value products once volume justifies it.
Level 3Contractual agreementsTurnkey projects and concessions. Subcontracting (Boeing). Licensing of patents, trademarks, technology: low capital, works behind import barriers, risks wrong partner and quality; co-marketing (joint promotion, Starbucks and Spotify) versus co-branding (a new joint product, Meta Ray-Ban, McFlurry Oreo). Franchising: franchisor gives the package, franchisee gives capital and local knowledge; fastest expansion, control issues. Strategic alliances and JVs: equity JV creates a new company; non-equity alliances are limited in scope and easier to dissolve. About 60 percent fail.
Level 4Foreign direct investmentRepresentative office (marketing only, cannot buy or sell). Branch (same activities as the parent, no separate legal entity, liabilities reach the parent, 100 percent owned). Subsidiary (own legal entity, taxed locally, activities can differ, liability limited). Build it greenfield (control, no technology leakage, slow) or by cross-border M&A (fast, income from day one, inherited risks and staff reactions).

Picture examples on the deck

  • Distributor: URBAR, a Spanish industrial vibration firm founded in 1960. Largest sogo shoshas by 2019 market value: Mitsubishi USD 42.5bn, Mitsui 27.7, Itochu 27.5, Sumitomo 17.9, Marubeni 12.3, Toyota Tsusho 11.6, Sojitz 4.3.
  • Turnkey: a motorway and a hydroelectric dam. Concessions: municipal refuse collection and a recycling plant. Subcontracting: GAP apparel and the Boeing 787, whose wings and center wing box come from Nagoya, center fuselage from Grottaglie in Italy, landing gear from Gloucester, doors from Toulouse and engines from GE in Ohio or Rolls-Royce in Derby.
  • Licensing: Olayan as Coca-Cola bottler; National Geographic stores, with worldwide brand rights subject to approval, an annual fee and a percentage of sales. The combined chain: National Geographic Society in Washington licenses the Spanish company, which franchises the store operators.
  • Co-marketing: Red Bull athletes, Starbucks with Spotify, Uber with Spotify. Co-branding: Apple Watch Nike+, Philadelphia Milka, the Santander Iberia card, Reebok x Bershka, McFlurry M&Ms and Kit Kat. Franchise logos: McDonald's, Pizza Hut, Burger King, KFC, Domino's, Arby's, A&W, Wendy's, Es Teler 77.
  • Self-driving car alliance map (Water Street Partners): automaker plus technology provider, Google and Ford; automakers together, BMW, Audi and Daimler, and GM and Honda; carmaker plus ride-sharing, GM and Lyft, Volvo and Uber; academic or government, Toyota and MIT, Nissan and NASA; suppliers together, Autoliv and Nissin; supplier plus technology, Baidu and Continental, NVIDIA and Bosch. Non-equity alliance example: General Kinematics of Chicago with URBAR of Spain.
  • Why alliances exist (slide 32): the readiness analysis asks whether the company can "acquire or obtain" the resources it lacks. Alliances are the way to obtain them.

Alliance checklist (contract negotiation): agreed objectives, contributions and rewards with penalties, integration with parent strategy, cultural and organizational fit, leverage of complementary strengths, exit strategy, monitoring. Partner selection needs strategic fit (complementarity) and organizational fit (chemistry, similar values, reputation, compatible decision systems, common time horizon). Put duration, notice period of 60 to 90 days, minimum sales and reporting into any intermediary contract. "Today's ally may be tomorrow's rival."

03

Aguirre's half: the risks of being abroad

Aguirre works at Coface, a trade credit insurer in over 60 countries, and has taught at IE since 1998. His sessions move from political and macro risk to credit crises, currency, ratings and banking, and trade finance. His exam questions come from the four Harvard and IE cases.

Managing risk and the shifting wealth of nations Sessions 3-4

  • Allies become enemies. Iran and Iraq swapped roles between 1979 (embassy seized, hostages 444 days), the 1980s, 1990 (Kuwait), 2003 and 2025. Political risk is not only emerging markets: Iberdrola's 80-turbine US project cancelled in Dec 2025; Naturgy expropriated in Colombia.
  • Developed versus developing threshold about USD 10,000 GDP per capita. China and Japan are the world's biggest lenders. Japan: debt over 220 percent of GDP held at home, first rate rise in 35 years in 2025.
  • Four risks on the deck: emerging-market capital flows and foreign-currency debt (original sin), commodity prices, debt, freight costs.
  • Strait of Hormuz: about 20m barrels a day transit; bypass pipelines carry only about 3.5m; about 27 percent of maritime trade; a third of global fertilizer and about 35 percent of aluminum made nearby. Malacca is the biggest strait by volume, Hormuz second.
  • Macro toolkit: GDP = C + I + G + NX; balance of payments = current, capital and financial accounts; PESTEL; PMI surveys about 50,000 purchasing managers; 2 percent inflation is healthy, Turkey at 30 to 40 percent is not; about 80 percent of loans are variable rate; exports are untaxed for the exporter everywhere except Argentina.
  • Mankiw's ten principles, summarized on the deck as: trade can make everyone better off, and living standards depend on productivity. Corporates are read by balance sheet and P&L, countries by balance of payments plus GDP.
  • Numbers to recognize: Asia-Pacific about 78 percent of world GDP growth 2016 to 2026; China, Germany and the US are the three biggest exporters; 1.52bn tourist arrivals in 2025, Spain 96.8m; Spain built 700,000 flats in 2007 and 70,000 in 2008 (non-productive investment versus Korea's R&D and education).

Charts on the slides (Coface)

  • Oil chokepoints, share of total supply / of maritime oil trade: Malacca 23 / 31, Hormuz 21 / 27, Suez 9 / 11, Bab el-Mandeb 8 / 11, Cape of Good Hope 6 / 8, Danish Straits 5 / 6, Turkish Straits 3 / 4, Panama 2 / 3.
  • Hormuz in 2025, share of global seaborne flows: fertilizer 33 percent, methanol 32, crude 31, minerals 24, natural gas liquids 23, LNG 19, refined products 13 to 14. Exports through the strait about 19 million barrels a day; rerouting capacity about 3.5 (Saudi East-West pipeline 3, Fujairah 0.5); 11.8 million barrels a day at risk. Ship transits collapsed from 80 to 115 a day to under 10 in March 2026. After the Red Sea crisis of late 2023, Suez transits fell from about 75 to 30 to 40 ships a day while Cape of Good Hope rose to 90 to 100.
  • Coface alternative scenario, a lasting 50 percent energy price shock: global growth down half a point to 2.1 percent, Europe to 0.5, the US to 1.8; inflation up 1.5 points; stagflation back; insolvencies rising fastest in Asia. Context: a fragile ceasefire after six weeks of conflict, Hormuz traffic near zero since 1 March 2026, and an unprecedented 400 million barrel release of emergency reserves by IEA members.
  • Energy in Europe: EU gas storage in 2026 fell to about 28 to 30 percent by late March, below the ten-year range. Share of electricity from gas: Ireland 48 percent, Italy 44, Greece 37, Netherlands 36, EU average 16, France 4 (68 percent nuclear), Sweden close to zero. Brent peaked near USD 130 in 2022 and spiked above 110 in early 2026; LME aluminium peaked near USD 3,850 a tonne in 2022.
  • Inflation and rates: 2022 peaks of 11.1 percent in the UK, 10.6 in the eurozone and 9 in the US. Policy rate peaks: Fed 5.5, Bank of England 5.25, ECB 4.0; the ECB rate was negative from 2014 to 2022. Eurozone manufacturing output prices jumped to 55.5 on the PMI in April 2026.
  • China and Europe: euro area imports from China peaked near USD 550bn in 2022 against exports of 240bn. Europe's industrial producer prices rose to about 129 (2019 = 100) while China's stayed near 100. Production cost gaps versus China: 50 to 60 percent in rubber, plastics and apparel; 30 to 40 in vehicles, metal products and chemicals; 20 to 30 in machinery, the largest sector. German manufacturing output is about 88 percent of its January 2020 level, Spain about 100.
  • "Reciprocal" tariffs: the rate "charged to the US" was the bilateral US trade deficit divided by that country's exports to the US, with a 10 percent floor; for the EU, 235 / 606 = 38.8, shown as 39 charged and 20 discounted. Poster examples: China 67 / 34, Vietnam 90 / 46, Taiwan 64 / 32, Japan 46 / 24, India 52 / 26, Cambodia 97 / 49; the UK, Brazil, Australia, Singapore, Turkey and Saudi Arabia 10 / 10. The observed US tariff on manufactured goods rose from 2.3 percent in January 2025 to 11.7 in October 2025; by February 2026 producer prices were up 4.6 percent, import prices 3.1 and consumer prices 1.3.
  • Foreign-currency corporate debt, Q2 2018: Turkey highest at about 36 percent of GDP (up 20 points since 2008), Hungary 33, Chile 32, Czech Republic 22, Mexico 17; China about 7 and India 8 lowest.
  • Patents (WIPO PCT filings, 2023): China 69,610, US 55,678, Japan 48,879, Korea 22,288, Germany 16,916, France 7,916. Top applicants: Huawei 6,494, Samsung 3,924, Qualcomm 3,410, Mitsubishi 2,152, BOE 1,988; CATL up 576 percent.
  • Asia: share of world GDP at purchasing power parity crossed 50 percent around 2020, from 34 percent in 2000. Regional contribution to world growth over the next ten years: Asia ex Japan 62.4 percent, North America 9.0, Western Europe 6.3, Africa 5.6, Eastern Europe 5.5, Latin America 5.5, Middle East 3.9, Japan 1.0. The slide caption's 78.7 percent for Asia-Pacific comes from a different source than the chart beside it. More people live inside a circle over South, Southeast and East Asia than outside it.
  • Globalization sentiment: "a force for good" in Vietnam 91 percent, Philippines 85, India 83; UK 46, US 40, France 37. "The world is getting worse": France 81 percent, China 33.
  • GDP growth (Coface): world 2020 minus 2.8, 2021 6.4, 2022 3.3, 2023 2.8, 2024 2.7, 2025 forecast 2.4. 2025 forecasts: US 1.5, Germany 0.2, France 0.5, Spain 2.6, China 4.3, India 5.9, Brazil 2.0.
  • PESTEL contents (slide 81): Politics, government type and policy, funding and grants; Economy, inflation and interest rates, labour and energy costs; Social, population, education, media, lifestyle and culture; Technology, emerging technologies, the web, information and communication; Legal, regulations and standards, employment law; Environment, weather, green and ethical issues, pollution, waste, recycling.
  • Other pictures: the 2017 unicorn map (Uber USD 68bn, Didi 50bn, Xiaomi 46bn, Airbnb 29.3bn, SpaceX 21.2bn, Spotify 8.5bn); the Brazil Economist covers "Brazil takes off" (2009), "Has Brazil blown it?" (2013), "The betrayal of Brazil" (2016); the Hobo-Dyer south-up equal-area map and a Chinese Pacific-centred map, used to argue that "how we see the world" is a choice; Marco Polo's route 1260 to 1295 via Hormuz; Arctic shipping routes (Northwest Passage, Northern Sea Route, Transpolar).

The ICC international contract

Eight points: parties (often including distributors), object, transport, terms of payment, guarantees of payment, courts, legislation, risks. The three transaction risks are transport, currency and credit. Use the destination country's courts; London arbitration only for big claims. Pro forma invoices need buyer approval. Cuba's average payment term is 360 days. Letters of credit, governed by the ICC, cover about 44 percent of corporate international trade. Reading: Peter Bernstein, Against the Gods.

The Asian financial crisis Session 10

Government causesFixed exchange rates; current account deficits; weak regulation and control.
Company and market causesToo many financial firms; dependence on short-term foreign funds; currency speculation; overpriced assets.
External causesGovernments paralysed by political uncertainty; the region seen as one unit; speculation; IMF conditions.

Class framing: 1992 to 1997 capital poured into economies growing above 9 percent; banks lend out 97 percent of deposits so mass withdrawals collapse liquidity; a surge in non-performing loans is the early warning; ICISA is the credit insurers' association (Allianz, Atradius, AXA). When a company is liquidated the government is paid first, then banks, then employees, then suppliers.

  • 5 Feb 1997Somprasong Land misses a USD 3.1m interest payment, the first Thai default.
  • 11 Mar 1997100bn baht bailout of finance companies; Camdessus says he sees no crisis.
  • 14 May 1997Thailand adopts selective capital controls to defend the baht.
  • 2 Jul 1997Baht floated for the first time since 1984; falls 15 percent immediately.
  • 14 Jul 1997Malaysia floats the ringgit. 15 Jul: Kia under bankruptcy protection.
  • 24 Jul 1997Mahathir blames George Soros; on 20 Sept calls currency trading "immoral".
  • 11 Aug 1997IMF USD 16bn for Thailand. 14 Aug: Indonesia floats the rupiah.
  • 23-28 Oct 1997Hong Kong market loses 25 percent; the won starts to fall.
  • 31 Oct 1997IMF USD 23bn for Indonesia (later 40bn); 16 banks closed.
  • 21 Nov 1997Korea "swallows its pride" and asks the IMF for USD 20bn.
  • 3 Dec 1997Korea gets USD 55bn (58bn on 23 Dec). 8 Dec: Thailand shuts 56 of 58 finance companies.
  • 22 Dec 1997Moody's cuts Indonesia, Korea and Thailand to junk. 23 Dec: Zhu Rongji rules out a yuan devaluation.
  • 23 Jan 1998Rupiah loses a third of its value in five days. 28 Jan: Korea rolls USD 24bn into guaranteed loans.
  • 23 Feb 1998Indonesia drops the currency board under IMF pressure. 24 Feb: IMF eases Thai conditions.
  • 13-21 May 1998Riots in Jakarta; Suharto resigns after 32 years, Habibie takes over.
  • 13-17 Jun 1998Japan in recession for the first time in 23 years; US and Fed buy yen.
  • 2 Sep 1998Malaysia imposes capital controls; Mahathir fires Anwar Ibrahim the next day.
  • 25 Nov 1998Camdessus: "the worst of the crisis is now over."

High rates as medicine (deck): Korea's 30 percent interbank rate caused bankruptcies, destroyed confidence and accelerated outflows until the IMF relented; Thailand starved firms of cash, the market fell 75 percent and 600,000 foreign workers went home; Indonesia saw defaults, inflation, riots and Suharto's exit; Malaysia rejected the IMF, pegged deposit rates to leading banks and suffered least.

Asian Tigers versus BRICS: the Tigers (Hong Kong, Singapore, Taiwan, Korea) were small, export-led after import substitution, US-dependent, with GNI per capita of about USD 8,000 to 23,000 in 1993 to 1995. The BRICs are large and diversified (Brazil cars and minerals, Russia oil and arms, India IT, China manufacturing). In 2008 Singapore and Taiwan were unscathed, Korea had NPLs and a crash, Hong Kong speculative attacks; BRIC markets fell then recovered from 2009. Class view: a simultaneous BRICS default is unlikely; risk is country by country. Sovereign debt treatments: Argentina-Russia (default, credit crunch), Turkey-Brazil (long fiscal adjustment, late public payments), India-Lebanon (banks hold the debt, crowding out).

Currency risk Session 11

Floating currencies are set by supply and demand, more efficient and more volatile. Fixed or pegged currencies need reserves covering the currency in circulation; pegs to the dollar have on average ended badly because only the Fed prints dollars. Convertibility is the ease of buying, selling or exchanging a currency (UN criteria in Top 25). There are 182 official currencies for 193 UN members. A currency future is a standardized exchange-traded contract, usually against USD in units like EUR 125,000, mostly closed before delivery. A forward is the over-the-counter bank hedge. Rising interest rates attract savings and appreciate the currency. The Big Mac Index is purchasing power parity shorthand. S&P, Moody's and Fitch remain the only credible rating agencies.

Credit ratings and German banking Session 12

Investment grade is BBB- and above. In 2012 CaixaBank, Sabadell and Bankinter fell below it when Spain neared default; Santander and BBVA kept it through global diversification. Public banks carry their sovereign's rating. The German case then asks whether a century-old relationship-banking system had to change.

Relationship (German) bankingCapital-market (Anglo-Saxon) banking
Hausbank accompanies the firm "from cradle to grave"; patient long-term credit; privacy; strong owner control; bank seats on supervisory boards; lending on trust and project qualityEquity and shareholder value; transparency; external ratings; arm's-length capital markets; analyzes the borrower's numbers, not the project
Funds firms through downturns; no dilutionCheaper for banks; startups with strong clients but weak balance sheets are rejected
Risk: thin equity, rising NPLs, low bank profitability, pro-cyclical squeeze under ratingsRisk: short-termism; Enron happened under this system too
  • Basel I (1988, in force end 1992): 8 percent capital to risk-weighted assets, a response to the 1980s debt crisis. Basel II (June 2001): same 8 percent, finer risk weights, three pillars, added market and operational risk. Fears: pro-cyclicality, penalizing low-equity SMEs and long-term loans, about 1,000 disclosure items, the power of three US agencies. July 2002 concessions listed in Top 25; deadline moved to Jan 2007. Basel III liquidity buffers; Basel IV current.
  • Mittelstand: hidden champions, mechanical engineering firms average 154 employees, Voith counts with 23,000 staff because the family owns 93 percent; one third loss-making in 2001; 500,000 successions due; 40 percent of firms rely on one bank; Porsche (Piech family 57 percent) refused quarterly reports and was dropped from the mid-cap index.
  • Three pillars: Sparkassen and 12 Landesbanken (state guarantees gave AAA or AA+ and 50 basis points cheaper loans, phased out after 2005), cooperatives (DZ Bank backed SAP's 1988 IPO), private commercial banks (Deutsche, Dresdner, Commerzbank, HVB). Overbanked: about 2,915 banks in 1990. "A graveyard for shareholder value" (Merrill Lynch).
  • Deutschland AG, five bank levers: lending, cross-shareholdings, securities issuance, supervisory board seats, proxy voting of bearer shares (banks voted about 90 percent at the largest 24 firms and rubber-stamped management). 2001 tax reform cut corporate tax to 25 percent and exempted capital gains on stake sales. Vodafone's hostile bid for Mannesmann in 2000 was "goodbye to Deutschland AG."
  • Capital markets: market cap 66.8 percent of GDP in 2000 versus 154.9 in the US and 330 in Switzerland; corporate bonds only 6 percent of bank loan volume; the Neuer Markt lost about 95 percent and closed in Sept 2002; of 540 listed firms only about 150 traded actively.
  • Downturn 2002: every big commercial bank except Deutsche posted losses; Ackermann floated a state bad bank; Schröder promised a Mittelstand bank. Closing line: banks lend you an umbrella when it is sunny and take it back when it rains.
  • From the exhibits: in 2002 the private commercial banks were 354 institutions with 28.4 percent of assets (the Big Four 16), the public savings banks and Landesbanken 547 with 36 percent, the cooperatives 1,621 with 8.7 percent, and 71 specialized banks held 26.9. Bank credit as a share of liabilities falls with firm size: about 40 percent for firms under five employees against 8 percent above 100. Return on equity of all German banks fell from 19.3 percent in 1998 to 4.4 in 2002 and the large banks were negative; German bank return on assets was 0.21 percent against 1.77 for US banks. Insolvencies rose from 25,530 in 1996 to 37,700 in 2002. Hidden champions: Krones 70 percent world share in bottle labeling machines, Brita 85 percent in water filters, Hohner 85 percent in harmonicas, Webasto 50 percent in sunroofs. In 1990, 85 percent of large listed industrial firms had a shareholder above 25 percent, but a bank was the largest holder in under 6 percent of them. Household share ownership fell from 47 percent in 1950 to 17 in 2000.

Trade finance and factoring Session 14

Factoring gives liquidity up to 90 percent of invoice value, debtor risk cover up to 100 percent, off-balance-sheet treatment and better ratios, and professional collections. The factor sets a credit limit per debtor, buys the guaranteed invoices, withholds a reserve for credit notes and pays the fundable amount up to the client's funding limit. Three misconceptions on the deck: it is too expensive (cheaper than running collections yourself), only weak companies use it (now a mainstream product), you lose control of clients (the relationship is professionalized). It ties you to one bank. Listed corporates factor at quarter-end to dress ratios; fintechs offer non-recourse lines of USD 100 to 200m with 25 staff; Coface insures the banks that buy receivables. Cash conversion cycle: cut DSO, trim idle inventory, stretch DPO; permanent current assets need long-term funding.

The cash gap model (slide 5)

Inventory arrives on day 0 and the supplier's invoice is paid on day 30. Goods ship and the buyer is invoiced on day 60; the buyer pays on day 120. Inventory period 60 days, payables 30, receivables 60, so the seller funds a 90-day cash gap from day 30 to day 120. The factor closes it by financing the receivables and collecting from the buyer. In factoring the client still notifies the debtor and keeps ledger management in house; the factor supplies financing and debtor risk cover, reconciles two monthly sales ledgers against cash in a trust account (in Coface's name) and pays again only if the comparison is positive.

Plamar, C.A.

IE GE1-015-I · June 2003 · Session 14

People. Francisco Martínez Sr. (born 1949 in Linares, chemical engineer from Barcelona Polytechnic) first went to Venezuela in 1969 for a PVC maker, consulted from 1976, founded a recycling and seals business in 1978 that reached 70 percent of the market, sold up in 1989, went bankrupt with a bag factory in Granada in 1991 and returned to Venezuela with an investor. Sons: Francisco Jr. runs administration and operations, Carlos sales and marketing (finishing an MBA in Madrid), Javier technology.

Business. Started in cleaning products, switched to plastics with a garage extruder repaired with a scrapyard gearbox. Packaging seals for paint containers (the only local rival closed). Metal handles from 1997 after Vicson refused wire and Galtreca, 600 km away, taught them the process; two Brazilian automatic machines cut staff from 18 to 6 and output rose from 50,000 to 300,000 a month. Industrial bags (35 plus competitors, PDVSA the only LDPE supplier) and shrink-wrap were added to smooth seasonality. Sales are personal relationships.

Money. No dividends for four years; every bank refused credit for lack of guarantees; suppliers and cash flow financed everything. 2002: domestic sales VEB 331m, exports 134m (handles 68m, seals 66m), net earnings 17.8m. Exports began opportunistically through a Venezuelan coatings exporter whose Dominican clients bought handles from the US and seals from Argentina; then Guatemala, then Bolivia by air.

Venezuela 2003. GDP expected to fall 12 percent; 60 percent of manufacturers closing; only USD 100m of foreign exchange authorized since February, three days of normal business; oil 50 percent of government revenue, 80 percent of exports, 25 percent of GDP. 2002: GDP minus 8.9 percent, bolívar down over 150 percent, unemployment 18 percent, inflation 22.4 percent. Today: about 7m emigrants, hyperinflation above 700 percent, Dutch disease, price controls.

The four options. Father: invest at home in bags and shrink-wrap or buy distressed rivals, or wait, worst case divest and return to Spain. Francisco Jr.: export harder; handles and seals earn the best margins; US and Argentine rivals ignore small markets; export know-how is an asset. Carlos: a plant in a neighbor country where over 10 prospects want reliable supply; cuts country risk, gives hard currency and bloc access; costs USD 300,000. Class answer: Guatemala.

Seals are the largest market segment at 27 percent, then packaging 18 and construction 16, so Plamar's two core products cover 45 percent of the market. Venezuela consumed 291,785 tonnes of plastic raw material, fifth in Latin America behind Brazil (3.45m), Mexico (2.9m), Argentina (1.03m) and Colombia (522,000). Société Générale (A): The Jérôme Kerviel Affair

HBS 9-110-029 · Session 11

Bank. Founded 1864, nationalized 1945, privatized 1987. Daniel Bouton CEO from 1993, chairman 1997, ENA graduate. SGCIB returned 48 percent on equity in 2006 against 26 percent for the group; equity derivatives were about 20 percent of 2007 profit, profitable every quarter since 1993, Equity Derivatives House of the Year in Jan 2008, 18.4 percent of the warrants market. A "soldier-monk" culture of engineers encouraged to take proprietary risk.

Desk and man. Delta One (products that move one for one with the underlying), head Martial Rouyère; Listed Products desk head Eric Cordelle from April 2007, a structurer who had never managed traders. Kerviel joined in 2000 in the middle office on about EUR 32,000, became a trading assistant in 2002 and a trader in 2005 on turbo warrants (knock-out options). No Grandes Écoles degree; felt an outsider. Salary EUR 48,000, bonus EUR 60,000 for 2006, asked EUR 600,000 for 2007. Reported EUR 25m proprietary earnings in 2007 (59 percent of the desk) against a true EUR 1.5bn; called the "cash machine".

Concealment. Fictitious offsetting trades cancelled before monthly checks; pairs offset in quantity but not price (SolarWorld 2,266,500 shares at 63 and 53, a fake EUR 22.7m loss); fraudulent provision flows; technical and internal counterparties (ClickOptions); deferred start dates; seven forged emails; other people's computers; a possibly complicit assistant who booked 15 percent of the fake trades.

Control failures. His supervisor resigned in Jan 2007 and nobody monitored the desk for two and a half months; Kerviel validated his own March earnings. Cordelle managed on trust; Rouyère gave no guidance. 74 alerts were handled by procedure. Eurex emailed in Oct 2007 about 6,000 contracts in two hours and wrote twice in Nov; compliance answered. The two-week vacation rule was waived after his father died. Ernst & Young and Deloitte reported no concerns while Delta One volumes doubled. Gross positions had no limit.

Discovery. A Basel II Cooke ratio anomaly on eight forwards; the claimed counterparty Deutsche Bank had no record. Summoned on Saturday 19 Jan 2008, he told Jean-Pierre Mustier he had found a "martingale". Maxime Kahn closed about EUR 50bn in three days with AMF permission to delay disclosure. On 24 Jan 2008: EUR 4.9bn plus about 2bn subprime; 2007 profit fell from EUR 5.2bn to 600 to 800m. Kerviel claimed tacit approval because his profits were impossible within his mandate. The French public sided with him.

Banking on Germany?

What Business Is Zara In?

Ivey W19157 · 2019 · Session 9
Neira's graded case. Zara is Inditex's flagship; the question is whether the model that beat Gap can beat Uniqlo and Boohoo.
FY2017 revenue

Story. Amancio Ortega started dressmaking in 1963 aged 16, opened the first Zara in La Coruña (246,000 people) in 1975, 1,000 stores in 17 years, IPO 23 May 2001. Sales grew from EUR 5.67bn in 2004 to 23.34bn in 2017; gross margin 57.4 percent versus an industry 38.3; 593 stores in China by 2014; a USD 280m SoHo store; stores revamped every four to five years; 0.62 net openings a day. Clothes cost about 20 percent more to make than rivals' offshore product and are priced about 15 percent lower.

Model. Link design to manufacturing and distribution for rapid response, with decentralized decisions. Three levels of "commercials": design teams of four (two product managers, two designers) with authority over design, fabric, quantities and price; regional commercials linking stores to La Coruña; store managers counting stock by hand and ordering twice a week. Small batches test demand; scarcity makes customers buy now. Everything ships from one center fed by 11 factories over 124 miles of underground monorail and reaches stores in two days. CEO Isla rejects "fast fashion": the point is accuracy, store by store, week by week.

Class VRIO. The automated distribution network (rare, capital-intensive, built since 1975), the three-tier commercial system (culturally embedded, decades of subcontractor relationships), and the vertically integrated supply chain in Spain, Morocco and Portugal all pass valuable, rare and costly to imitate, and the single centralized system organizes them, so the advantage is sustained. The industry's key risk is the fashion miss; Zara reacts instead of predicting. Traditional and Zara-style models can coexist. Competitors: Uniqlo (3,445 stores, "a technology company"), Boohoo (GBP 580m sales, 100 new products a day), Gap (USD 673m advertising, 4.2 percent of sales).

Exhibits. McKinsey's "Emerging 440" cities: households rise from 330 million in 2010 to 521 million in 2025 while household income rises from USD 7.9 trillion to 20.2 trillion, twice the pace; the above-USD-70,000 segment grows fastest at 8 percent a year, and the 20,000 to 70,000 segment becomes the largest income pool. Women's apparel growth accelerates from 3.3 percent a year (2004 to 2010) to 4.8 (2010 to 2025), with emerging markets reaching 55 percent of midmarket sales and 28 percent of luxury by 2025. Inditex 2017 by brand: Zara EUR 16,620m, Bershka 2,227m, Massimo Dutti 1,765m, Pull&Bear 1,747m, Stradivarius 1,480m, Zara Home 830m, Oysho 570m, Uterque 97m; net cash EUR 6.4bn.

Distance Still Matters

Ghemawat · HBR Sept 2001 · Session 7
Full treatment in Neira's chapter above.

Country portfolio analysis counts potential sales and ignores the cost of distance. Distance has four dimensions and each hits industries differently (electricity is sensitive to administrative and geographic distance but not cultural; TV is sensitive to cultural distance; "TV is hardly cement"). The gravity model explains up to two thirds of trade variation. Company features change distance: cosmopolitan managers shrink cultural distance; Tricon already owned four fifths of its Mexican outlets with a 38 percent share. Focused Maytag outperformed far-flung Electrolux and Whirlpool.

Session 5: Benefits and reasons to internationalize (Prof. Pablo Neira)

This unit is the first step of Neira's four-step method for expanding abroad (benefits and reasons, ready?, where?, how?). The deck is a catalogue of reasons a company may have for going international, grouped into five main drivers on the opening slide (home market, foreign market, competition, product, economies of scale and scope) plus a sixth bucket that applies to both home and foreign markets. Each reason comes with a company example, most of them drawn from Neira's own career (the port terminal in Guatemala, the Metrocompost plant in Vietnam, General Kinematics, the steel wire rod plant, URBAR, National Geographic). What the professor said matters most: the list is not exhaustive, but before you walk into a board meeting saying "we should expand", you must be able to name which of these reasons you are pursuing and what you are trying to achieve. Taught on 21 September 2026 in the second half of a double session; the first half was a recap of the global trends material from sessions 1-2, summarised at the end of these notes.

Slide-by-slide

Slide 1: Title

  • "How to Expand Internationally", Prof. Pablo Neira, IE University, Session 5, March 2026. Subtitle: "Benefits and reasons to internationalize."

Slide 2: Course map

  • An arrow with five boxes in order: Global trends, Benefits and reasons to internationalize, Ready to internationalize?, Where?, How?
  • Global trends is shaded green (already covered); this session is the second box.
  • In class Neira framed the sequence as four questions: why do I want to go (benefits), is my company ready, which country, and by which entry mode (franchise, agent, subsidiary, and so on, covered later).

Slide 3: Main drivers

  • Five main drivers, numbered on the slide:
    1. Home market
    2. Foreign market
    3. Competition
    4. Product
    5. Economies of scale and scope
  • Note the deck then presents them in a different order: foreign market first, then home market, then "both home/foreign markets" (a sixth group not on this list), then product, competition, and economies of scale and scope. The section numbers on later slides (2. Home market, 3. Both, 4. Product, 5. Competition, 6. Economies) follow that presentation order.

Slide 4: Foreign market 1, growth

  • Seek opportunities for growth in new markets: increase sales and benefits ("benefits" here means profits).
  • The most basic reason. Neira: a for-profit company wants more money, so look for more places to sell.

Slide 5: Foreign market 2, resource seeking (a to c)

  • Resource seeking opportunities: access to capital, raw material, low labor costs and new technologies.
  • a) Be close to supply sources: minerals (oil, zinc, copper) or agricultural products (rubber, tobacco, sugar). These resources are sometimes central to the survival of a company.
  • b) Global sourcing advantages and flexibility in product sourcing: purchasing from the most appropriate supplier around the world regardless of its location.
  • c) Availability of new technology and capacity: some companies source overseas because domestic suppliers lack the capacity and are not making the investments needed to stay competitive.

Slide 6: Resource seeking (d and e)

  • d) Superior quality products: search for quality inputs not available from domestic suppliers.
  • e) Gain access to lower-cost or better value factors of production.
  • Picture: a large call centre full of agents in blue shirts. The point: labour is a factor of production that can be sourced abroad at lower cost (Neira's example in class was Spanish call centres relocated to Latin America).

Slide 7: Resource seeking (f), strategic assets

  • f) Access to strategic assets. Grey text on the slide: "PM-Guatemala".
  • Picture: a container port terminal with ship-to-shore cranes and a container ship at berth.
  • The point: sometimes the reason to go abroad is a unique asset (a port concession) you could not obtain at home.

Slide 8: Resource seeking (g), talent pools

  • g) Access to new talent pools. International labour can offer unique advantages: increased productivity, technical skills, advanced language skills, diverse educational backgrounds and others.
  • Pictures: the orange logo of the app YoVivo! ("All your photos. All your clouds. All in one place.") and its App Store screenshots (Organize, Enjoy, Encrypt, Share), with the caption "Featured as a Best New App in 31 countries in July 2015".
  • The point: the app's founders in London hired their programmers in the Philippines (story in the class section).

Slide 9: Foreign market 3, specific opportunity

  • To exploit a specific business or market opportunity. Example: Metrocompost in Vietnam.
  • Picture: a screenshot of the MetroCompost website ("recycling and environment", "more than 20 years of commitment, since 1990") showing a green composting plant and a project sheet: location Hai Duong, Vietnam; year of operation 2011; treatment capacity 29,500 t/a; material: organic fraction of municipal solid waste; composting system: static trenches; scope of supply: pretreatment installation, composting in static trenches, refining line, machinery (loaders, trucks).
  • The point: a one-off tender can take a company to a country that was never in its strategy.

Slide 10: Foreign market 4, partners

  • Invest in a potentially rewarding relationship with foreign partners:
    • Create joint ventures with profitable partners.
    • Develop partnerships to grow business in a specific country. Grey text: General Kinematics.
    • Build trust with local players.
  • Quote on the slide: "One reason for Netflix to establish an office in France was the company's need to win the trust of the French industry; to build ties with content-makers, filmmakers, producers and sales agents..."

Slide 11: Foreign market 5, serving global customers

  • Serving global customers. In several industries the primary driver of globalization has been the need to service global customers who demand the same product, service and quality at various locations around the world.
  • Pictures (three groups of examples):
    • A supplier map of the Ford S-Max (Automotive News Europe) naming dozens of component suppliers (Mazzucconi, ABC Group, ThyssenKrupp, Mitsubishi Electric, Federal-Mogul, Webasto, Omron, Magneti Marelli, ZF, Getrag and others). Component makers follow the carmaker.
    • The Big Four auditors (PwC, Deloitte, EY, KPMG) and global banks (Goldman Sachs, HSBC, JPMorgan Chase, Lazard, Deutsche Bank, Merrill Lynch, Morgan Stanley, RBC Royal Bank, State Street).
    • "Top 10 advertising agencies in the world": Ogilvy & Mather, Mullen, Publicis Groupe, BBDO, Dentsu, Grey Global, Havas, Droga5, McCann Worldgroup, Young & Rubicam.
  • The point: professional services, banks, ad agencies and auto suppliers internationalize because their clients do.

Slide 12: Foreign market 6, learning (a)

  • Learning benefits. a) Gain ideas about products, services and business methods that arise from being in foreign markets.
  • Quote from the CEO of IKEA Japan: "One reason for us to enter the Japanese market, apart from hopefully doing very good business, is to expose ourselves to the toughest competition in the world. By doing so, we feel that we are expanding the quality issues for IKEA all over the world."
  • Picture: the entrance of an IKEA store in Japan ("Welcome to IKEA", opening hours 10:00 to 20:00).

Slide 13: Learning (b and c)

  • b) Access to new technologies which may significantly improve operations.
  • c) Integration of knowledge from different locations and the creation of new knowledge through interacting with different national environments.
  • Critical requirement for exploiting these learning benefits: the company must possess some form of global infrastructure for managing knowledge that permits new experiences, ideas and practices to be integrated and diffused.
  • Picture: Starbucks ("The best coffee for the best YOU"). The point: Starbucks observes consumer behaviour in each country, sends it to the parent, and diffuses what works to other stores.

Slide 14: Foreign market 7, entry barriers and tariffs

  • Changes in entry barriers / avoid tariffs.
  • Picture: a The Local/AFP news article dated 3 October 2019: "Cava, queso, olive oil and mariscos: Trump slaps extra tariffs on Spanish produce", with a photo of olive oil and Manchego cheese.
  • The point: when a tariff is raised against your country, producing or routing from inside the barrier (or from another country) is a reason to internationalize.

Slide 15: Foreign market 8, high demand

  • Countries where there is a high demand for the offering (grey text: consumer goods/food; healthcare; housing).
  • The study guide and class call this the "pull effect": the foreign market pulls you in because demand is there and unsupplied.

Slide 16: Home market 1 and 2

  • Section heading "2. Home market".
  • 1. Local market is small. Pictures: an aerial photo of a motorway (the Spanish highway network) and Google Maps of Singapore and its position in Southeast Asia (the island is tiny next to Malaysia and Indonesia).
  • 2. Slow growth on the domestic market.
  • The point: a market can be small physically (Singapore), small because the need is already met (Spain's highways are built), or small because people do not consume the product.

Slide 17: Home market 3, saturation

  • When saturation in the home market occurs. Grey text: "consumer goods, Z" (Z for Zara in Spain, per the study guide).
  • Definition on the slide: a saturated market is the situation when demand has been fully satisfied. The only ways to sell more on a saturated market are:
    • substitution or replacement of the existing product;
    • taking over market share at the expense of other competitors;
    • innovation of a product in such a way as to move to an unsaturated market or to create an entirely new target market.
  • Internationalization is the fourth way out: take the same product to a market that is not saturated.

Slide 18: Home market 4, seasonality

  • To level out seasonal fluctuations in demand.
  • Text on the slide: IDE Technologies provides "snowmaking" to ski resorts around the world. It operates in both hemispheres (e.g. Switzerland and South Africa) to maintain consistent revenue: when it is summer in one part of the world and they cannot operate, they focus on the part where it is winter.
  • Pictures: a snow cannon, a Spanish jamón (cured ham leg), and a row of cava bottles. Ham and cava are Christmas products in Spain; selling abroad fills the rest of the year.

Slide 19: Home market 5, excess capacity

  • Make use of excess capacity (fill capacity).
  • Pictures: the website of Celsa Group / Global Steel Wire (GSW), coils of steel wire rod, and a hot rolling mill.
  • The point: a plant with huge fixed costs must run near full capacity; export orders fill the gap when domestic orders fall short.

Slide 20: Home market 6, 7, 8

  • 6. Excessive regulation at home.
  • 7. Economic problems or recession. Grey text: URBAR (Neira's industrial company, which went to Argentina after the 2008 Spanish recession).
  • 8. Diversification: risk reduction:
    • To reduce dependence on home market sales.
    • To offset negative growth in one market by operating successfully in another.

Slide 21: Both home and foreign markets

  • Section "3. Both home/foreign markets". Three reasons that can arise on either side:
    1. Changes in regulation. Grey text: UBER SPAIN.
    2. Tax reasons.
    3. Governmental reasons: incentives to companies to internationalize (the home government pushing you out, or a foreign government pulling you in).
  • Distinguish from slide 20: slide 20 is excessive regulation that already exists at home; slide 21 is regulation that changes after you have started operating, forcing you to move.

Slide 22: Product 1, extend the life cycle

  • To extend the product's life cycle: provide products and services which have reached maturity at home. Grey text: "fatmilk/cereals/coke".
  • Picture: the product life cycle chart with four stages on a sales-versus-time curve: introduction (blue), growth (green), maturity (yellow, the peak), decline (red).
  • The point: a product at maturity or entering decline at home can be at introduction or growth in another country (full-fat milk is declining in developed countries but still in high demand elsewhere).

Slide 23: Product 2, exclusive product

  • To exploit an exclusive product or technology.
  • Neira: if you have something unique, do not test it in one country first; launch it across the planet.

Slide 24: Competition 1 to 3

  • Section "5. Competition".
  • 1. Competition in the home market is intense or growing. Some companies find easier markets abroad than locally.
  • 2. Lower degree of competition abroad. Many markets are still developing and have no strong structure of competitors.
  • 3. First-mover advantage: businesses that expand into markets where their competitors do not operate often get a first-mover advantage that lets them build strong brand awareness with consumers before their competitors arrive.

Slide 25: Competition 4, follower move

  • As a reaction to competitors' moves. The follower move: entering a market because a major competitor has done so, driven by the belief that the competitor would gain a significant advantage if allowed to operate alone in that market.
  • Text box on the slide: "H&M opened its first stores in India in 2017 after Zara expanded to India in 2010, where it now has 13 stores. In 2 out of the 3 years since Zara opened in India it has made profits. This was a signal for H&M that it could also be successful in India's market. Its aim is to take Zara's spot as the world's number one apparel retailer."
  • Pictures: a Zara logo, a Zara store, an H&M store.
  • Order to remember: Zara first (2010), H&M the follower (2017). The class recording garbled this; trust the deck.

Slide 26: Competition 4, offense as defense

  • "Offense as defense": a company enters the home market of a competitor, usually in retaliation for an earlier entry into its own domestic market. The objective is also to force the competitor to allocate increased resources to an intensified level of competition at home.
  • Pictures: Kodak vs Fujifilm (film canisters and logos) and Michelin vs Goodyear logos.
  • The point: when Fuji entered the US, Kodak attacked Japan; Michelin (French) and Goodyear (American) did the same to each other.

Slide 27: Economies of scale and scope, definitions

  • Section "6. Economies of scale & scope". Footer text: "M MNCs" (this driver mainly applies to multinational corporations).
  • Economies of scale: savings in cost of production by increasing the scale of production (increasing the number of units produced). In areas like sourcing, production, marketing, R&D.
  • Economies of scope: savings in cost by producing multiple products using the same resource or capability.
    • Tangible resources (distribution networks).
    • Intangible resources (global brand recognition or management capabilities).

Slide 28: Develop economies of scale

  • 1. Develop economies of scale (in sourcing, production, marketing, R&D):
    • a) Reducing costs per unit: costs are spread over a larger sales base, so profit per unit increases.
    • b) ROI: large investment projects (R&D, etc.) may require global markets to justify the capital spent; recover the cost across the maximum number of countries.

Slide 29: Economies of scope, operational

  • 2. Develop economies of scope: operational and strategic.
  • a) Operational: synergies from sharing resources across businesses.
    • Sharing tangible resources (research labs, distribution networks) across multiple businesses.
    • Sharing intangible resources (brands, corporate reputation and technology) across multiple businesses.
    • Global brand recognition: the benefit that derives from having a brand that is recognized throughout the world.
  • Picture: a National Geographic branded retail store (clothing, bags, merchandise). The point: a brand built in television and magazines can be stretched into retail products and stores in several countries.

Slide 30: Economies of scope, strategic

  • b) Strategic: synergies from the ability to apply common management capabilities to different businesses.
    • Transferring functional / organizational capabilities (marketing, product development) across businesses.
    • Applying core capabilities in general management to different businesses.
  • Operational scope shares a resource; strategic scope transfers a capability. That is the distinction to remember.

What the professor added in class

Opening brainstorm and the growth reason

  • Before showing the list Neira asked the class for reasons. Students offered: access to credit and funding, finding a market to reduce costs, friendlier regulation and taxes, raw materials, labour and energy, building an international brand, accessing technology, finding lower competition, and the reverse case of bringing a product found abroad back to the home market. He said all of them fit somewhere on the list.
  • Growth: "this is a for-profit company, the more money you make the better", so the first reason is simply more sales.

Resource seeking

  • Flexibility of sourcing: if you depend on one supplier and its factory burns down, your production stops. Having suppliers in several countries gives flexibility in cost and quality, not only security.
  • New technology and quality: sometimes no manufacturer in your home country can make a specific part or provide a service at the quality you need, so you have to look abroad.
  • Lower cost: until recently the call centres of Spanish phone companies and utilities were moved abroad (you hear the accent is not Spanish); the reason was lower labour cost.
  • Strategic asset (slide 7): a Spanish port-handling company (PM) that manages about 80 percent of loading and unloading in Spanish ports was not planning to go to Central America. An agent asked whether they wanted to bid for a port terminal tender; they bid and won. Neira first said Colombia and corrected himself to Guatemala. Lesson: sometimes the reason is a unique asset you get to know about through an agent.
  • Talent pool (slide 8): in 2013 Neira was external advisor to the YoVivo founders, Javad (from Iran) and Filippo (from Italy), based in London, who had been running Deutsche Bank's IT. The app gathered your photos from phone, cloud and Dropbox, removed duplicates and organised them; it was best new app in 31 countries in July 2015. They did not program it in London (too expensive, and they could not find programmers of the same quality and speed). They kept a pool of 20 to 25 programmers in the Philippines, cut the work into pieces, assigned each piece to a group and followed them weekly, firing and replacing as needed. "Sometimes you need special talent that you do not have at home."

Specific opportunity and partners

  • Metrocompost (slide 9): when Neira ran a listed industrial manufacturing company it had a division that built turnkey waste-treatment and waste-to-energy plants. An agent brought a tender in Vietnam. "Was it within our strategy to go to Vietnam? Of course not." They bid and won. A waste plant can be simple (manual screening) or sophisticated (X-ray sorting of glass by colour, separating glass from plastic), depending on what the local government wants to spend.
  • General Kinematics (slide 10): the same company had a division designing equipment for moving components and parts, medium to small size. General Kinematics in the US made similar equipment but much larger. During the 2007-2008 crisis in Spain they agreed: we sell your equipment in Spain and Europe, you sell ours in the States. Lesson: a partner can even be a competitor with overlapping products if the combination works.
  • Netflix in France: when Netflix arrived there was a strongly negative reaction from local players in a very local industry. Netflix opened an office, did marketing, hired and grew local people. "This was the key": build trust.

Serving global customers

  • Audit firms: if a client opens a subsidiary in a new country, a big audit firm will accompany it rather than risk losing the client. For a tiny client with a EUR 10,000 audit they will not bother; for a large phone company they will.
  • Investment banks (Goldman Sachs, Bank of America) follow clients into new countries; so do advertising agencies.
  • Automotive: when Volkswagen set up a factory in Mexico, its German component suppliers literally opened new plants around it. "They follow the customer, when it makes sense."

Learning

  • IKEA in Japan: do-it-yourself furniture is widespread in Japan and competition is terrible; IKEA was reluctant. The decision was: go, maybe we are not successful, but we will learn how the Japanese do business.
  • Starbucks (slide 13): enter a country to observe how consumers behave, capture it, send it to the parent, and see whether it can be diffused to stores in other countries. Neira said this learning driver is really for large multinationals with presence in many countries, not for a startup or SME.

Entry barriers and high demand

  • Tariffs (slide 14): "this is not about norms, it is about customs duties." When Trump put tariffs on Spanish cheese and olive oil, many Spanish producers shipped the product to Italy, put an Italian sticker on it, and exported from there. They do not ship directly from Spain any more.
  • High demand (slide 15): the example is regular (full-fat) milk. In developed countries consumption of regular milk is falling and semi-skimmed and skimmed are rising, but in other countries demand for regular milk is still very high. Also healthcare products and consumer goods.

Home market reasons

  • Small market (slide 16): students suggested three meanings: your capacity exceeds what the home market buys; the population is small; or people simply do not consume much of the product. Neira added Spain's highways: the network is built, so for the 5 or 6 big Spanish construction companies the home market is already small and they went to Latin America and Asia. A student added Nigeria: a huge market, but Nigerians prefer powdered milk, so dairy companies there export fresh milk and Nigerians import powder. Singapore: physically small.
  • Saturation (slide 17): "no matter how much you produce and how much you try to sell, you will not sell more." Milk in Spain: people drink what they drink; a lower price will not make them go from 3 litres a week to 6. Same with Coke and Coke Zero: cutting the price per can does not raise consumption. So you must look at your excess capacity and find other countries.
  • Seasonality (slide 18): snowmaking companies run in Switzerland and Europe in winter and go to Chile and Argentina in summer (the slide says South Africa; both illustrate the opposite hemisphere). Students added: a Kenyan fintech whose biggest market was Tanzania sold enormously in the tourist season (Serengeti, Zanzibar) and nothing in low season, so it had to expand to new markets and sectors; Italians who open ice cream shops in Germany for 4 or 5 months of summer and return to Italy. Neira: Spanish ham companies concentrate about 70 percent of sales in December and January (Christmas gifts to clients), and cava likewise, so they need other markets for the rest of the year.
  • Fill capacity (slide 19): Neira's company produced steel wire rod. The investment in a plant is enormous and you only break even at 85 percent of capacity. When orders for the next two or three months fell below that, they went to new markets, even ones they had never sold to, sometimes at a lower price with no margin, just to break even. "Sometimes you are simply obliged to look for alternative markets."
  • Excessive regulation (slide 20): find countries where the regulation is not so tough.
  • Recession (slide 20, URBAR): in 2007-2008 about 85 percent of the company's sales were in Spain, spread across 15 or 16 sectors. They had always assumed all sectors could not go bad at the same time; it happened. They looked at Argentina and Chile and established in Argentina.
  • Diversification: "all your apples in the same basket." Do not wait for the crisis; anticipate and de-risk.

Both markets

  • Changing regulation (slide 21): the deck says Uber Spain; in class Neira told the Uber in Colombia story: Uber started, after two years the taxi industry brought a claim, Uber had to stop and leave, and came back years later in a different form. The point is the same: you start under one set of rules and the rules change.
  • Tax: many large Spanish companies have set themselves up in Ireland (Neira said "Northern Ireland") because of corporate income tax. New taxes on your business at home can also push you out.
  • Government incentives: in Spain the government body ICEX (Neira said "IFEX") helps Spanish companies internationalize. The reverse also exists: a foreign government offering incentives to attract companies.

Product

  • Life cycle (slide 22): a product entering decline at home, where no amount of extra production or cost-cutting sells more, can be revived in another market (milk again).
  • Exclusive product (slide 23): companies with a unique new product do not start in the USA and see how it goes; they launch across the planet.

Competition

  • A Turkish student: he invested in confectionery production in Ethiopia. In Turkey it would have been impossible to compete with hundreds of small, medium and large producers; in Ethiopia a small-scale operation could compete. This is slide 24 point 2.
  • First mover: with a decent product you get a customer advantage from being the first newcomer in a country.
  • Follower (slide 25): H&M was reluctant about India because fast fashion there seemed complex. Zara went in (2010), was doing "okay, okay, okay" and then grew well; when H&M saw its competitor succeeding it changed its mind and followed. (The recording muddled who went first; the deck is the reference: Zara 2010, H&M 2017.)
  • Offense as defense (slide 26): Kodak (US) and Fuji (Japan): when the Japanese company came to the US market, Kodak reacted by going into Japan. Same story with tyres: Michelin (French) and Goodyear (American) entered each other's home markets, and both are doing well in different countries.

Economies of scale and scope

  • A student defined economies of scale as decreasing the cost per unit by producing more; Neira accepted it.
  • Scope: his illustration was a logistics warehouse that stores one type of product and sells spare capacity to store other products.
  • ROI: healthcare (pharma) and similar companies with huge investments need customers from everywhere to pay back the investment.
  • National Geographic (slide 29): a Spanish family office Neira worked with licensed the National Geographic brand for something the owner had never thought of: merchandise (t-shirts, trousers, shoes, climbing glasses) and branded stores. They opened stores in Madrid (Gran Vía), London and Panama and could open franchises. National Geographic had to approve every layout, design and colour. The channel has an estimated 250 million TV followers and the brand is about 80 years old. This is economies of scope from an intangible resource, the global brand.
  • Strategic scope (slide 30): if your marketing or commercial department is "magic" with any product you give it, use it to promote more products. Neira is "fully convinced" that good general management capabilities are fully transferable across industries: a good general manager moved to another sector needs about six months to adapt and then performs. So a company with two or three such managers can widen its scope of businesses and hand them the new ones.

Closing

  • A student noted that some Indian companies export simply because the weak rupee means euro or dollar prices are worth far more than the local price. Neira: the list is not exhaustive; access to funding and currency reasons also exist.
  • EXAM: Neira's closing rule: "you want to expand, wonderful, but you need to have clear and solid reasons why." Do not go to a board or your boss saying "we should expand here and there" without knowing what you are trying to achieve. This is only the first step of the method, but it must be done.

Global trends recap (sessions 1-2 and the first half of sessions 5-6, no deck uploaded)

Course framing (session 1)

  • Neira (economics, Harvard MBA 1991, about 36 years of experience: Unilever, consulting, CEO of a listed industrial manufacturer, family offices, now BlackRock investments in Spain including a tungsten mine) teaches the strategy half; Mikel Aguirre teaches economic, geopolitical and country risk.
