Fifteen sessions; exam in session 15; Neira's graded work is a report plus class discussion on the Zara case; Aguirre has 4 or 5 cases.
  • Tungsten aside: 85 percent of world deposits are in China; the largest mine outside China is in western Spain (Extremadura).

The Fortune 500 dilemma (mortality rate)

  • About half of today's Fortune 500 will be off the list in a few years (Neira said "less than 5 years" in class; the study guide says 7). Almost 90 percent of the 1955 list is gone. Average lifespan on the list used to be 30 to 35 years. Of the top 12 companies by market cap in 2000, only Microsoft is still in the top 12.
  • Market caps have gone from hundreds of billions to trillions; the three largest companies together are worth about the GDP of Spain (unclear figure on the recording). Tesla's valuation implies far more cars than it sells; expectations drive it.
  • Why: industry disruption, forces based on new technology, new ideas and new ways of doing business that enter traditional sectors, blur their boundaries and bring new competitors. Not only technology: Airbnb also shifted power away from hotels.
  • Disruption is both uncomfortable and destructive (layoffs, new factories) and an opportunity for companies and consumers.
  • The invisible competitor challenge: new competitors come through another door, are not classified as competitors, and you notice them too late (a student's marketing agency lost clients to ChatGPT in 2022). Ask what a hotel, a taxi, a bank or a dentist is now; motor vehicles versus mobility: carmakers used to compete on engine power, now on the dashboard.

Three primary roots of disruption

  • Technology: the great enabler. Not new: the locomotive disrupted the stagecoach; steam (1784), electricity (mass production), computing, roughly every 100 years. Two critical impacts today: data has been opened to everyone ("data is the new oil"), and companies cannot use it all: Tesla analyses only about 15 percent of the data its cars capture.
  • Demographics: the silent force. Urbanisation: world population 8.3 billion (India overtook China last year); around 2010 urban and rural populations were equal and urban keeps rising. Cities generate 80 to 85 percent of GDP and attract talent and ideas. Video shown: half of humanity lives in cities, two thirds by 2050; cities generate more than 80 percent of world GDP; Europe needs more than EUR 600 billion a year of infrastructure investment; megacities (over 10 million people): only New York and Tokyo in 1950; Mexico City, São Paulo and Osaka joined by 1980; over 20 in 2010; 32 today, Asia has over half; 41 megacities by 2030 holding nearly 9 percent of world population; fastest future urbanisation in Africa. Also rising life expectancy (people born after 2000 may pass 100; population heading to 9 or 10 billion even with flat birth rates) and immigration, both forcing companies to serve more people with limited resources.
  • Globalization: the amplifier. Trade liberalization, the trend of the last 50 years, now carries a question mark (Trump, trade wars, tariffs on Spanish products announced within 24 hours of a political spat). New competitors from emerging markets produce decent quality at very low prices. McKinsey: about 60 percent of cross-border purchase decisions are driven by lower price.

What is different now

  • Two ideas: accelerating industry disruption and a global growth shift.
  • Acceleration: technology explosion (printing, telescope, steam engine, then in the last two decades new technologies every month; a 2013 McKinsey list of potentially disruptive technologies; self-assembling robots, brain-to-vehicle interfaces, molecular robots, facial recognition (needed to activate a SIM card in China), extended reality (augmented, mixed, virtual; used by Nike, Amazon, IKEA to sell), hotel delivery robots in China, a guide robot in the Plaza Norte mall, police robots in Singapore, delivery robots at Purdue).
  • Combinatory technology: technologies are now open and easy to combine. Amazon Go (2017): computer vision, deep learning and sensor fusion ("Just Walk Out") so you grab goods and leave with no checkout. A student noted it needed over 1,000 people in India reviewing video and was largely wound down; Amazon now sells the technology to supermarkets in Europe. The lesson is the combination, not the success.
  • B2C to C2B: customers now tell companies what to sell. "Consumer articulation": things we used to pay for are free (international calls via Skype and WhatsApp; the 20-volume encyclopedia Neira sold for EUR 25). 90 percent of shoppers say reviews influence their buying; most trusted sources are family and friends (60 percent) and customer reviews (60 percent); only 12 percent look at what the supplier says. Companies respond with referral marketing (reward fans who share; Revolut-style invite bonuses). Both customers and companies will have more choices.
  • New business models: from the linear value chain to horizontal platforms (a strong technology platform lets Apple go from PCs to iPod, iPhone, Apple TV, Watch and cars; Google from Maps and Mail to healthcare and cars) and then to ecosystems (the Uber ecosystem combining cloud, payments, maps). Most are asset-light: Alibaba, the world's largest retailer, owns no warehouse; Airbnb owns no hotels; Uber owns no taxis. This lets them diversify and enter new geographies at a speed never seen before.
  • Global growth shift: cross-border data flows have exploded since 2015; in 2008 devices roughly equalled people; now 8.3 billion people and an estimated 28 billion devices within 5 years. But data localisation rules are rising (a Kenyan fintech had to build local data centres in Tanzania and Uganda). Technology now connects people, not just devices, yet use is mostly domestic: Facebook about 50 percent cross-border, YouTube about 20 percent, e-commerce 11 to 15 percent. Ghemawat's HBR article: distance still matters, the hard reality of expansion; beliefs, religion, culture and taste still differ, and US firms have failed abroad by assuming what sells at home sells in China.
  • Numbers to remember: world population about 8.2 to 8.3 billion; 5.5 billion internet users; only 12 percent of internet users buy cross-border; cross-border e-commerce about USD 700 billion, reaching only about 8 percent of the population. Neira's point: going from 8 to 20 or 25 percent is realistic, so the opportunity is enormous, and not only for Apple or Tesla but for SMEs and startups that pick the right country.
  • Growth engines: in the past BRIC (Brazil, Russia, India, China); now India, China, Africa and Southeast Asia, about 60 percent of world population and 50 percent of expected global urban growth; Europe, Latin America and North America are flat. A student: Prudential followed exactly this path, from the UK to the US and now headquartered in Asia (China, Indonesia, Vietnam) and Africa.
  • Resources: limited or unlimited? Population growth raises consumption; technology helps by reducing consumption and by creating alternative resources (electric cars reduce fuel use, but in Spain they are only about 10 percent of the market against an expected 30 to 35 percent, real range is 200 to 250 km against claimed 350, and nickel for batteries has its own externalities). "Can innovation make the planet resource-rich?" Neira has no answer but believes each shortage attracts investment in alternatives: a seed of opportunity.

Impact on businesses and leaders

  • Global competition is greater than ever; competitors from Vietnam and China arrive with decent quality at much lower prices. Chinese car brands took close to 15 percent of the Spanish market in 5 years, fully equipped, and are moving upmarket. US versus China trade has reshaped the map since 2000. On the demand side, countries never considered as markets now have enough customers to matter.
  • "The future is much faster than we think." No company can do everything in-house; some piece of the global value chain is always done better by someone else; be humble enough to use them.
  • Incumbents must ask hard questions (a healthcare company's customer may now be the patient on an app, not the hospital). Doing nothing means "continuing our slow decline into obsolescence." Kodak had the data on digital and did nothing; Blockbuster turned down Netflix; Nokia and Steve Ballmer laughed at the iPhone ("USD 500 subsidised, no keyboard, not a good email machine; the Motorola Q is USD 99; I like our strategy"). In all three cases the data was available; the failure was cultural: they thought they were immune and had internal resistance from the CEO, executive team and board.
  • New competitors grow flat for a year or two and then "go to the roof" in years three and four. Big companies now run departments that scan for digital competitors and buy or ally with them; small companies must at least stay alert. In Spain listed large manufacturers are only about 15 percent of GDP; thousands of smaller firms lack those resources.
  • Marketing myopia (HBR, raised by a student): define yourself by the need you satisfy, not the product (Uber is logistics and transportation, Amazon is a marketplace), so you can disrupt yourself.
  • Rules: see disruption as positive; be vigilant; keep an anticipatory mindset; try things without 100 percent certainty; disrupt yourself before somebody else disrupts you. Famous misjudgements: IBM's president in 1943 ("a world market for about 5 computers"), DEC's president ("no reason for any individual to have a computer"), Bill Gates ("640K should be enough").

Likely exam angles

  • Know that the deck lists five main drivers: home market, foreign market, competition, product, economies of scale and scope, and that a sixth group ("both home/foreign markets") holds changes in regulation, tax reasons and government incentives.
  • Know that foreign market reasons are pull factors: growth, resource seeking, a specific opportunity, partnerships and trust, serving global customers, learning, entry barriers and tariffs, high demand ("pull effect").
  • Know that home market reasons are push factors: small market, slow growth, saturation, seasonality, excess capacity, excessive regulation, recession, diversification and risk reduction.
  • Know the seven sub-points of resource seeking (a to g): close to supply, global sourcing flexibility, new technology and capacity, superior quality, lower-cost factors, strategic assets, talent pools.
  • Know which example goes with which reason: PM Guatemala port terminal = strategic asset; YoVivo and Philippine programmers = talent pool; Metrocompost Vietnam = specific opportunity; General Kinematics = partnership; Netflix France = build trust; Ford S-Max suppliers, Big Four, banks, ad agencies = serving global customers; IKEA Japan = learning (toughest competition); Starbucks = knowledge integration; Trump tariffs on cava, cheese, olive oil (3 October 2019) = entry barriers; IDE Technologies snowmaking, ham, cava = seasonality; Celsa Global Steel Wire = fill capacity; Singapore and Spanish highways = small home market; URBAR = recession; Uber Spain = changes in regulation; full-fat milk, cereals, Coke = product life cycle; Zara and H&M India = follower move; Kodak vs Fujifilm and Michelin vs Goodyear = offense as defense; National Geographic stores = economies of scope from a global brand.
  • Know the definition of a saturated market (demand fully satisfied) and the three ways to sell more in one: substitute or replace the product, take share from competitors, innovate into an unsaturated or new market.
  • Know the four stages of the product life cycle (introduction, growth, maturity, decline) and that internationalization extends a product that has reached maturity at home.
  • Know that IDE Technologies operates in both hemispheres (Switzerland and South Africa) to level out seasonal demand.
  • Know that H&M entered India in 2017 after Zara in 2010; Zara had 13 stores and was profitable in 2 of 3 years; that was the signal for H&M (follower move).
  • Know that offense as defense means entering a competitor's home market in retaliation to force it to spend resources defending at home.
  • Know that first-mover advantage is about building brand awareness before competitors arrive.
  • Know that the learning benefit requires a global infrastructure for managing knowledge so ideas can be integrated and diffused.
  • Know the definitions: economies of scale = lower unit cost from more units; economies of scope = savings from using the same resource or capability for multiple products.
  • Know that economies of scale have two sub-benefits: lower cost per unit and justifying the ROI of large investments (R&D) across many countries.
  • Know that economies of scope split into operational (sharing tangible resources such as labs and distribution networks, and intangible resources such as brands, reputation and technology) and strategic (transferring functional capabilities such as marketing and product development, and general management capabilities).
  • Know that global brand recognition is an intangible resource and a distribution network is a tangible one.
  • Know the steel wire rod rule of thumb: break-even at 85 percent of capacity; and that URBAR had 85 percent of sales in Spain across 15 or 16 sectors in 2008 and went to Argentina.
  • Know the global trends numbers: three drivers (technology the enabler, demographics the silent force, globalization the amplifier); 90 percent of the 1955 Fortune 500 gone; only Microsoft left from the 2000 top 12; Tesla analyses 15 percent of its data; cities generate 80 to 85 percent of GDP; 32 megacities today, 41 by 2030, Asia over half; McKinsey 60 percent buy abroad for lower price; 90 percent of shoppers influenced by reviews, only 12 percent trust the supplier; 12 percent of internet users buy cross-border; cross-border e-commerce about USD 700 billion, about 8 percent of the population; Facebook 50 percent, YouTube 20 percent, e-commerce 11 to 15 percent cross-border; Chinese cars about 15 percent of the Spanish market in 5 years.
  • Know that Kodak, Blockbuster and Nokia had the data; their failure was cultural, not informational.
  • Know Neira's rule: have clear, solid reasons before proposing expansion; this is the first step before "ready", "where" and "how".

Traps and look-alikes

  • Home market vs foreign market reasons: the same word can appear on both sides. "Slow growth" and "saturation" are home (push); "high demand" and "growth opportunities" are foreign (pull). Excess capacity is home; serving global customers is foreign.
  • Excessive regulation (home market, slide 20) vs changes in regulation (both markets, slide 21): the first is rules that are already too tough at home; the second is rules that change after you start (Uber Spain). Tax reasons and government incentives sit with "changes in regulation" in the "both" group, not under home market.
  • Entry barriers / tariffs (foreign market reason 7) vs changes in regulation: tariffs are customs duties, Neira stressed, not norms. The deck files tariffs under foreign market, with the Trump 2019 article.
  • Saturation vs small market vs slow growth: small = the market was never big (Singapore, highways built); slow growth = big but not growing; saturated = demand fully satisfied, so even price cuts do not raise volume (milk, Coke).
  • Seasonality vs excess capacity: both are about filling the plant, but seasonality is a predictable calendar swing (snowmaking, ham, cava, ice cream) and excess capacity is structural volume above home demand (steel wire rod needing 85 percent utilisation).
  • Recession (home reason 7) vs diversification (home reason 8): recession is reacting to a crisis that has already hit (URBAR 2008); diversification is anticipating it to reduce dependence on home sales and offset negative growth in one market with another.
  • Strategic asset (resource seeking f) vs specific business opportunity (foreign reason 3): the port terminal is an asset you gain access to; the Metrocompost plant is a one-off project or tender. Both arrived through agents; the deck keeps them in separate reasons.
  • Talent pool (resource seeking g) vs lower-cost factors (resource seeking e): Philippine programmers were chosen for quality and speed as much as cost (talent pool); call centres moved purely for labour cost (lower-cost factors).
  • Learning (a) gaining ideas vs (c) knowledge integration: IKEA Japan illustrates exposing yourself to tough competition to gain ideas; Starbucks illustrates integrating knowledge across locations, which needs a global knowledge infrastructure.
  • Follower move vs offense as defense: both are reactions to a competitor. Follower = go where the competitor went, so it does not enjoy that market alone (H&M following Zara into India). Offense as defense = go into the competitor's home market in retaliation to make it spend at home (Kodak into Japan, Fuji into the US; Michelin and Goodyear).
  • First-mover advantage vs lower competition abroad: lower competition is a static condition of the foreign market (Ethiopian confectionery); first-mover advantage is the benefit of arriving before your known rivals and building brand awareness first.
  • Economies of scale vs economies of scope: scale = same product, more units, lower unit cost (and ROI on big investments); scope = different products, same resource or capability.
  • Operational scope vs strategic scope: operational shares a resource (tangible: labs, distribution networks; intangible: brand, reputation, technology; National Geographic). Strategic transfers a capability (functional such as marketing or product development; general management).
  • Tangible vs intangible resources: distribution networks and research labs are tangible; brands, corporate reputation, technology and management capabilities are intangible.
  • Zara and H&M order: Zara 2010, H&M 2017. The class recording reversed it; the deck is right.
  • IDE Technologies hemispheres: the slide says Switzerland and South Africa; Neira said Chile and Argentina in class. Either way the point is both hemispheres; if a question quotes the deck, South Africa.
  • Uber example: deck says Uber Spain; class story was Uber Colombia. Same lesson: regulation changed after entry.
  • PM port terminal country: Guatemala (the deck says PM-Guatemala; Neira first said Colombia and corrected himself).
  • Three drivers of disruption: technology is the enabler, demographics the silent force, globalization the amplifier. Do not swap the labels.
  • Reviews statistics: 90 percent are influenced by reviews; 60 percent trust family and friends; 60 percent trust customer reviews; only 12 percent trust the supplier. Separately, 12 percent of internet users buy cross-border. Same number, different facts.
Session 6 (taught 2 Oct) · complete notes · 6204 words

Session 6: Ready to internationalize? (Prof. Pablo Neira, deck dated October 2026, taught 2 Oct 2026 as session 8)

This unit is the third box in the course roadmap (global trends, benefits and reasons, ready to internationalize?, where, how). It asks one question: before a company picks a country or an entry mode, is it actually ready to go abroad? The deck answers with a strategic analysis in the home country built from three pieces: (1) external analysis of the industry with Porter's Five Forces, (2) internal analysis of how the company competes, using Porter's generic strategies and the Ansoff matrix, and (3) resources and capabilities analysis using the Resource Based View (RBV) and the VRIO test. In class Neira said these are not the only frameworks, but the three areas (industry, how you compete, resources and capabilities) are the ones you must cover. His closing emphasis: look inside; most successful companies win because of resources and capabilities that give a sustained competitive advantage, and a temporary advantage is "no good." He also stressed being realistic about funding and the 6 to 18 month ramp-up before a new market makes money.

Slide-by-slide

Slide 1: Title

  • "Ready to internationalize?" Prof. Pablo Neira, IE University, October 2026.

Slide 2: How to Expand Internationally (course roadmap)

  • Five boxes along an arrow: Global trends, Benefits and reasons to internationalize, Ready to internationalize?, Where?, How?
  • This deck is the third box. Where and How are the next two decks (Sessions 7 and 9).

Slides 3 to 4: Ready to internationalise? How to evaluate it?

  • Section dividers. The question of the unit: how do you evaluate whether a company is ready?

Slide 5: MNCs international strategy process, Strategic analysis in home country

  • Readiness is judged by a strategic analysis in the home country (also called "strategic analysis in local market" on later slides). The analysis is done at home, before going abroad.

Slides 6 to 7: What is strategy?

  • The deck first clears up what strategy is not, with three groups of wrong answers:
  • 1. Strategy is different than goals. Wrong examples: "our strategy is to be #1 or #2", "to grow", "to produce superior returns to our shareholders", "to be the world leader."
  • 2. Strategy is more than a particular action. Wrong examples: "our strategy is to merge", "buy another company", "outsource", "consolidate the industry."
  • 3. Strategy is not the same as vision or values. Wrong examples: "to meet the financial needs and goals of our customers", "to serve our customers meeting the highest standards of integrity."
  • The definition: Strategy is the approach and ways to compete and the competitive advantages on which it will be based; how are we going to be unique.

Slide 8: Strategic analysis in home country, the three analyses

  • A diagram with three boxes inside the home-country analysis:
  • 1. External analysis: industry situation. Question: how attractive is the industry where we compete?
  • 2. Internal analysis: company situation. Questions: how are we competing? What is my current strategy? How successful am I?
  • 3. Resources and capabilities analysis going global. Question: what are my resources and capabilities?
  • Arrows run 1 to 3 and 2 to 3: both the external and internal views feed the resources and capabilities judgement.
  • Bottom line on the slide: understanding internal and external factors will enable formulating an international strategy.

Slide 9: 1. External analysis (framing)

  • External analysis, industry situation, uses the Porter framework.
  • Core question: how attractive is the industry where we compete?

Slide 10: Five Forces Porter's model

  • Banner slide introducing the tool.

Slide 11: Industry analysis, Porter's Five Forces Competition Framework, objectives

  • Four objectives of the industry analysis:
  • How attractive is the industry where we compete?
  • What are the key success factors in the industry?
  • Evidence of changes in the industry that might affect future profitability.
  • Are we in the right business? Should we consider changes before going abroad?
  • Note the last point: the readiness check can conclude that the company must fix or change its business at home before internationalizing.

Slide 12: What determines the level of profit in an industry? Who is Michael Porter?

  • Michael Porter (born 1947) is a management guru and professor at Harvard Business School.
  • Engineer, PhD in Economics and MBA, both from Harvard; bestselling author; founder of the consulting firm Monitor.
  • He redefined how business people think about competition by bringing the language and concepts of economics into corporate strategy.
  • He began by simplifying the notion of competitive advantage, then built a framework for how to achieve it.
  • His approach rests on the overall economics and structure of complex systems rather than individual parts.
  • The test for each force: "Is it sufficiently strong to reduce or eliminate industry profits?" (highlighted on the slide).
  • The diagram on the right shows the five forces around industry competitors (rivalry among existing firms) in the centre, lettered: a Substitutes (threat of substitutes, from the right), b Potential entrants (threat of new entrants, from the left), c Industry competitors (centre), d Buyers (bargaining power of buyers, from below), e Suppliers (bargaining power of suppliers, from above).

Slide 13: Porter's Five Forces Competition Framework (diagram)

  • Same picture, full size: suppliers above, buyers below, potential entrants left, substitutes right, rivalry in the middle. The point: profit in an industry is squeezed from five directions, not only by direct rivals.

Slide 14: 5 Porter's forces summary and how to apply the model

  • This slide lists the determinants of each force (image only, transcribed here):
  • Supplier power: buyers' price sensitivity, relative bargaining power (see buyer power for detail, the logic mirrors it).
  • Threat of entry: capital requirements, economies of scale, absolute cost advantages, product differentiation, access to distribution, legal barriers, retaliation.
  • Industry rivalry: concentration, diversity of competitors, product differentiation, excess capacity and exit barriers, cost conditions.
  • Substitute competition: buyers' propensity to substitute, relative prices and performance of substitutes.
  • Buyer power: two parts. Price sensitivity: cost of product relative to total cost, product differentiation, competition between buyers. Bargaining power: size and concentration of buyers relative to producers, buyers' switching costs, buyers' information, buyers' ability to backward integrate.
  • HOW TO APPLY THE MODEL (three steps): 1. Identification of the industry. 2. Identification of the players in the industry. 3. Sequential analysis of each force.

Slide 15: (a) Substitutes: products with equivalent function

  • Definition of a substitute: a product with an equivalent function.
  • Two drivers, each with high and low substitution examples:
DriverLogicHigh substitutionLow substitution
Number of close substitutesThe more substitutes, the more competitive the industry and the lower the prices, because the customer can switch to another product when prices riseNewspapers, travel agency, urban transportationGasoline, cigarettes
Buyers' propensity to substituteDriven by similar performance and price, similar occasion for use, same geographic marketAudi Q5 vs Land Rover, pizza vs burger, Amazon vs El Corte InglésSpeed train vs bus, orange juice vs cola, cement in Madrid and Paris
  • What the pairs illustrate: Audi Q5 and Land Rover have similar performance and price (easy to switch); pizza and burger share the occasion for use; Amazon and El Corte Inglés compete in the same market. Cement in Madrid and in Paris is low substitution because they are not in the same geographic market; a high-speed train and a bus differ in performance and price.

Slide 16: (b) Potential entrants: new firms and firms diversifying from other industries

  • Seven barriers to entry, each with a definition and an example:
BarrierDefinitionExample
Capital requirementInitial investment needed to enter the industryBoeing and Airbus (high investment); smartphone apps (low cost of developing)
Economies of scaleLarge indivisible investments that must be amortized over a large volume of outputNew development cost of the A380, estimated at USD 18 billion, requires at least 400 units to break even
Absolute cost advantageEstablished firms may have advantages over new entrants: ownership of low-cost sources and economies of learningAramco (low price of raw reserves); Intel's experience in microprocessors (learning economies)
Product differentiationBrand recognition and customer loyalty for established firmsCosmetics (high product differentiation); low-cost carriers (limited differentiation)
Access to channel distributionMainly for consumer goods, which depend on the retailer; the internet has diminished this barrierMercadona (leader in distribution in Spain) limits the brands that appear on its shelf space
Government and legal barriersSome economists claim these are the only truly effective barriers to entryTraffic rights between countries limit new airlines' entry and the frequencies offered
RetaliationThe entrant's expectation of the established firms' reactionAirlines frequently react with price-cutting on former routes when another airline starts operating

Slide 17: (c) Rivalry between existing competitors: major determinant of profitability

  • Rivalry is called the major determinant of profitability. Four factors:
FactorDefinitionExample
Seller concentrationNumber and size of firms competing in a market; market share of the largest 4 is the indicator. In a monopoly the firm can exercise high price influence; in a duopoly firms tend to have similar prices and compete on advertising and innovationGillette dominates razor blades; Coca-Cola and Pepsi are a duopoly with similar prices and a focus on marketing
Product differentiationIf there is no differentiation the product becomes a commodity and firms compete on priceRestaurants differ significantly (type of food, dishes, atmosphere, location); petrol stations cannot differentiate their core product (they compete on location, convenience)
Excess capacity and exit barriersImbalance between demand and capacity pushes firms to cut prices to stimulate demand; exit barriers are the costs of reducing capacity (job protection, infrastructure)Seaside hotels cut prices in winter to stimulate demand and improve occupancy
Scale economies and fixed vs variable costsHigh fixed cost relative to variable cost causes price competition; more scale economies push companies to grow and compete on priceScale efficiency in the automotive industry is core (low margin, high volume)

Slide 18: (d, e) Bargaining power and price sensitivity: competition in the market for inputs and outputs

  • Buyers' power has two components.
  • Price sensitivity depends on: 1. importance of the product relative to cost; 2. competition between buyers; 3. differentiation of the product. Examples: automakers as buyers of car components (components are a big share of their cost, so they are price sensitive); El Corte Inglés buying T-shirts.
  • Bargaining power depends on: 1. size and concentration of buyers vs suppliers (few buyers making big purchases means a high cost of losing one); 2. buyers' information (more informed buyers find lower prices more easily); 3. vertical integration (do it yourself vs depend on the supplier). Examples: 1. a customer has low bargaining power negotiating with electrical contractors; 2. travel search engines (Booking.com, KAYAK) let buyers compare fares easily; 3. unlike Gap and H&M, which buy their clothes from suppliers, Zara makes most of its own.
  • Suppliers' power (price sensitivity and bargaining power again): the analysis of relative power between producers and their suppliers is precisely analogous to the producer-buyer analysis. The only difference is that now the firms are the buyers and the producers of inputs are the suppliers.

Slide 19: External analysis (repeat framing)

  • Transition slide repeating: external analysis, Porter framework, how attractive is the industry.

Slide 20: 2. Internal analysis

  • Questions: How is the company competing? Is it a solid and proven successful strategy?
  • Tool 1: Porter strategies.

Slide 21: Porter strategies, Two competitive advantages

  • Questions: what is the strategy of the company? What are the sources of competitive advantage of the company?
  • Diagram (image only): Competitive advantage splits into two:
  • Cost advantage = "similar product at lower cost."
  • Differentiation advantage = "price premium from unique product."

Slides 22 to 25: Positioning: Porter's generic strategies

  • A 2 by 2 matrix. Horizontal axis: competitive advantage ("what makes the company strong?"): costs or differentiation. Vertical axis: market scope ("what part of the market is being targeted?"): entire market or a segment.
  • Each slide lights up one cell with its definition and a company logo:
  • Cost leadership (costs, entire market): "Be the most competitive company in cost in the entire market." Example on the slide: Amazon.
  • Differentiation (differentiation, entire market): "Be a distinctive company, recognized for its uniqueness, quality or personality." Example: Apple.
  • Cost focus (costs, a segment): "Be very competitive in cost in a particular product or niche." Example: Lidl.
  • Differentiation focus (differentiation, a segment): "Have a differentiated product or market niche." Example: Ferrari.
CostsDifferentiation
Entire marketCost leadership (Amazon)Differentiation (Apple)
A segmentCost focus (Lidl)Differentiation focus (Ferrari)

Slide 26: 2. Internal analysis (second tool added)

  • Same framing: how is the company competing, is the strategy solid and proven? Tools: 1) Porter strategies, 2) Ansoff matrix.

Slide 27: Ansoff matrix, why

  • What growth strategy is the company currently using in its local market?
  • Is it sustainable and transferable to foreign markets? Should the company change the growth strategy?
  • The matrix helps businesses decide their market growth strategy: entering into new foreign markets?

Slide 28: Ansoff matrix, the two levers

  • Only two approaches to any growth strategy, varying: 1. what is sold; 2. to whom it is sold.
  • Boxed: Selling new or existing products in new or existing markets.
  • Footer note: it is all about choice; business strategy is not either or (companies can combine).

Slide 29: Ansoff matrix (picture)

  • Axes: Products (current, new) across; Market (current, new) down.
  • Bottom left: Market penetration (current product, current market). Bottom right: Product development (new product, current market). Top left: Market development (current product, new market). Top right: Diversification (new product, new market).

Slide 30: Market penetration and product development

  • MARKET PENETRATION: selling an existing product in an existing market.
  • Only possible in a growing market which is not yet saturated.
  • Seeks four main objectives: a) maintain or increase the market share of current products; b) secure dominance of growth markets; c) restructure a mature market by driving out competitors, typically with an aggressive pricing strategy; d) increase usage by existing customers.
  • Footer note: open new locations; less risky because you know the customer; organic growth.
  • Pictures: Aldi store and Domino's pizza (chains that grow by opening more outlets).
  • PRODUCT DEVELOPMENT: developing new products to sell in existing markets. Usually employed with branded goods, so that the qualities of the new product are linked to the customer's confidence in the established brand.
  • Pictures: the Coca-Cola range (Coca-Cola, light, Diet Coke, zero) and the McDonald's McSalad ad.

Slide 31: Diversification

  • DIVERSIFICATION: selling new products to new markets. This can lead into entering new countries.
  • One of the main reasons for diversification: efficiency gains from applying the organization's existing resources or capabilities to new markets and products or services, that is economies of scope.
  • Footer examples: Alphabet, Samsung. Picture: Apple iPod range.

Slide 32: Market development

  • MARKET DEVELOPMENT: offering an existing product in a new market.
  • Three forms: new segments (from discount to premium); new users (new channel: e-commerce); new geographies, the prime example is internationalization.
  • Pictures: Starbucks in China (store and Chinese-language drinks such as Fortune Chestnut Molten Mocha, Ice Cream Plus) and Kellogg's Corn Flakes in Chinese packaging: existing products taken to a new country.

Slide 33: 3. Resource analysis

  • Tool: Resource Based View.
  • Central question: does the company have resources and capabilities to go international?
  • Sub-questions: what uniqueness can we bring into the new markets? Does the company have sufficient resources for international markets? If not, will the company be able to acquire these in order to execute its international business plan?

Slide 34: Resource Based View (RBV)

  • Firms should look inside for the sources of competitive advantage.
  • Resources are the main reason that explains why companies achieve higher organizational performance.
  • Boxed question: what resources of the company generate competitive advantage?

Slide 35: RBV 1st step, identify the firm's resources and capabilities

  • Resources are the productive assets owned by the firm. Two types:
  • 1. Tangible: financial resources and physical assets. Understand their potential to generate profit.
  • 2. Intangible: trademarks, patents, copyrights, access to information, know-how, organizational culture.
  • On their own, resources are non-productive. To perform a task, resources must work together (that is what a capability is).
  • Example: Disney has tangible resources (theme parks, hotels, movie studios) and an intangible one: the enduring affection of millions of people across generations for Disney and its characters.
  • Table of capabilities by functional area (second half of the slide):
  • Corporate functions: financial control; strategic management of multiple businesses; strategic innovation; multidivisional coordination; acquisition management; international management.
  • Management information: comprehensive integrated network linked to managerial decision making.
  • Research and development: research; innovative new product development; fast-cycle new product development.
  • Operations: efficiency in volume manufacturing; continuous improvement in manufacturing; flexibility and speed of response.
  • Product design: design capability.
  • Marketing: brand management; promoting reputation for quality; responsiveness to market trends.
  • Sales and distribution: effective sales promotions and execution; efficiency and speed of order processing; speed of distribution; quality and efficiency of customer service.

Slide 36: RBV 1st step, questions to find resources and capabilities

  • Which activities lower the cost of production without decreasing perceived customer value?
  • Which activities increase product or service differentiation and perceived customer value?
  • Do you have access to scarce raw materials or hard-to-get distribution channels?
  • Do you have a special relationship with key players, organizations or suppliers in your sector?
  • Do you have an integrated order and distribution platform powered by unique software that joins stakeholders?
  • Do you have employees with unique skills and capabilities?
  • Do you have brand reputation for quality, innovation, customer service?
  • Do you perform any tasks better than your competitors do? (Benchmarking is useful here.)

Slide 37: RBV 2nd step, check if they meet critical requirements

  • Two types of resources:
  • Tangible assets: can be bought in markets, so little advantage. Physical things like land, buildings, equipment and capital.
  • Intangible assets: the main source of sustainable competitive advantage. Brand reputation, trademarks, intellectual property.
  • Resources must be:
  • Heterogeneous: competitive advantage comes from a different bundle of resources.
  • Immobile: resources such as brand image, process knowledge or intellectual property usually do not move from company to company and cannot be replicated, at least in the short term.
  • The RBV chain diagram: Resource-based view relies on resources (tangible, intangible), that must be heterogeneous and immobile, and have VRIO attributes to become VRIO resources, that provide competitive advantage.

Slide 38: VRIO framework

  • Resources must have 4 attributes to become a source of sustainable competitive advantage: Valuable, Rare, Imperfectly imitable, company Organized to capture the value.

Slide 39: RBV 3rd step, evaluate resources and capabilities (VRIO framework by J. Barney)

  • A flowchart of four yes/no questions, each "no" exits to an outcome:
  • Valuable? Is the resource valuable to exploit opportunities? Does it increase perceived customer value? Does it increase differentiation or decrease the cost of production? No: competitive disadvantage.
  • Rare? Can the resource be acquired by only one or few firms? Is it unique or owned by several firms? No: competitive parity.
  • Costly to imitate? Hard to imitate because: developed over a long period of time; causal ambiguity (written "casual ambiguity" on the slide); social complexity, based on company culture. No: temporary competitive advantage.
  • Organized to capture value? Resources by themselves do not confer any advantage if the company is not organized to capture the value from them: management systems, processes, policies, organizational structure and culture. No: temporary competitive advantage.
  • All four yes: sustained competitive advantage.
ValuableRareCostly to imitateOrganizedOutcome
NoCompetitive disadvantage
YesNoCompetitive parity
YesYesNoTemporary competitive advantage
YesYesYesNoTemporary competitive advantage
YesYesYesYesSustained competitive advantage

Slide 40: 3. Resource analysis (repeat)

  • Does the company have resources and capabilities to go international?

Slides 41 to 42: Conclusions, Strategic analysis in home country (summary picture)

  • One picture tying the unit together: 1. External analysis, industry situation = Porter 5 Forces (five forces diagram). 2. Internal analysis, company situation = Porter strategies and Ansoff matrix (generic strategies matrix: cost leadership, differentiation, focus; and the Ansoff 2 by 2). 3. Resources and capabilities analysis = Resource Based View (VRIO flowchart: valuable, rare, costly to imitate, organized to capture value, leading to competitive disadvantage, parity, temporary advantage, temporary advantage, sustained advantage).
  • Note the generic strategies picture on this slide uses the older three-cell version (cost leadership, differentiation, and a single "focus" row for a single segment), while slides 22 to 25 split focus into cost focus and differentiation focus.

What the professor added in class (2 Oct 2026)

Framing and the three areas

  • It sounds nice in a boardroom to say "we want to go global" and start debating when and where, without knowing whether the company is ready. Readiness comes first.
  • There are many ways to evaluate readiness; the frameworks in the deck are the ones he uses when running or advising companies, not the only ones. But three areas must be covered: what industry am I in and how profitable or captive is it; how am I competing (my strategy); what are my resources and capabilities.
  • The concepts may feel like high school material, but companies still skip them.
  • EXAM: the three analyses are external (industry, Porter Five Forces), internal (how you compete: Porter strategies and growth strategy with Ansoff), and resources and capabilities (RBV, VRIO).

External analysis

  • He adds a sixth angle Porter did not have: disruption or disruptors. Include it when analysing the industry.
  • Sometimes the analysis concludes the industry is not attractive (too many competitors, too many potential entrants) and the company must readapt or redirect its strategy at home before going abroad. Do your homework first.
  • The worst thing is to find the benefits and reasons and then jump at the 195 to 200 countries. Maybe you are not ready: not enough skills, not the right people, or simply not enough funding.
  • Porter video shown in class: you fight for profits not only with direct competitors but with customers and suppliers who have bargaining power, new entrants, and substitutes that cap profitability and growth. Five Forces is a holistic way to see the structural drivers of profitability, what is causing profitability, and which trends will change the game.
  • Define the industry boundaries first. If you are Iberia, what is "the airline industry" you are analysing? Companies often start the analysis without setting this clearly (this is step 1 of "how to apply the model").
  • Student discussion on airlines and India: existing competitors can lobby to block new airports within 100 to 200 km to keep entrants out; government and political barriers shape the number of flights per route. Neira: this is why country choice (Session 7) needs an industry analysis for that specific country.
  • Student example, Southwest Airlines: low cost plus a differentiated model (short-haul only, no food, first come first served seating, no business class) gives a 20-minute turnaround versus about an hour for others. Neira: they found their niche.
  • Customizing the offer (for example menus) is also a way to shape the forces when entering; once you are established, the threat from entry is lower.

Internal analysis: Porter generic strategies

  • Two major ways to compete, or a combination: cost leadership or differentiation, crossed with whole market or a specific segment.
  • Cost leadership, whole market: class named Walmart (always lower cost, all customers) and Amazon (sells to rich, medium and low income alike). The slide uses Amazon.
  • Differentiation, whole market: Apple. iPhones are expensive, yet the whole market, not only wealthy families, pays the premium.
  • Cost focus: Lidl, Aldi. You go in expecting the lowest prices; they do not target the medium-to-high-end segment. Contrast in Madrid: Sánchez Romero supermarkets (one in Goya), premium brands, wealthy customers, perhaps 20, 30 or 40 percent more for the same goods.
  • Differentiation focus: targeting only the rich top of the wealth pyramid with something unique. Cars: Ferrari, Porsche, Tesla were named.
  • Real companies are often in a grey zone: Apple has very expensive models and cheaper ones; car makers have high-end and small cars. The matrix is a simplification. Start by understanding the industry, then place the company.

Internal analysis: Ansoff matrix

  • The growth strategy question: what is it, and is it transferable or copyable into the market you want to enter? Does it make sense there, or do you need to change it?
  • Only two levers: change what you sell or to whom you sell. Companies are often in a grey area between cells.
  • Market penetration: same products, same customers, grow by presence. Examples: a Kenyan fintech growing from Nairobi into Western, Northern and coastal Kenya (student); supermarkets opening more locations in Madrid, then second-tier cities; fast food chains (Domino's, McDonald's) opening more stores.
  • Product development: new product to the existing customer base. Student offered Apple credit cards and iPods. Neira's examples: Coke adding new flavours and types; McDonald's adding salads, coffee, donuts: same stores, same customers, new products. Loyalty makes customers try the new product.
  • Diversification: new product and new market at once; the most complicated cell because two unknowns are being tested at the same time (will the product succeed, and will customers who never bought from you buy it). Apple launching new products in countries where it had no presence; Netflix entering streaming in new countries where people did not know it (student example, endorsed).
  • Market development: current portfolio into a new market, the typical cell for international expansion, new geographies. Student example Uber: in the US it is private drivers with their own cars; in Spain it was sued and had to operate under the VTC licence model, owning cars and paying drivers as contractors. Neira: same product, new market, with adaptation.

Funding and the ramp-up (student question: do companies expect to lose money at first?)

  • EXAM: a rigorous plan assumes a ramp-up period of 6, 8 or 18 months, sometimes a year or two depending on the product, during which the venture loses money. You must have enough funding and capabilities to hold through it.
  • Be realistic; do not lie to yourself or play tricks in the spreadsheet. "On a spreadsheet you can write whatever you want." Spanish saying quoted: reality is what it is. If the plan is not funded, go back and raise money first.
  • The temptation when presenting to the board or shareholders is to show profits rising from month one. Resist it.
  • His own example: a mine in Spain (name unclear in the recording) restarting once permits arrive; shareholders were told 18 months before it begins to produce, needing capex (equipment, roads) plus working capital for salaries and monthly payments during those 18 months. Shareholders judged it still worth funding.

Resources and capabilities

  • Resources are tangible and intangible; capabilities relate more to people and functional areas (strong technical team, strong marketing team, strong finance team). Use the questions on slide 36 to dig deeper.
  • VRIO walked through: valuable? If everybody has the same resource it is not rare, so you are in competitive parity. Then costly to imitate?
  • Starbucks example: the first store in Seattle was successful; the founder could have stopped there but opened more, saw it get more profitable and expanded to thousands of stores worldwide. Store managers send weekly feedback to headquarters; anything unique that works in one store is analysed and disseminated to the others (an organization set up to capture value).
  • Debate: what matters more, inside or outside? Conclusion: in most successful cases it is the skills, resources and capabilities that make the company unique and give a sustainable advantage. The industry helps, but the inside view is what you can play with.
  • EXAM: a temporary advantage is "no good." You need something that is very complicated for competitors to copy in the long term. In the very long run everything can be replicated (someone said even a 30-year-old Japanese company could be copied), but that is a rare situation.
  • Closing recap: look at three areas; do the industry analysis with Five Forces or any model; do the internal analysis (how you compete, growth strategy); know your resources and capabilities and whether they give a sustained competitive advantage.

Likely exam angles

  • Know that strategy is the approach and ways to compete and the competitive advantages on which it is based (how to be unique); it is not goals, not a single action, not vision or values.
  • Know that the readiness check is a strategic analysis in the home country with three parts: external (industry, Five Forces), internal (company, Porter strategies and Ansoff) and resources and capabilities (RBV, VRIO).
  • Know the four objectives of the Five Forces analysis: industry attractiveness, key success factors, changes affecting future profitability, and whether we are in the right business before going abroad.
  • Know the five forces and their letters on the slide: a substitutes, b potential entrants, c rivalry among existing competitors, d buyers, e suppliers, and that each is tested by asking whether it is strong enough to reduce or eliminate industry profits.
  • Know the three steps to apply the model: identify the industry, identify the players, analyse each force in sequence.
  • Know Michael Porter's facts: born 1947, Harvard Business School, engineer with Harvard PhD in Economics and MBA, founded Monitor.
  • Know that rivalry is called the major determinant of profitability, that seller concentration is measured by the market share of the largest 4 firms, and that no differentiation makes a product a commodity sold on price.
  • Know the seven entry barriers and their examples, especially the A380: about USD 18 billion development cost, at least 400 units to break even (economies of scale), Mercadona (access to distribution), traffic rights (government and legal, claimed by some economists to be the only truly effective barriers), airline price cuts (retaliation).
  • Know the substitutes table: newspapers, travel agencies and urban transport are high substitution; gasoline and cigarettes are low; cement in Madrid versus Paris is low because of different geographic markets.
  • Know buyer power = price sensitivity (product cost relative to total, competition between buyers, differentiation) plus bargaining power (size and concentration, information, vertical integration or backward integration, switching costs), and that supplier power is the mirror image.
  • Know Zara makes most of its own clothes (vertical integration) while Gap and H&M buy from suppliers; Booking.com and KAYAK are the buyer information example.
  • Know the two competitive advantages: cost advantage (similar product at lower cost) and differentiation advantage (price premium from a unique product).
  • Know the generic strategies grid and the slide examples: cost leadership Amazon, differentiation Apple, cost focus Lidl, differentiation focus Ferrari; the axes are competitive advantage (costs or differentiation) and market scope (entire or a segment).
  • Know Ansoff's two levers (what is sold, to whom) and the four cells: penetration (existing, existing), product development (new product, existing market), market development (existing product, new market), diversification (new, new).
  • Know that market penetration is only possible in a growing, unsaturated market, has four objectives, and is the least risky; diversification is the most complex and is justified by economies of scope (Alphabet, Samsung).
  • Know that market development has three forms (new segments, new users or channels, new geographies) and that internationalization is its prime example.
  • Know RBV: look inside; resources are the main reason for higher performance; tangible assets can be bought so they give little advantage; intangible assets are the main source of sustainable advantage; resources must be heterogeneous and immobile.
  • Know VRIO by J. Barney and the outcomes: not valuable = competitive disadvantage; not rare = competitive parity; not costly to imitate = temporary advantage; not organized = temporary advantage; all four = sustained advantage.
  • Know the three sources of imitation difficulty: time, causal ambiguity, social complexity (culture), and that organization means systems, processes, policies, structure and culture.
  • Know the Disney example (theme parks, hotels, studios plus enduring affection for its characters) and that resources on their own are non-productive and must work together.
  • Know Neira's class rule: plan for a 6 to 18 month loss-making ramp-up, fund capex and working capital, and do not trust optimistic spreadsheets.

Traps and look-alikes

  • Strategy vs goal: "be number 1" or "grow" is a goal; strategy says how you will compete and be unique.
  • Strategy vs action: "merge" or "outsource" is one action, not a strategy.
  • Cost advantage vs differentiation advantage: cost = similar product at lower cost; differentiation = price premium from a unique product. Both can be aimed at the whole market or a segment.
  • Cost leadership vs cost focus: same cost advantage; leadership targets the entire market (Amazon), focus targets a segment or niche (Lidl).
  • Differentiation vs differentiation focus: Apple serves the whole market with a unique product; Ferrari serves a niche.
  • Slide examples vs class examples: the slide says Amazon and Lidl; in class Neira also said Walmart, Aldi, Porsche and Tesla. If a question quotes the deck, answer Amazon, Apple, Lidl, Ferrari.
  • Market development vs diversification: both are new markets; market development keeps the existing product (internationalization is the prime example), diversification also changes the product and is the riskiest cell.
  • Market penetration vs market development: penetration = existing product, existing market (more stores in the same market, more usage); development = existing product, new market (new segment, new channel, new country). A student's "new region of Kenya" example was treated as penetration in class because the customer type and country stayed the same; a new country is market development.
  • Product development vs diversification: both involve a new product; product development sells it to existing customers, leaning on brand trust (Coke flavours, McSalad); diversification sells it to new customers.
  • Economies of scale vs economies of scope: scale is an entry barrier from spreading large fixed investments over volume (A380); scope is the efficiency reason for diversification, applying existing resources to new products and markets.
  • Entry barrier vs exit barrier: entry barriers (seven on slide 16) deter new firms; exit barriers (job protection, infrastructure) keep excess capacity in the industry and intensify rivalry.
  • Price sensitivity vs bargaining power: both are halves of buyer power; sensitivity is about how much the buyer cares about price, bargaining power is about whether the buyer can force a lower price (size, information, integration).
  • Buyer power vs supplier power: same determinants, mirror image; with suppliers the firm is the buyer.
  • High vs low substitution: high when products have similar performance and price, the same occasion for use and the same geographic market; cement in Madrid vs Paris is low because the markets differ.
  • Tangible vs intangible resources: tangible (land, buildings, equipment, capital, financial resources) can be bought, so little advantage; intangible (brand, trademarks, IP, know-how, culture) are the sustainable source.
  • Resources vs capabilities: resources are assets owned; capabilities are what the firm does with them, organised by functional area; resources alone are non-productive.
  • Heterogeneous vs immobile: heterogeneous means firms hold different bundles; immobile means the resources cannot move between firms or be replicated in the short term.
  • Competitive parity vs temporary advantage vs sustained advantage (VRIO): parity = valuable but not rare; temporary = valuable and rare but either imitable or not organized to capture value; sustained = all four attributes.
  • Imperfectly imitable vs costly to imitate: the same VRIO attribute, worded differently on slides 38 and 39.
  • Five Forces as in the deck vs in class: the deck has five forces; Neira adds disruption as an extra angle in class, not a sixth force on the slide.
Session 7 + Ghemawat · complete notes · 8819 words

Session 7: International market selection, Where? (Neira, 28 Sep 2026) plus Ghemawat, "Distance Still Matters" (HBR 2001)

This unit is the third step of the course's internationalization framework: global trends, benefits and reasons, ready?, where?, how?. It answers "which country?" with a staged funnel that starts from roughly 200 countries and ends with one: earliest screening (start from your own business), preliminary screening (macro, PESTEL), second screening (distance, CAGE), in-depth screening (industry attractiveness and barriers with Porter's five forces, then a detailed market analysis), and final selection (the competitive advantage equation: company resources and capabilities matched with country specifics and industry success factors). Cost of entry, resource constraints and the main goals are kept in mind the whole way. The assigned article, Pankaj Ghemawat's "Distance Still Matters", supplies the second-screening tool: the CAGE framework (cultural, administrative, geographic, economic distance), the Frankel and Rose numbers on how much each kind of distance changes trade, the Star TV failure, the China sidebar, the industry sensitivity table and the Tricon Restaurants case where Mexico moves from 16th of 20 to 2nd once distance is counted. The professor's emphasis in class: selecting the country is one of the most critical steps; do the analysis for the right reasons with SMART goals; distance is not only physical; if you cannot get data on one ingredient, swap it for another; and company capabilities must match the market, because strength in one element cannot compensate for weakness in another.

Part 1: The deck, slide by slide

Slide 1: Internationalization strategy (course map)

  • Five boxes on an arrow: Global trends, Benefits and reasons to internationalize, Ready to internationalize?, Where?, How?. Where? and How? are highlighted: this session covers Where?, the next covers How?.
  • In class he recapped: last session grouped the reasons to go international into things in the home market, things in the foreign market, competition, products, and economies of scale and scope. "Ready?" (the internal analysis) is a separate session that may be covered later; you can still do the Where? analysis without it.

Slide 2: Title

  • "How to Expand Internationally", Session 7, September 2026. International Market Selection: A Strategic Framework for Business Expansion. Where to Go. When to Go. How to Go.

Slide 3: Ghemawat quote

  • "Companies routinely exaggerate the attractiveness of foreign markets and that can lead to expensive mistakes." Pankaj Ghemawat. Slide adds: "...if you don't do a correct analysis."
  • Class: Ghemawat is a Harvard professor who has studied internationalization and entry barriers. Going international takes time, resources, people and consultancy; if you do it for the wrong reasons or without the right steps it is a waste of time and money.

Slide 4: International strategy for business (strategy design process)

  • Flow: Strategic analysis (input) then the STRATEGY DESIGN box: Set main goals and objectives, Select potential markets, Set country/market specific goals, Entry strategy, then Implementation (output).
  • "Set main goals and objectives" is highlighted, with the question: What are the core reasons of the business to enter another country?

Slide 5: Set main goals

  • Companies need clear specific goals and objectives: the main reasons why they want to go international.
  • To achieve them, goals should be in line with their resources and capabilities.
  • Class: not generic ("I want to grow"); be specific. A tiny startup that says "I want to be the market leader in that country" has goals out of line with its resources and capabilities.

Slide 6: Goals should be SMART

  • Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant, Time-limited, plus "flexible to some degree as priorities change". Caption: SMART objectives can be applied anywhere in your life, professionally and personally.
  • Class examples for each letter:
    • Specific: "next year you should sell more" is not a goal; without specificity you can never track whether it was achieved.
    • Measurable: "increase customer satisfaction next year" fails unless you define how to measure it (polls, etc.).
    • Achievable: a goal so far from reality demotivates the team; nobody is challenged to reach it.
    • Relevant: "paint all the warehouses red" is specific and measurable but irrelevant to the business.
    • Time-limited: always set a period (6, 12, 18 months); he said he would insist on this all course long; applies to careers too ("12 months after the master's to get into this sector, then switch").
    • Flexible: COVID is the example; every company had budgets and goals and had to change them.
  • Class, student question (when should a company not go international / losing track of the SMART goal): his experience is that with many people throwing input the team gets paralysed; the fix was a weekly (not monthly) review against the plan. Startups can do a lot in one month, so weekly follow-up avoids wasting time.

Slide 7: Strategy process (select potential country highlighted)

  • Same flow as slide 4 with Select potential country highlighted. This is the step the rest of the deck covers.

Slide 8: Górecka quote

  • "The selection of foreign markets is one of the most critical decisions in international market entry strategy." Dorota Górecka.

Slide 9: Select potential market, goal

  • Goal: Identify foreign markets that present the greatest business opportunities for the company.
  • Picture: "How many countries are there in the world?!" Class: 190-something; 195, 196 or about 200 depending on who counts (some organisations count Andorra and similar). So the question is how to go from about 200 countries to the one that gives the most opportunities.

Slide 10: Country evaluation screening process (four stages shown)

  • Stages drawn as arrows: Earliest screening, Second screening, In-depth screening, Final selection (circle).
  • Below, a long arrow: To be considered during the whole process: Cost of entry; Resource constraints; Main goals and objectives.
  • Class: keep three things in the back of your mind the whole time. How much will it cost (funding is not unlimited); resource constraints (the right team, the right assets); and your main goals, because people fall in love with a country and after weeks realise they lack the funding or capabilities, or that it does not serve the goals.

Slide 11: Earliest screening, the URBAR example

  • Picture only: the website of URBAR Soluciones de Ingeniería ("since 1960 developing custom industrial vibrating applications"), an engineering plant and an engineering team. Point: the earliest screening starts from your own business, not from country data.
  • Class story: he worked at URBAR, an industrial manufacturing company in Spain that designs equipment to move components. Sales were engineers talking to the customers' technical and purchasing departments. About 85 percent of sales were in Spain and the Spanish economic crisis forced them to expand. The technical team was very strong but did not speak English, so the only way to expand was to countries where the team could communicate: they focused on Spanish-speaking Central and South America. That one or two criteria from your business model cuts 200 countries to a group of 5, 10 or 12 (he also said 8 to 10).
  • Student remark: that is already CAGE (language). He agreed you could argue so, but the first step is simply to look at your business model and find the key criteria before any framework.

Slides 12 and 13: Second screening, the distance approach

  • Second screening = the "Distance" approach: CAGE analysis.
  • Source: article "Distance Still Matters: The Hard Reality of Global Expansion", Pankaj Ghemawat.
  • Class: between earliest and second screening there is a preliminary screening from a macro perspective (PESTEL) to see how your company fits the dynamics of the country (slide 33 shows it).

Slide 14: CAGE distance framework, what it does

  • Analysis of the distance between home and potential countries.
  • Helps identify and prioritize the differences between countries when developing international strategies.
  • Details how easy or not it is for the company to adapt and operate in the target country: to REPLICATE their business in the foreign country.
  • Class: it gives you a comparison of the issues that are critical to your company across candidate countries. Student question on where to get objective data (for example on cultural differences): sometimes the data is not there; if an ingredient would take too long or you will never get enough data points, drop that ingredient and find an alternative one. It is not an easy analysis.

Slide 15: CAGE video

  • Picture: Pankaj Ghemawat on video (Carlson School of Management, University of Minnesota) explaining CAGE. Content of the clip (played in class): C cultural, A administrative/political, G geographic, E economic. Most interactions, not just trade, are hindered by differences and helped by similarities on these dimensions. Two countries with the same official language, in the same regional trading arrangement, sharing a border and with similar per capita income can be expected to trade 10 to 15 times as much as similarly sized countries without those commonalities. The framework gives an imperfect but useful metric: is Canada closer to home than Mexico? Canada is still the US's largest bilateral trading partner although only about the tenth largest economy, because of CAGE commonalities.

Slide 16 (repeated as slide 25): CAGE worksheet, Country A versus Country B

  • A table with one row per dimension and empty bullet columns for Country A and Country B. Row texts:
    • C, Cultural distance: list the cultural norms, values and social beliefs (the unwritten rules) that shape the behavior of individuals and organizations. Societies also differ in attitudes toward globalization and market power, with consequences for formal trade regulations and general attitudes to how businesses are run.
    • A, Administrative distance: list differences in history and politics, especially where countries do not share colonial ties. A lack of shared currency, political hostilities and government corruption also add administrative distance.
    • G, Geographic distance: not only physical distance but a country's physical size, whether it shares borders with hostile or non-hostile neighbors, and access to trade routes such as the ocean and other topographical features. List these attributes.
    • E, Economic distance: the two biggest determinants are the cost of labor and the level of consumer wealth. It is more difficult for a company from a wealthy country to enter a poorer country and succeed, but not impossible. List these determinants.
  • Point: this is the working template. You fill it for each candidate pair and see which country is closer to you on the dimensions that matter for your product.

Slide 17: CAGE four boxes

  • Picture of the four boxes as the deck names them: Cultural distance; Administrative and political distance; Geographic distance; Economic/wealth distance.

Slide 18: Administrative and political distance

  • Drivers: tariffs, weak institutions, currency, associations between countries (colony-colonizer), trade agreements, regulation related to the company's industry, legal systems.
  • Most affects: products that the foreign government views as vital to national security (telecommunications) or as building national reputation (aerospace); products or services affected by regulation (taxi services).
  • Class: ask "if I go into that country, how much will the way I do business be influenced by administrative issues?" Example: selling weapons or anything related to defence; the government will be reluctant or impose norms.

Slide 19: Corruption Perceptions Index 2020 (Transparency International)

  • Picture: world map plus the full ranking, "perceived levels of public sector corruption in 180 countries/territories". Note: the deck's text layer still carries an older embedded file name "corruption index 2017, 170 countries"; the slide shown is the 2020 edition with 180 countries.
  • Scores (higher is cleaner): Denmark and New Zealand 88 (rank 1); Finland, Singapore, Sweden, Switzerland 85; Norway 84; Netherlands 82; Germany and Luxembourg 80; Australia, Canada, Hong Kong, United Kingdom 77; Japan 74; United States 67 (rank 25); Spain 62 (rank 32); Italy 53; Saudi Arabia 53; China 42 (rank 78); India 40; Brazil 38; Mexico 31; Russia 30; Guatemala 25; Venezuela 15; Somalia and South Sudan 12 (rank 179).
  • Class: published regularly for most countries; how important it is for your business depends on how your company wants to do business. See the bribery discussion under "What the professor added".

Slide 20: Economic and wealth distance

  • Drivers: consumer wealth and income, the cost of labor, availability (or lack) of resources, inputs, infrastructure, organizational capabilities, and their cost.
  • Most affects: products for which demand varies with income (cars); industries where natural resources, labor, financial resources or other sources differ in cost and quality.

Slide 21: Coface Country Risk Assessment Map, January 2018

  • Picture: Coface (a trade credit insurer) map of 160 countries, labelled "Country ratings". Scale of business defaulting risk: A1 very low, A2 low, A3 satisfactory, A4 reasonable, B fairly high, C high, D very high, E extreme. "A unique methodology": macroeconomic expertise, comprehension of the business environment, microeconomic data over 70 years of payment experience.
  • Upgrades that month: Brazil B (recovery from private consumption, falling unemployment, low inflation, monetary easing), Greece B (agreement with creditors restored confidence), Netherlands A1 (growth above 2 percent, insolvencies falling for the fifth year), Singapore A2, South Korea A2 (robust thanks to exports and budget support), Ukraine C (growth about 3 percent, IMF-pressed reforms moving slowly). Downgrade: Saudi Arabia C (dependent on oil prices, internal political tensions).
  • Point: country ratings like this are a ready-made input for the administrative and economic dimensions. Class: a student asked what kind of risk it measures; the map legend says business defaulting risk, and he said the information is there in these country ratings.

Slide 22: Geographic distance

  • Definition: more than just how far two countries are from each other: the country's physical size, within-country distances to borders, access to the ocean, topography, and even time zones.
  • Most affects: heavy or bulky products (transport costs); fragile or perishable products (glass, fruit); businesses in which communications are critical (financial services).
  • Class: also think about moving goods inside the country (from the port by boat, then bus), poor connections, landlocked countries with no ocean border, warehouse and distribution logistics.

Slide 23: Cultural distance

  • Definition: language, beliefs, religion, values and social norms, the unwritten, unspoken rules of the game, that shape the behavior of individuals and organizations.
  • Most affects: products with high linguistic content (TV); products related to national identity (food); consumer durable goods (Japan: small cars and appliances).
  • Class: are you selling food? Then you probably need to adapt to local taste. Many companies have failed entering another country on this point (he mentioned spicy sauces as an example).

Slide 24: CAGE table from the article, "Distance between two countries increases with..."

  • Cultural: different languages, ethnicities, religions, social norms; lack of connective ethnic or social networks.
  • Administrative and political: absence of shared monetary or political association; political hostilities; weak legal and financial institutions.
  • Geographic: lack of common border, waterway access, adequate transportation or communication links; physical remoteness; different climates.
  • Economic: different consumer incomes; different costs and quality of natural, financial and human resources; different information or knowledge.
  • Class: distance is never only physical; it increases with every one of these. Focus on the items that are critical to your product or service (inflation, interest rates, taxes, whatever matters for you).

Slide 25: CAGE worksheet repeated

  • Same Country A versus Country B template as slide 16. Class: for URBAR's list of Latin American countries, do the cultural, administrative, geographic and economic analysis for each, compare, see which is closer, and screen. After this step you should ideally be down to three or four countries. Even without full data there are always ways to reach a decision.

Slide 26: Screening process, in-depth screening highlighted

  • The funnel again with In-depth screening boxed as Country INDUSTRY specifics (the earlier stages are country macro specifics).

Slide 27: In-depth screening, industry situation in pre-selected countries

  • Two branches: (1) Understand INDUSTRY ATTRACTIVENESS and barriers to entry using Porter's 5 forces; (2) DETAILED MARKET ANALYSIS related to the product/service. "Barriers to entry" is boxed in red on this slide.
  • Class: take the two (or three) remaining countries and understand how your industry works there. Porter's five forces will be covered properly in a couple of weeks.

Slide 28: Key concept, barriers to entry

  • Definition: obstacles that make it difficult and costly for new competitors to enter a market.
  • High barriers (less attractive): high capital requirements; strong brand loyalty; economies of scale; proprietary technology.
  • Low barriers (more attractive): easy market access; low capital needs; fragmented competition; growing market demand.
  • Class: the ideal scenario is low capital: a product you make at home with minimum customisation, ship it, and sign an agreement with a local logistics supplier. High capital requirements (for example having to produce locally) make entry much harder.

Slide 29: In-depth screening, industry situation in targeted countries

  • Same two branches, now with DETAILED MARKET ANALYSIS boxed in red.

Slide 30: Detailed market analysis, the three questions

  • How will the potential target country affect the firm's product?
  • Need to adapt?
  • How should the product/service be offered?
  • Class: do you need to adapt the product, the language, the packaging? The size of the changes drives capital requirements, so it feeds back into barriers to entry.

Slide 31: Detailed market analysis, example areas (1)

  • Market size: estimated industry sales for the year; estimated sales for your company for the year; how many potential buyers; is demand likely to grow or shrink.
  • The product: are there a lot of products already in the market that will compete with yours; assessment of the product as an innovation (how it is perceived relative to the market's technology level); problems and resistance to product acceptance based on the preceding evaluation.
  • The market: geographical region(s); transportation and communication available in the region(s) (if relevant); consumer buying habits (where, how and why they buy); product feature preferences.
  • Class: will there be resistance from local customers to a product coming from your country?

Slide 32: Detailed market analysis, example areas (2)

  • Pricing strategy: customary markups; types of discounts available; compare and contrast your product with competitors' products (brand name, features, packaging) and competitors' prices; can you match or beat the prices of your competitors; competitors' promotion and advertising methods; competitors' distribution channels.
  • Distribution of the product: will shipping to the market be expensive and logistically complex; retail or wholesale outlets through which the product is normally sold; product sales by other intermediaries; advertising and promotion; advertising media usually used to reach your target market(s); sales promotions customarily used (sampling, coupons, etc.).
  • Class: looking at local prices alone can decide it: after producing, shipping and distributing, will you have any margin or EBITDA?

Slide 33: The full five-stage funnel

  • Country MACRO specifics: Earliest screening, Preliminary screening (macro perspective: PESTEL analysis), Second screening (distance approach: CAGE analysis).
  • Country INDUSTRY specifics: In-depth screening.
  • Final selection (highlighted).
  • Memorise this: earliest, preliminary, second, in-depth, final. Earliest starts from the company's own business model; preliminary is PESTEL; second is CAGE; in-depth is Porter plus detailed market analysis; final is the competitive advantage equation.

Slide 34: In international markets, how do you achieve competitive advantage?

  • Answer on the next slide: The Competitive Advantage Equation.

Slide 35: The Competitive Advantage Equation (final selection)

  • Competitive advantage is achieved when 1. Company resources and capabilities are MATCHED WITH 2. Country specifics and 3. Industry success factors.
