  • All three elements must align. Strength in one cannot compensate for weakness in another.

Slide 36: The Competitive Advantage Equation, comparing Country A and Country B

  • For the two finalists, compare: 1. Their country specifics; 2. Their industry success factors and attractiveness; 3. Cost of entry.
  • Against the company: 1. Resources and capabilities; 2. Main goals and objectives.
  • Result: Match or Gap (if a gap, how complex is it to correct).
  • Class: it is very unlikely that a country matches perfectly; there is normally a gap. The question is how big it is and how complicated to close. Always keep your goals in mind.

Slide 37: Strategy process, company specifics

  • The flow again with Set country/market specific goals highlighted and labelled COMPANY specifics. Once the country is chosen, set specific goals for that market.

Slide 38: Example of goals per area (a to e)

  • a. Market objectives: expected sales; profit expectations, forecast and budgets; market penetration and coverage (which areas of the country you target and how much the firm should emphasise sales there).
  • b. What product or activities, and product adaptation or modification (how and why the product should be adapted): core component, packaging, support services.
  • c. Marketing communications: advertising (objectives, media mix, messaging appropriate for the market, costs); sales promotions (if appropriate: objectives, types, costs); personal selling (style appropriate for the market, needed adaptations); other communication methods.
  • d. Distribution (from origin to destination): ports (origin port, destination port); mode (ocean, rail, air or highway, advantages and disadvantages of each; in most cases the firm will use ocean).
  • e. Packaging: marking and labelling regulations, containerization, costs.

Slide 39: Example of goals per area (f to m)

  • f. Documentation: bill of lading, commercial invoice, invoice, export declaration, certificate of origin, insurance, special documentation.
  • g. Freight forwarder: in most cases the firm will need one; recommend some, with names and addresses.
  • h. Warehousing: type, location.
  • i. Final price(s): must incorporate the cost of getting the product to the final customer: shipping cost, inland transportation cost, insurance, tariffs, local taxes, markups, and desired local markup.
  • j. Terms of sale: e.g. Ex Works, FOB, CIF.
  • k. Payment method(s): e.g. cash in advance, open account, or letter of credit.
  • l. Marketing budget: selling expense, marketing communications expense, distribution expense, product cost, other costs.
  • m. Resource requirements: finance, personnel, production capacity.
  • Class: this is just an example list; market goals, product, marketing, packaging, customisation. From 200 countries you end with one and then set specific goals for your product in that country.

Slide 40: Strategy framework, Where?

  • The flow with Set main goals and objectives, Select potential markets, Set country/market specific goals boxed as COUNTRY/MARKET SELECTION: Where?; input READY?; Entry strategy highlighted as the next session (How?).

Slide 41: Key takeaways

  • 1. Systematic analysis beats intuition. Use frameworks (CAGE, Porter) to reduce bias and risk.
  • 2. Progressive screening saves resources. Eliminate unsuitable markets early, focus deep analysis on genuine opportunities.
  • 3. Alignment is critical. Company capabilities must match market opportunities. One strength cannot compensate for weaknesses.
  • 4. Risk-return trade-off matters. Higher opportunity often means higher complexity. Match entry mode to your risk tolerance.

Slide 42: Closing

  • Górecka quote repeated, then: "Get it right, and unlock global growth."

Part 2: Ghemawat, "Distance Still Matters: The Hard Reality of Global Expansion" (HBR, September 2001, reprint R0108K)

Idea in brief

  • Companies routinely overestimate the attractiveness of foreign markets because they are dazzled by size and use tools that count only potential sales. Distance has four dimensions: cultural, administrative/political, geographic, economic. Different types of distance affect different industries differently (religion shapes food preferences but not cement). The more two countries differ on these dimensions, the riskier the market; similarities suggest potential (a common currency boosts trade more than 300 percent).

Star TV: the opening failure

  • Launched 1991: deliver TV to a "media-starved" Asian audience, targeting the top 5 percent of Asia's socioeconomic pyramid, a newly rich elite that could pay and was an attractive advertising market. Because English was the second language of most targets, Star would use cheap, readily available English-language programming instead of investing in local content, and satellites would sidestep geographic distance.
  • Rupert Murdoch's News Corporation bought out Star's founders for USD 825 million between 1993 and 1995, attracted by leveraging the Twentieth Century Fox film library across Asia.
  • Results: fiscal year to 30 June 1999, loss of USD 141 million pretax on revenues of USD 111 million; losses in fiscal 1996 to 1999 about USD 500 million, not counting joint ventures such as Phoenix TV in China; no positive operating profit expected until 2002.
  • Two mistakes identified later in the article: (1) ignoring cultural distance: assuming TV was culture-insensitive, despite European evidence that mass audiences in countries large enough to support local content prefer local programming; China and India would have needed heavy localisation ("TV is hardly cement"). (2) Ignoring administrative and political sensitivities: foreign ownership of broadcasting is politically loaded everywhere (Murdoch himself had to become a US citizen to buy the stations that became Fox). Shortly after the acquisition Murdoch declared satellite TV "an unambiguous threat to totalitarian regimes everywhere"; the Chinese government then banned reception of foreign satellite TV. China accounts for nearly 60 percent of Star's potential customers.

Country portfolio analysis (CPA) and why it fails

  • CPA: the "hoary but still widely used" technique. Plots actual and potential markets on a grid: per capita income on one axis, a product performance measure (often penetration rate) on the other; bubble size = total market size (GDP or absolute consumption). It focuses on national GDP, consumer wealth and propensity to consume, so it places all the emphasis on potential sales and ignores the costs and risks of doing business in the new market.
  • Most of those costs and risks come from distance, and distance is not only geographic.

Measuring the impact of distance: Frankel and Rose

  • Economists use the gravity theory of trade: trade rises with economic size and falls with distance. Gravity models explain up to two thirds of observed variation in trade between country pairs. Jeffrey Frankel and Andrew Rose (working paper, May 2000) estimated these effects.
Distance attributeChange in international trade
Income level: GDP per capita, 1 percent increase+0.7 percent
Economic size: GDP, 1 percent increase+0.8 percent
Physical distance, 1 percent increase-1.1 percent
Physical size, 1 percent increase (*)-0.2 percent
Access to ocean (*)+50 percent
Common border+80 percent
Common language+200 percent
Common regional trading bloc+330 percent
Colony-colonizer relationship+900 percent
Common colonizer+190 percent
Common polity+300 percent
Common currency+340 percent
  • (*) Footnote: the starred estimates exclude the last four variables in the table.
  • Headline facts in the text: trade between countries 5,000 miles apart is only 20 percent of what it would be at 1,000 miles; a company trades ten times as much with a former colony; common currency +340 percent; common trading bloc +330 percent; shared language makes trade three times greater.
  • "The death of distance" (IT and global communications shrinking the world) is not just wrong for business, it is dangerous. CPA must be tempered by an evaluation of distance.
  • Industries differ: geographic distance matters most for heavy or bulky products and for operations needing coordination of dispersed people; cultural distance matters for consumer goods and media but far less for cement or steel.

Cultural distance

  • Attributes: differences in religion, race/ethnicity, social norms, language; lack of connective ethnic or social networks. Language is easy to see; social norms (deep, unspoken principles guiding everyday choices) are nearly invisible even to those who follow them.
  • Example of a hidden norm: Chinese tolerance of copyright infringement. William Alford (To Steal a Book Is an Elegant Offense, Stanford, 1995) traces it not to communism but to a Confucian precept favouring replication of past intellectual work ("I transmit rather than create; I believe in and love the Ancients"). In the 1920s Merriam Webster found the Commercial Press in Shanghai already distributing its own version of Merriam Webster's bilingual dictionary; a Chinese court imposed a small fine for using the seal but did not stop publication.
  • How culture usually creates distance: it shapes choices between substitute products through feature preferences. Colour tastes: the word "red" in Russian also means beautiful. Consumer durables are especially sensitive: the Japanese prefer small cars and appliances, a norm in countries where space is valued.
  • Sometimes products touch identity and whole categories are affected: food is sensitive to religion (Hindus do not eat beef); in Japan rice carries enormous cultural baggage while Americans treat it as a commodity.
  • Industries most affected (CAGE table): high linguistic content (TV); products affecting cultural or national identity (foods); products whose features vary by size (cars), standards (electrical appliances), packaging; products carrying country-specific quality associations (wines).

Administrative or political distance

  • Attributes: absence of colonial ties; absence of shared monetary or political association; political hostility; government policies; institutional weakness.
  • Effects: colony-colonizer links boost trade by 900 percent (Britain and the Commonwealth, France and the franc zone of West Africa, Spain and Latin America). Preferential trading arrangements, common currency and political union each raise trade by more than 300 percent. The European Union is the leading example of deliberately reducing administrative distance. Ties must be friendly: India and Pakistan share colonial history, a border and linguistic ties, yet trade is virtually nil.
  • Unilateral measures: policies of individual governments are the most common barriers to cross-border competition. Sometimes the home country is the problem: US prohibitions on bribery and health, safety and environmental rules dampen US firms' international business. More commonly the target government raises barriers: tariffs, trade quotas, restrictions on FDI, and preferences for domestic competitors (subsidies, favouritism in regulation and procurement).
  • Governments protect a domestic industry when it is:
    • a large employer (large voting blocs: Europe's farmers);
    • a national champion (symbol of modernity and competitiveness: Boeing versus Airbus could spark a trade war; the more a government has invested in an industry, the more protective it is);
    • vital to national security (high-tech such as telecommunications and aerospace; the FBI delayed Deutsche Telekom's acquisition of VoiceStream);
    • a producer of staples (food staples, fuel, electricity);
    • a producer of an "entitlement" good or service (health care; governments set quality standards and control prices);
    • an exploiter of natural resources (physical assets seen as national heritage; foreigners seen as robbers; nationalisation a constant threat to oil and mining multinationals);
    • involving high sunk-cost commitments (oil refineries, aluminium smelters, railway lines; irreversibility creates scope for hold-ups once the investment is made).
  • Weak institutional infrastructure (corruption, social conflict) depresses trade and investment more than any explicit policy or restriction; a strong legal system makes a country much more attractive.
  • Industries most affected (CAGE table): government involvement is high in staples (electricity), "entitlements" (drugs), large employers (farming), large suppliers to government (mass transportation), national champions (aerospace), vital to national security (telecommunications), exploiters of natural resources (oil, mining), subject to high sunk costs (infrastructure).

Sidebar: How far away is China, really?

  • Survey of nearly 100 multinationals: 54 percent said performance in China was "worse than planned" versus 25 percent "better than planned"; 62 percent had overestimated market potential.
  • Culturally China is far from nearly everywhere: many dialects hard for foreigners, limited local foreign-language skills; business culture based on personal connections (guanxi) versus Westerners' transaction focus; Chinese consumers may be "home-biased" (less preference for foreign brands than in India); greater China plays a disproportionate role in China's economic relations.
  • Administrative barriers probably matter more: American Chamber of Commerce members flagged market-access restrictions, high taxes and customs duties as the biggest barriers to profitability; high state involvement, loss-making state-owned enterprises and technically insolvent state banks. Transparency International 2000: China 63rd of 90 (a rating of 1 = least perceived corruption). Standard and Poor's political-risk ranking 5 in 2000, with 6 the worst.
  • Conclusion: China is a big market, but distance matters along many dimensions.

Geographic distance

  • Attributes: physical remoteness; lack of a common border; lack of sea or river access; size of the country; average within-country distances to borders; topography; weak transportation or communication links (man-made infrastructure); differences in climate.
  • Effects: transport cost for low value-to-weight or bulk products (steel, cement); costs for fragile or perishable products rise with distance.
  • Intangibles too: cross-border equity flows fall significantly as geographic distance rises. This cannot be transport cost (capital is not physical); it is explained by the level of information infrastructure (crudely measured by telephone traffic and the number of branches of multinational banks).
  • Firms that find geography a barrier to trade are expected to switch to direct investment in local plant, but research suggests geographic distance also dampens investment flows. Keep both information networks and transport infrastructure in mind.
  • Industries most affected (CAGE table): low value-to-weight or bulk ratio (cement); fragile or perishable (glass, fruit); communications and connectivity important (financial services); local supervision and operational requirements high (many services).

Economic distance

  • The wealth or income of consumers is the most important economic attribute creating distance. Rich countries do relatively more cross-border activity relative to their size, mostly with other rich countries (positive correlation between per capita GDP and trade). Poor countries also trade more with rich countries than with other poor ones.
  • Behind this are differences in cost and quality of financial, human and other resources. Two strategies:
    • Replication: companies relying on economies of experience, scale and standardization should focus on countries with similar economic profiles, because they must replicate their business model. Wal-Mart in India would be a very different business from Wal-Mart in the United States; Wal-Mart in Canada is virtually a carbon copy.
    • Arbitrage: competitive advantage from exploiting cost and price differentials between markets; industries whose major cost components vary widely across countries (garments, footwear, where labour cost matters) target countries with different economic profiles.
  • For both, supply chain and distribution channel disparities are a significant barrier. A study found that distribution margins within the United States (domestic transport, wholesaling, retailing) are a bigger barrier to imports into the US, on average, than international transport costs and tariffs combined.
  • Cross-country complexity puts a premium on responsiveness and agility; replicators struggle to match locally focused competitors. In home appliances, Maytag (few geographies) produced far better investor returns than Electrolux and Whirlpool, whose spread cost them simplicity and profitability.
  • Industries most affected (CAGE table): demand varies with income (cars); economies of standardization or scale important (mobile phones); labour and other factor cost differences salient (garments); distribution or business systems different (insurance); companies need to be responsive and agile (home appliances).

Industry sensitivity to distance (Ghemawat and Rajiv Mallick)

  • Method: regressed trade between every pair of countries in each of 70 industries (SIC) on each dimension of distance. Results confirm the need to separate the components: electricity is highly sensitive to administrative and geographic distance but not at all to cultural distance.
Dimension (measure)More sensitiveLess sensitive
Cultural (linguistic ties)meat and meat preparations; cereals and cereal preparations; miscellaneous edible products and preparations; tobacco and tobacco products; office machines and automatic data-processing equipmentphotographic apparatuses, optical goods, watches; road vehicles; cork and wood; metalworking machinery; electricity current
Administrative (preferential trading agreements)gold, nonmonetary; electricity current; coffee, tea, cocoa, spices; textile fibers; sugar, sugar preparations and honeygas, natural and manufactured; travel goods, handbags; footwear; sanitary, plumbing, heating and lighting fixtures; furniture and furniture parts
Geographic (physical remoteness)electricity current; gas, natural and manufactured; paper, paperboard; live animals; sugar, sugar preparations and honeypulp and waste paper; photographic apparatuses, optical goods, watches; telecommunications and sound-recording apparatuses; coffee, tea, cocoa, spices; gold, nonmonetary
Economic (wealth differences)Economic distance decreases trade: nonferrous metals; manufactured fertilizers; meat and meat preparations; iron and steel; pulp and waste paperEconomic distance increases trade: coffee, tea, cocoa, spices; animal oils and fats; office machines and automatic data-processing equipment; power-generating machinery and equipment; photographic apparatuses, optical goods, watches
  • Note the economic column is different in kind: it does not rank sensitivity but splits industries into those where wealth differences cut trade (replication-type goods) and those where wealth differences raise trade (arbitrage-type goods such as coffee, tea, cocoa, spices).

Case study in distance: Tricon Restaurants International (TRI)

  • Tricon manages Pizza Hut, Taco Bell and KFC; spun off from Pepsico in 1997. TRI is its international arm, based in Dallas.
  • At spin-off: restaurants in 27 countries; two thirds of revenues and an even higher share of profits from just seven markets; limited operating cash flow plus Tricon's debt service left TRI with less than one tenth of the money that McDonald's International had to invest outside the US. In 1998 president Pete Bassi decided to rationalise by concentrating equity investment in a limited number of markets.
  • CPA chart ("A Flawed Approach"): 20 non-US fast-food markets plotted by per capita income (x axis, 0 to 40,000 dollars) against per capita fast-food consumption (y axis, 0 to 400 dollars), bubble size = total consumption. Key: 1 Japan, 2 Korea, 3 Taiwan, 4 Puerto Rico, 5 Malaysia, 6 Australia, 7 Thailand, 8 New Zealand, 9 South Africa, 10 Singapore, 11 Saudi Arabia, 12 Poland, 13 Belgium, 14 France, 15 Germany, 16 Spain, 17 UK, 18 Canada, 19 Mexico, 20 China. Puerto Rico has the highest per capita consumption, Canada next; the big bubbles (biggest opportunities) sit centre-right: Japan and Germany the largest. On CPA, Mexico (total fast-food consumption USD 700 million) ranks 16th of 20, which would imply disposing of the Mexican investments.
  • Adjusted for distance: adjusting each country's consumption for geographic distance from Dallas, Mexico's consumption falls less than any other country's and Mexico jumps to 6th. Adding the common land border and membership in a trade agreement with the US pushes Mexico to 2nd, after Canada. Not all adjustments are positive: adjusting for common language (which Mexico lacks) drops Mexico to a tie for second with the United Kingdom. Mexico, which had been less than one tenth the size of Japan and Germany, ends up the second largest opportunity. Bassi: "Mexico is one of TRI's top two or three priorities."
  • Company-specific features change distance too: firms with many cosmopolitan managers are less affected by cultural differences. TRI already owned more than four fifths of its Mexican outlets and had a 38 percent share of the local market, well ahead of McDonald's, making Mexico even more attractive.

Closing

  • Factoring industry effects of distance is only a first step; a full analysis considers how the company's own characteristics increase or reduce distance. The CAGE framework is necessarily subjective but an important complement to the usual portfolio tools. "Technology may indeed be making the world a smaller place, but it is not eliminating the very real, and often very high, costs of distance."
  • Further reading listed with the article: Sebenius, "The Hidden Challenge of Cross-Border Negotiations" (HBR March 2002), on how negotiation styles differ across regions; Porter, "Clusters and the New Economics of Competition" (HBR Nov-Dec 1998), on how geographic, cultural and institutional proximity creates clusters (Silicon Valley, Hollywood) that raise productivity, drive innovation and spawn new businesses.

What the professor added in class

Framing and goals

  • Selecting the country is one of the most critical steps; done wrongly you spend lots of time and money analysing something useless.
  • Goals must be SMART and aligned with resources and capabilities; he gave the examples under slide 6 (sell more, customer satisfaction, painted warehouses, 6/12/18 months) and the COVID flexibility example.
  • When a project loses direction because too many people give input: weekly review meetings against the plan, not monthly.
  • The number of countries: about 190 to 200 depending on the count (Andorra and similar).
  • Three things in the back of your mind during the whole funnel: cost, resource constraints (funding, team, assets) and main goals.

Earliest and preliminary screening

  • URBAR story (slide 11): industrial equipment maker in Spain, 85 percent of sales in Spain, crisis, engineers who spoke no English, so Spanish-speaking Latin America became the shortlist. One or two criteria from your business model take you from 200 countries to 8 to 12.
  • Preliminary screening: macro dynamics of the country (PESTEL) and how your company fits them.
  • EXAM: he said he would review CAGE because the exam and the group work rely on it: the group report is group work; the individual grade is the exam. (He also said the syllabus group project due that day was postponed and he would email the new arrangement.)

CAGE in class

  • Video: shared language, trading bloc, border and similar income can mean 10 to 15 times more trade; Canada is the US's biggest trading partner though only about the tenth largest economy.
  • Data problem: if you cannot get enough data points for one ingredient, drop it and use an alternative indicator.
  • Administrative: defence and weapons as an example of government reluctance; corruption index; how much corruption matters depends on how the company wants to do business.
  • Bribery discussion (a student asked about an official demanding an under-the-table payment in an otherwise perfect country): it depends on the company's policy; Spanish companies must sign anti-bribery policies, gifts over about EUR 30 must be returned; another student said some US companies in India pay an external agency a fee to deal with such things; the professor noted it is complicated and systemic ("everyone does it, so it is normal" was the student view, not his recommendation).
  • Geographic: internal logistics (port, boat, bus), poor connections, landlocked countries, warehousing and distribution.
  • Cultural examples from students: in Ethiopia people signal "I understand" with a sharp inhale instead of "uh-huh"; in Japan arriving exactly on time counts as late and business cards are given with two hands; in Germany and much of Europe contacting people after hours or on weekends or holidays is rude, whereas in the US you are expected to respond (investment banking and consulting are another story); he recalled a Bank of America banker in Spain calling on a Sunday about a syndicated loan; in India the lunch hour is a full hour; Walmart's US self-checkout would not work in India, it is cheaper to pay a cashier; Caterpillar gives three free meals a day in India but not in the US; McDonald's in India rebuilt the menu around chicken and vegetarian options (no beef).
  • Reverse view from a student: instead of asking whether the country fits your product, ask whether the product fits the country; many companies run an "export only" product line with different regulations and packaging.
  • After CAGE you should be down to three or four countries.

In-depth screening and final selection

  • Take the two countries left and understand the industry there: attractiveness (Porter's five forces, to be covered in about two weeks) and barriers to entry; the ideal is low capital: home-made product, minimum customisation, shipped, local logistics partner.
  • Detailed market analysis: do you need to adapt the product, language, packaging; will local customers resist a foreign product; can you match local prices and still have margin or EBITDA after shipping and distribution.
  • Final selection: compare the two countries on macro specifics, industry success factors and attractiveness (including barriers and cost of entry) against your resources, capabilities and goals; find the gap; it is very unlikely a country matches fully; ask how complicated the gap is to correct.
  • Then set specific goals for the chosen market (market, product, marketing, packaging, customisation).

Likely exam angles

  • Know that the course map is global trends, benefits and reasons, ready?, where?, how?, and that this session is "where?".
  • Know that the strategy design process is strategic analysis, set main goals and objectives, select potential markets, set country/market specific goals, entry strategy, implementation.
  • Know that SMART means specific, measurable, achievable, relevant, time-limited, plus some flexibility as priorities change (COVID).
  • Know the five-stage funnel in order: earliest screening, preliminary screening (PESTEL, macro), second screening (CAGE, distance), in-depth screening (Porter five forces and barriers to entry, plus detailed market analysis), final selection (competitive advantage equation).
  • Know that earliest, preliminary and second screening cover country macro specifics; in-depth screening covers country industry specifics.
  • Know that cost of entry, resource constraints and main goals and objectives are considered during the whole process.
  • Know that CAGE = cultural, administrative (and political), geographic, economic (wealth) distance, from Ghemawat's "Distance Still Matters" (HBR 2001), and that its purpose is to identify and prioritize differences between countries and show how easy it is to replicate the business abroad.
  • Know which industries each distance most affects: cultural = TV (linguistic content), food (national identity), consumer durables (Japan small cars and appliances), wines (quality associations); administrative = telecommunications (national security), aerospace (national reputation), taxi services (regulation), electricity (staples), drugs (entitlements), farming (employer); geographic = heavy or bulky goods such as cement and steel, glass and fruit (fragile, perishable), financial services (communications); economic = cars (demand varies with income), garments (labour cost), mobile phones (scale), insurance (distribution systems).
  • Know the Frankel and Rose numbers: colony-colonizer +900 percent, common currency +340, common trading bloc +330, common polity +300, common language +200, common colonizer +190, common border +80, ocean access +50; physical distance 1 percent up cuts trade 1.1 percent; GDP 1 percent up adds 0.8, GDP per capita 1 percent up adds 0.7.
  • Know that trade between countries 5,000 miles apart is 20 percent of what it would be at 1,000 miles, and that gravity models explain up to two thirds of trade variation.
  • Know the Star TV facts: launched 1991, News Corp paid USD 825 million (1993 to 1995), lost about USD 500 million in fiscal 1996 to 1999, USD 141 million loss on USD 111 million revenue in FY1999, assumed Asians wanted English programming, Murdoch's "threat to totalitarian regimes" remark led China to ban foreign satellite TV, China is nearly 60 percent of Star's potential customers.
  • Know that CPA plots per capita income against product penetration with bubble size for market size and is flawed because it counts only potential sales and ignores the costs and risks of distance.
  • Know the Tricon case: Pizza Hut, Taco Bell, KFC, spun off from Pepsico 1997, 27 countries, seven markets gave two thirds of revenue, less than one tenth of McDonald's investment money, president Pete Bassi 1998; Mexico 16th of 20 on CPA (USD 700 million consumption), 6th after geographic adjustment, 2nd after Canada with border and trade agreement, tied 2nd with the UK after the common-language adjustment; TRI owned more than four fifths of its Mexican outlets with a 38 percent share.
  • Know the China sidebar: 54 percent worse than planned, 25 percent better, 62 percent overestimated potential; guanxi; Transparency International 63rd of 90 in 2000; S&P political risk 5 of 6.
  • Know that Wal-Mart Canada is a carbon copy and Wal-Mart India would be a different business (replicators go to similar economies; arbitrageurs such as garments and footwear go to different ones).
  • Know that US domestic distribution margins are a bigger import barrier than international transport and tariffs combined, and that Maytag beat Electrolux and Whirlpool by staying focused.
  • Know that electricity is highly sensitive to administrative and geographic distance but not to cultural distance, and that the most culturally sensitive industries are meat, cereals, edible products, tobacco and office machines.
  • Know that weak institutions and corruption depress trade and investment more than explicit administrative policies, and that India and Pakistan trade almost nothing despite shared history, border and language.
  • Know the barriers-to-entry lists: high (less attractive) = high capital requirements, strong brand loyalty, economies of scale, proprietary technology; low (more attractive) = easy market access, low capital needs, fragmented competition, growing demand.
  • Know the competitive advantage equation: company resources and capabilities matched with country specifics and industry success factors; all three must align; strength in one cannot compensate for weakness in another; compare countries on country specifics, industry success factors and attractiveness, and cost of entry; look for match or gap and how complex the gap is to correct.
  • Know the country-specific goal areas, especially terms of sale (Ex Works, FOB, CIF), payment methods (cash in advance, open account, letter of credit), documentation (bill of lading, commercial invoice, export declaration, certificate of origin), and that in most cases the firm ships by ocean and uses a freight forwarder.
  • Know the four key takeaways: systematic analysis beats intuition; progressive screening saves resources; alignment is critical; risk-return trade-off, match entry mode to risk tolerance.
  • Know the Corruption Perceptions Index on the slide is Transparency International 2020, 180 countries (Denmark and New Zealand 88, US 67, Spain 62, China 42, Mexico 31, Somalia and South Sudan 12), and that the Coface map (January 2018, 160 countries) rates business defaulting risk from A1 (very low) to E (extreme).

Traps and look-alikes

  • Earliest versus preliminary screening: earliest starts from your own business model (URBAR: Spanish-speaking countries); preliminary is the macro country view with PESTEL. Both are "macro specifics" but only preliminary uses PESTEL.
  • Second versus in-depth screening: second = CAGE distance, a country-level comparison; in-depth = industry-level (Porter five forces, barriers to entry, detailed market analysis). CAGE is not an industry tool and Porter is not a distance tool.
  • Country macro specifics versus country industry specifics versus company specifics: the first three funnel stages are macro, in-depth is industry, and setting country/market specific goals is company specifics.
  • Administrative versus cultural distance: language, religion, social norms, ethnicity are cultural; colonial ties, currency, trading blocs, political hostility, corruption, legal systems, tariffs are administrative. India and Pakistan are an administrative (hostility) case even though they share a language.
  • Geographic distance versus physical distance: geographic includes size, internal distances, sea or river access, topography, climate, time zones and transport and communication infrastructure, not just miles.
  • Economic distance versus consumer wealth: wealth or income is the most important economic attribute, but the dimension also covers cost and quality of natural, financial and human resources, inputs, infrastructure and knowledge.
  • Replication versus arbitrage: replicators (scale, standardisation, Wal-Mart) want similar economies; arbitrageurs (garments, footwear) want different economies. Economic distance hurts the first and helps the second.
  • Cultural distance "most affects" examples: TV (linguistic content), food (identity), cars and appliances (size), wines (quality association). Cement is the standard example of a product insensitive to culture but sensitive to geography.
  • Administrative "most affects" examples on the deck versus the article: deck gives telecommunications (national security), aerospace (national reputation), taxi services (regulation); the article's longer list adds electricity, drugs, farming, mass transportation, oil and mining, infrastructure.
  • Frankel and Rose magnitudes: colony-colonizer (+900) is far bigger than common currency (+340), trading bloc (+330), polity (+300), language (+200), colonizer shared (+190), border (+80), ocean (+50). Do not confuse "common colonizer" (+190) with "colony-colonizer relationship" (+900).
  • Star TV numbers: USD 825 million is what News Corp paid; USD 500 million is the 1996 to 1999 loss; USD 141 million is the FY1999 loss; USD 111 million is FY1999 revenue.
  • Tricon rankings: 16th of 20 (CPA), 6th (geographic distance only), 2nd after Canada (border and trade agreement), tied 2nd with the UK (after common-language adjustment). Mexico's company-specific factor was four fifths ownership and 38 percent share, not the ranking.
  • China sidebar percentages: 54 percent worse than planned (versus 25 percent better) and 62 percent overestimated potential; 63rd of 90 on corruption (2000); S&P political risk 5 of 6 (6 worst).
  • CPA axes: per capita income on x, per capita consumption (penetration) on y, bubble = total market size. CPA is not wrong about size; it is incomplete because it ignores distance costs.
  • High versus low barriers to entry: high barriers make a market less attractive for a new entrant; low barriers more attractive. (Do not mix with the Session 6 view where high barriers protect an incumbent.)
  • Corruption index editions: the slide shows TI 2020 with 180 countries; the deck's hidden file name says 2017 with 170. Answer 2020 and 180 if asked what the slide shows. In the article, the China figure is the 2000 index with 90 countries.
  • Coface versus Transparency International: Coface rates business defaulting (country) risk A1 to E; TI scores perceived public-sector corruption 0 to 100.
  • Match or gap: the final selection does not expect a perfect match; it asks whether the gap can be corrected and how complex that is.
Session 9 · complete notes · 7365 words

Session 9: How? Country entry alternatives (Prof. Pablo Neira)

This unit is the last step of Neira's internationalization sequence (global trends, benefits and reasons, ready?, where?, how?). It catalogues the ways a company can enter a chosen country, arranged on a ladder from lowest to highest resource commitment, risk and return: indirect export, direct export, contractual agreements and foreign direct investment (FDI). Each rung has sub-types with their own advantages and risks. What the professor stressed most in class: who "owns" the customer under each intermediary (agent versus distributor), doing real due diligence on any intermediary or partner, always writing duration and exit terms into contracts, that licensing and franchising can be combined (his own National Geographic experience), that alliances rest on complementarity and trust (60 percent fail), and that FDI is the most risky and most expensive route but also the one that keeps the whole margin, so it is a realistic option only after you know the market as an exporter. The deck was taught across 28 September (indirect and direct export, contractual agreements) and 5 October 2026 (alliances and FDI).

Slide-by-slide

Slide 1: Internationalization strategy (roadmap)

  • Five boxes in an arrow: Global trends, Benefits and reasons to internationalize, Ready to internationalize?, Where?, How?
  • This deck covers the last box, How? (the image highlights Where?, the previous deck, but the title slide that follows makes the subject of this deck clear).

Slide 2: Title

  • "How to Expand Internationally", Prof. Pablo Neira, IE University. HOW? Country Entry Alternatives.

Slide 3: Entry strategies ladder

  • Four levels, top to bottom: Indirect export, Direct export, Contractual agreements, Foreign direct investments.
  • A vertical arrow beside them runs from low (indirect export) to high (FDI) on three dimensions:
    1. Resource commitment
    2. Risk
    3. Return / benefits
  • Point: the further down the ladder you go, the more you commit and risk, and the more you can earn.

Slide 4: 1. Indirect export, a) Importers

  • Indirect export: the company sells to a buyer (cross-border intermediaries or middlemen) which in turn exports the product. These intermediaries normally have deep expertise in a specific product or service and market.
  • a) Importers (also called export management companies): they work as the export department of the company.
    • Familiar with local conditions; help find customers, distribution channels, handle documentation, clear goods through customs and provide after-sales service.
    • Marketing: may take full or partial responsibility for promotion of the goods.
    • Can work under the name of the company, so customers are often unaware they are not dealing directly with the company.
    • May receive exclusive rights, either to sell in a specific market or for a specific product line.
    • A low cost option.

Slide 5: 1. Indirect export, b) Agents and representatives

  • An agent is an individual or firm you employ, usually on commission, to sell your product to wholesalers, retailers and sometimes end users in the target market.
  • Agents do not buy your products.
  • Customers "are" of the exporter. Agents may also handle products that compete with yours.
  • A representative is a specialized agent who operates within a specific geographic area and/or goods.
Advantages of agentsDisadvantages of agents
Low entry costLow profitability of the transactions
Requires low staffingHigh dependence on the intermediary
Intermediary overcomes difficulties of entryInability to gain international experience
Gives immediate presence in the target market
Gives you control over product/service

Slide 6: 1. Indirect export, c) Distributors

  • Distributors buy your product from you and then sell it on to the end users.
  • They may handle competing products.
  • Usually they will want exclusive rights for a specific territory.
  • Customers "are" of the distributor.
  • Can perform various tasks, not only sale: logistics, customs, distribution.
  • Picture: the website of URBAR, a Spanish distributor showing the products it distributes (vibrating motors, pumps, hydraulic equipment). This is the professor's own company, used as the example of a distributor.

Slide 7: 1. Indirect export, d) Trading companies

  • Give full service: cover the sale process from purchasing, logistics and customs to warehousing and selling.
  • They buy from you on behalf of foreign clients: no "loyalty" to the exporter; they seek the best terms for their clients.
  • The largest and most extended are in Japan: the Sogo Shoshas.
    • Conglomerates that sell everything from metals to grains and textiles.
    • Represent 50% of Japan's exports and 75% of imports.

Slide 8: Largest Sogo Shoshas

  • Logos of Itochu, Sumitomo, Marubeni, Mitsui & Co., Mitsubishi Corporation.
  • Bar chart, 2019 market value in billion US dollars: Mitsubishi 42.5, Mitsui 27.7, Itochu 27.5, Sumitomo 17.9, Marubeni 12.3, Toyota Tsusho 11.6, Sojitz 4.3.
  • Point: these trading houses are huge companies in their own right; if you want to sell into Japan you typically go through one of them.

Slide 9: 1. Indirect export (video still)

  • A still frame of a video (London skyline at sunset). No written content; a video was shown in class (unclear on the slide what the video was about).

Slide 10: Correct channel selection is key

  • Exercise due diligence when selecting the intermediary:
    1. Be sure they have the marketing knowledge, industry expertise, financial capacity and facilities (showrooms, staff, warehousing) required to represent you properly.
    2. Find out if they pay promptly.
    3. If they represent products that compete head-to-head with yours, find out how they will resolve this potential conflict.
    4. Always check their reputations and references.

Slide 11: Set goals for the international trade

  1. Volume, market share, profit margin requirements.
  2. Financial and personnel commitments to developing the trade.
    • Capital requirements: the cash flow associated (for example providing initial inventories).
    • Cost: investment on developing the channel and on maintaining it.
  3. Degree of control, terms of sale and channel ownership.
  4. Coverage: geography and market segments.
  5. Duration / continuity with the intermediaries.

Slides 12 and 13: Summary of entry strategies (build slides)

  • Indirect export = Importer, Agent, Distributor, Trading house. Left margin repeats the three selection criteria: resource commitment, risk, return. Slide 13 highlights Direct export as the next block.

Slide 14: Direct export (1 to 3)

  1. Internet: initial focus on the home market, but companies started receiving unplanned orders from other countries, which made them actively redesign websites and catalogues in new languages and adapt them to specific markets.
  2. Wholesaler: selling to wholesalers, department stores, large supermarkets and purchasing groups. It is not a direct sale to the final customer.
  3. Branded manufacturers: a manufacturer makes and sells via a retailer chain in the foreign market, maintaining the brand name (example: Lee and Wrangler).
  4. Pictures: a confectionery wholesaler advert ("National coverage with award winning localised service") and a Wrangler in-store display.

Slide 15: Direct export, 4. Export department (B2B)

  • Particularly for high-technology and/or big value industrial products with a complex sales process.
  • Used when the company has developed international trade via indirect exports to such a level that it pays to manage it internally.
  • Picture: a large mobile crushing/screening plant, the kind of high-value industrial equipment that needs the company's own export department.

Slide 16: Summary (build slide)

  • Indirect export: 1. Importer, 2. Trading house, 3. Agent, 4. Distributor. Direct export: 1. Internet, 2. Wholesaler, 3. Branded manufacturers, 4. Export department (B2B). Contractual agreements highlighted next.

Slide 17: Contractual agreements, definition and types

  • Long term associations between a company and another company (or a government) in a foreign market.
  • Involve the transfer of knowledge (technology, process, trademarks and/or human skills), construction or manufacturing capabilities.
  • Five types:
    1. Turn-key projects
    2. Subcontracting
    3. Licensing
    4. Franchising
    5. Strategic alliances (JV)

Slide 18: 1.A Turn-key operations

  • Any complete construction of any industrial plant or infrastructure abroad. The contractor builds it and hands over the key.
  • Pictures: a motorway under construction and a hydroelectric dam.

Slide 19: 1.B Concessions

  • Only the heading and pictures: a refuse collection truck and a waste recycling plant. The point (explained in class) is that a concession is a long-term right granted by a public body (for example a municipality) to run a service such as waste collection or treatment.

Slide 20: 2. Subcontracting

  • Contractual agreements here are described as long term non-equity associations between a company and another in a foreign market, involving transfer of knowledge (technology, process, trademarks and/or human skills).
  • Subcontracting: subcontracting a local manufacturer to produce your goods.
  • Picture: a GAP hoodie (GAP designs, local manufacturers produce).

Slide 21: Boeing 787 Dreamliner, parts from around the globe

  • A map of the 787 showing which supplier makes each part: wing tips Busan Korea; wing, fixed trailing edge, center wing box and landing gear wheel well Nagoya Japan; moveable trailing edge Melbourne Australia; flap support fairings Busan Korea; tail fin Frederickson WA; tail cone Auburn WA; aft fuselage Busan Korea and Charleston SC; horizontal stabilizer Foggia Italy; center fuselage Grottaglie Italy; passenger entry doors Toulouse France; nacelles Chula Vista CA; mid forward fuselage Nagoya; forward fuselage Wichita KS; cargo access doors Linköping Sweden; wing/body fairing and landing gear doors Winnipeg Canada; landing gear Gloucester UK; fixed and moveable leading edge Tulsa OK; engines GE (Evendale, Ohio) and Rolls Royce (Derby, UK).
  • Suppliers by region: US (Boeing, Spirit, GE, Goodrich), Asia (Fuji, Mitsubishi, Kawasaki, KAL-ASD), Europe (Safran Landing Systems, Rolls Royce, Latécoère, Alenia, Saab).
  • Point: subcontracting at global scale; Boeing is essentially an assembler of parts made by subcontractors worldwide.

Slide 22: 3. Licensing

  • A license is the grant of certain rights to another company: patents, trademarks, brand names, rights to use technology, etc.
  • Allows the other business to use your proprietary technology / intellectual property for specific purposes in a specific country or region.
  • Examples of what can be licensed: patents, domain names, industrial design, confidential information, inventions, database rights, works of authorship, service marks, logos, trademarks, design rights, business or trade names, commercial secrets, computer software.
  • Proprietary technology: all proprietary processes, formulae, inventions, trade secrets, know-how and other proprietary rights used in the development, license, sale, marketing, distribution or maintenance of a product.
  • Intellectual property: the series of rights that creators and other owners (artists, producers, radio broadcasting organisations, etc.) have over the works and benefits that stem from their creation. Includes literary, scientific and artistic creations. Unlike industrial property, intellectual property comes into being at the same time as the creation and does not have to be registered; this is known as "copyright".

Slide 23: OLAYAN

  • Picture of a Coca-Cola bottling line with the word OLAYAN. Olayan is a Saudi group that bottles Coca-Cola under licence: the Coca-Cola Company supplies the concentrate and the brand, local licensed bottlers produce and distribute.

Slide 24: 3. Licensing (cont.), advantages, risks and the National Geographic example

Advantages of licensingRisks of licensing
Low capital requirementChoosing wrong partners
Works where import restrictions forbid other ways of entryQuality and other production problems
Key in countries sensitive to foreign ownershipPayment problems
Loss of marketing control
  • Example on the slide: a National Geographic store and shopping bag. Terms of the licence the professor's company held:
    • Worldwide rights to use the brand name on any product, subject to prior National Geographic Society approval.
    • An annual fee.
    • A % commission on sales.

Slides 25 and 26: Co-marketing

  • Co-marketing: lets you and your partner take advantage of each other's existing distribution networks and domestic markets. It is in fact joint promotional activities.
  • Pictures: a skier in a Red Bull helmet (Red Bull with GoPro), Starbucks with Spotify ("Now playing"), Uber with Spotify.
  • Point: two separate products promoted together; no new product is created.

Slide 27: Co-branding

  • Co-branding: two companies agree to create a new product or service combining products already well known in their respective markets.
  • Pictures: Apple Watch Nike+, Philadelphia Milka, Santander Iberia Classic card, Reebok x Bershka trainers, McFlurry M&Ms and McFlurry Kit Kat.

Slide 28: 4. Franchising

  • A form of licensing in which:
    • The franchiser provides a standard package of products, systems and management services.
    • The franchisee provides market knowledge, capital and personal involvement in management, in accordance with the franchising agreement.
  • Provides a blending of skill centralization (at the franchiser) and operational decentralization (at the franchisee).
  • Logos: McDonald's, Pizza Hut, Burger King, KFC, Domino's, Arby's, A&W, Wendy's, Es Teler 77.

Slide 29: 4. Franchising (cont.)

Advantages of franchisingRisks of franchising
Fast system of expansion (fastest of all!)Need to accommodate local culture and taste differences
Low investment requiredControl issues
Normally friendly regulation, as governments foster local ownership, operations and employment

Slide 30: Combined option: licensing and franchising

  • Chain: National Geographic Society (Washington) <-> licensing contract <-> The company (Spain) <-> franchise contract <-> The franchisee.
  • The Spanish company (circled) sits on both sides: it is the licensee of National Geographic and the franchiser of the store operators. Pictures: National Geographic logo and a National Geographic store.

Slide 31: 5. Strategic international alliances, John Browne quote

  • John Browne, CEO of BP: "Any organization that thinks it does everything the best and need not learn from others is incredibly arrogant and foolish. You have to recognize that others may actually know more than you do about something, that you can learn from them."
  • Point: the rationale for alliances is learning and obtaining what you lack.

Slide 32: Alliances and the readiness analysis

  • Reproduces the Session 6 readiness diagram: external analysis (industry situation), internal analysis (company situation), resources and capabilities analysis (Resource Based View, VRAIO framework).
  • "Does the company have capabilities to go international? What uniqueness can we bring into the new markets? Does the company have sufficient resources for international markets? If not, will the company be able to acquire or obtain these in order to properly execute its international business plan?" The phrase "able to acquire or obtain" is circled.
  • Point: an alliance is one way to obtain missing resources and capabilities. Footer reads "Managing MNCs" (the source course).

Slide 33: Strategic international alliances, definition

  • A business relationship established by two or more companies to cooperate out of mutual need and to share/reduce risk in achieving a common objective, towards achieving competitive strength.
  • Allows expanding your business in a current or new market or gaining access to resources that would be difficult to acquire by yourself.
  • Complementarity of partners is crucial.

Slides 34 and 35: 3 key elements that distinguish alliances from other interfirm relationships

  1. Partner companies worry about themselves and their partners because success of the alliance depends on collaborative efforts.
  2. The relationship involves the exchange of knowledge associated with technologies, skills or products.
  3. Trust and cooperation play a key role in the management of the alliance:
    • a) When knowledge is exchanged there is a risk that it could be used opportunistically by one of the partners.
    • b) Reality of strategic alliances: a contract cannot predict all the potential competitive and organizational risks an alliance creates.
    • c) As a result, firms going into an alliance must be prepared to deal with risk, which is why trust is key.

Slide 36: Unavoidable issues with alliances

  • Alliances involve uncertainty and ambiguity: this implies significant coordination costs.
  • The partner relationship will evolve in ways hard to predict. Alliances are formed for strategic reasons and as strategies and competitive environments evolve, so do alliances.
  • The partners will eventually go their separate ways: alliances eventually will end, so firms must be realistic about alliance longevity and termination terms.
  • "Today's ally may be tomorrow's rival."

Slide 37: SIA formation process (steps 1 to 3)

  1. Do I need a SIA? Based on your strategy, do I require special expertise or market presence where an alliance would make sense?
  2. Define form and objectives of the SIA: how should it work to achieve the goals.
  3. Partner selection:
    • Strategic fit: complementarity of partners is key.
    • Organizational fit: you build relationships between people, not just a relationship between your organization and a company. Look for:
      • Good chemistry between key managers
      • Similar corporate cultures and values
      • Partners that value public reputation
      • Compatible control and decision-making systems
      • Common time horizon

Slides 38 and 39: SIA formation process, 4. Contract negotiation: key issues

  1. Are there clearly understood agreed-upon objectives? Each party must understand the other side's reasons for the alliance.
  2. What will be each partner's contribution and rewards; penalties if poor performance; arbitration if necessary?
  3. How will the alliance be integrated with the parent firm's strategy?
  4. Will there be cultural compatibility and organizational fit between the partners?
  5. Does the alliance leverage the complementary strengths of the partners?
  6. What and when will be the exit strategy? Alliances eventually will end; be realistic about alliance longevity.
  7. What will be the monitoring process?
  8. But alliances are difficult to manage: 60% failure.
  9. Main reason: poor selection of alliance partner and lack of trust.

Slide 40: Types of strategic alliances, 1. Equity joint venture

  • The "classic" alliance: two or more firms pool a portion of their resources in a separate, jointly owned organization.
  • Goal: to achieve a specific business objective which may not be achievable by any one partner alone.

Slide 41: Self driving cars: players and alliances

  • Six partnership segments (source: Water Street Partners, news articles and journals):
    • Automakers and technology providers: Google and Ford (Toyota also shown in this column).
    • Two or more automakers: BMW, Audi, Daimler; GM and Honda.
    • Carmaker and ride-sharing firms: GM and Lyft; Volvo and Uber.
    • Academic or government institution: Toyota and MIT; Nissan and NASA.
    • Suppliers and other suppliers or carmakers: Autoliv-Nissin brake systems.
    • Suppliers of carmakers and technology providers: Baidu and Continental; NVIDIA and Bosch.
  • Point: one industry where almost every player has needed an alliance to obtain capabilities it lacks.

Slide 42: Types of strategic alliances, 2. Non-equity alliances

  • A simple partnership that is limited in scope/duration.
  • Involves no exchange of equity and no new company is formed.
  • Examples: technology exchange, joint R&D, joint product development, joint distribution or marketing, among others.
  • Easier to form and dissolve, and typically involve less complex corporate governance and partner management issues.

Slide 43: Non-equity alliances (cont.)

  • Example pictures: General Kinematics (Chicago, vibratory equipment maker) and URBAR (Spain, "from our knowledge and experience we build all kinds of installations related to vibration technology"). A simple partnership limited in scope between the US manufacturer and the professor's Spanish company.

Slide 44: Joint venture, advantages and risks

Advantages of a JVRisks of a JV
Speed of actionPartner opportunistic actions (sharing knowledge)
Risk sharingInability of a partner to execute its share of the agreement
Economies of scale / cost sharingResources dedicated to the relationship
Learning new skills or technologyManagement time required
Exploration of new opportunities
Positive employee reactions

Slide 45: Uber and Volvo

  • Picture of a Volvo XC90 self-driving car with the Uber logo: the carmaker plus ride-sharing alliance from slide 41.

Slide 46: Summary of entry strategies (full)

  • Indirect export: Importer, Trading house, Agent, Distributor.
  • Direct export: Internet, Wholesaler, Branded marketers, Branded manufacturers, Export department (B2B). (Note: "Branded marketers" appears only on the summary slides, not as its own content slide.)
  • Contractual agreements: Turn-key projects, Subcontracting, Licensing, Franchising, Strategic alliances (JV).
  • Foreign direct investments highlighted as the next block. Criteria in the margin: resource commitment, risk, return.

Slide 47: Foreign direct investments

  • An internationalization strategy in which the firm establishes a physical presence abroad.
  • Represents greater resource commitment and entails substantial risk and uncertainty.
  • Advantages: access foreign markets more effectively; serve customers better; can join a global or regional supply chain; secure sources of supply; gain access to new technology.
  • Box: a realistic option after you have established yourself as an exporter and have become familiar with your foreign market.

Slide 48: FDI types: representative office and branch

  • Three chevrons in sequence: Representative office -> Branch (sales office) -> Subsidiary. The side list reads: representative office, sales office, subsidiary fully owned.
  • Representative office:
    • An office opened in a foreign market as a first step for establishing a relationship with potential customers or suppliers.
    • Used only and exclusively in marketing and promotional activities.
    • Cannot conduct production activities or buy or sell directly; it acts only on behalf of the company.
  • Branch (sales office):
    • An extension of the parent company in another country.
    • Carries out the same activities performed by the head office.
    • Does not have a separate legal entity from the parent company.
    • Can perform all of the activities of the parent company, including buying or selling directly.

Slide 49: Subsidiary, and branch versus subsidiary

  • Subsidiary: a company owned by a firm abroad but which operates as a local company with respect to regulations, laws and taxes.
BranchSubsidiary
LegalNot a separate legal entity from the parent companyHas its own legal entity
TaxationDouble taxation agreementsIn the foreign country where it is formed
ActivitiesSame as the parent companyCan be different
Ownership100% by the parent company> 50% to 100%
LiabilitiesExtend to the parent companyLimited to the subsidiary

Slide 50: Two ways to create a subsidiary

  • The subsidiary chevron branches into Green field and Cross border mergers and acquisitions (M&A).

Slide 51: Greenfield versus M&A

  • Greenfield: expanding operations in a foreign market starting from zero; requires obtaining everything locally, from assets to employees.
Greenfield advantagesGreenfield disadvantages
No risk of losing technology to a competitorLengthy process from scratch
Tight control of operationsFaces competition before it is set up
Well perceived: creates jobs in the local marketTime researching beforehand
  • Merger: two businesses are combined into one firm.
  • Acquisition: a firm purchases a % of the target company's stock, normally to achieve control of the local firm.
M&A advantagesM&A disadvantages
Faster start: ability to expand rapidly, immediate access to marketReaction of directors and employees
Shorter payback time: investor gets income from day 1Risks of the acquired firm passed to the acquiring firm
Learn from the acquired company and benefit from its assets

Slide 52: Which entry strategy to choose?

  • Full list of the four levels and their sub-types against an arrow from Low to High.
  • Decide on four criteria:
    1. Resource commitment, and the barriers involved
    2. Risk
    3. Return / benefits
    4. Time frame / speed required (added as a fourth criterion on this final slide)

What the professor added in class

Framing and the ladder (28 Sep)

  • The sequence of the course: global trends, benefits and reasons, ready?, where?, and finally how? Once you have reasons, are ready and know where, "how do I enter into that country? There are so many ways."
  • The list is not exhaustive; which option fits "goes case by case depending on the country" and the product.
  • Up the ladder (indirect export) you need little funding and take little risk, but benefits are lower. Down the ladder (FDI) you need a lot of funding and take more risk, but the benefits can be much higher.
  • A student asked whether online sales without physical presence count: yes, that is direct export via the internet (the Netflix discussion: subscribing from Spain to a service that has no local operations).
  • Student clarification accepted by the professor: indirect export is sending to the market the same product you sell domestically; direct export involves customizing it a little and handling the sale yourself.

Importers

  • The importer says "I will do everything: marketing, handling of the goods, invoicing, the whole process, as much as you tell me to do." The potential customer, for example in Nigeria, will not detect that there is someone in the middle.
  • Very low cost because they work largely on the margin of the goods.
  • All middlemen ask for exclusivity. Reason: they do not want to develop a market for you for six months and then find you gave the same mandate to someone else. "If I do this effort for you, give me exclusive rights for a period of time."

Agents and representatives

  • An agent can be a single person. The agent tells customers "I work for this company, it has these products, I can put you in contact." Once the contact is made, the company deals directly with the customer. The agent finds customers and connects you; the agent cannot close on your behalf without telling you.
  • Paid on commission; sometimes a small fixed or retainer fee plus commission. If nothing sells, the agent earns nothing.
  • Because you must come in with attractive prices to win those customers, the margins are low: that is the low profitability disadvantage.
  • Immediate presence: with the right agent, "in one month you will already be talking to potential customers."
  • The agent is not responsible for execution: no logistics, no distribution. You may still need an importer or distributor alongside the agent, which can conflict with exclusivity someone else has asked for.
  • Agents also ask for exclusivity, often renewed on an annual basis.
  • Dependence is total: if you chose the wrong agent you discover it after eight months of weak leads, and you are locked in by the exclusivity you granted.

Distributors

  • The difference with the agent: the distributor buys the product and sets the prices. "I sell it to you for this; I do not know if you are selling it for 2 euros or 10 euros." Customers are the distributor's.
  • Personal experience: his company (URBAR) was distributor for several manufacturers, including a Swedish pump maker, with agreements lasting years. The manufacturer had no idea who the end customers were, what discounts or marketing were used; it only saw orders from the distributor.
  • Exclusivity works both ways: if a local customer contacted the manufacturer directly, the manufacturer was obliged to send them back to the distributor.

Trading companies

  • Sogo shoshas: 50% of Japan's exports and 75% of imports. Mitsubishi was valued at about 42 billion dollars (chart from six years ago). "You want to sell something into Japan? Go through one of those trading companies."

Due diligence and contract terms for intermediaries

  • They all arrive saying "I will be your man" with wonderful presentations. You must verify: real knowledge of the market and customers; for distributors, financial solvency so they pay rapidly and on time; whether they already carry competing products; and always check references. Asking for references is itself a test: the reaction of someone with no real history gives them away.
  • Student question on minimum sales quotas: "Everything is open." Distributors typically ask for exclusivity for three years and say "give us at least one year, or eighteen months, to develop the business." You can set minimum sales, commission percentages, whatever you negotiate.
  • Student question: is it better to pick a distributor already selling similar products, or one with country experience but no similar product? His preference was distributors already in the sector with complementary catalogues (not competing ones): a competing line turns the relationship into a question of price, and you cannot position as premium.
  • Goals to put in writing: volume, number of units; for agents, a required number of visits per week or month plus monthly reports listing the customers visited with names and contacts, so you can check the visits are real.
  • Duration and exit: always set a duration and how the contract can be terminated. A notice period of 60 or 90 days is reasonable, not ten days. Define how termination works to avoid legal claims later.

Direct export

  • Internet: companies received foreign orders without ever planning to export, then adapted websites and catalogues.
  • Branded manufacturers: Lee and Wrangler jeans sold outside the US are made and sold by a local manufacturer that receives the designs and the fabrics to use, and also takes care of selling, under the Lee or Wrangler brand.
  • Export department: for complex, high-value assets (he mentioned windmills and large infrastructure) an agent or a B2B intermediary cannot handle the complex sales process; the manufacturer itself must meet the potential customers. "There are occasions where you just have to be yourself."

Contractual agreements in general

  • Each side puts capabilities on the table so that combining them gives a good outcome. The transfer of knowledge must be handled carefully so it is not used against you: a partner that sold his products later began producing a similar product under another brand name.

Turn-key and concessions

  • Turn-key example from his company: water treatment plants for municipalities in Vietnam. They signed with the municipality, built the plant in containers, assembled it on site and handed it over.
  • Concessions: his company holds concessions to collect waste in several municipalities outside Spain. The municipality says "I will give you ten years of the concession to treat the waste of my municipality; it will not cost me anything." You organize everything from collection to treatment, run the numbers, make the expensive investment and recover it over the years of the concession. It made sense to seek concessions where they already had a plant.

Subcontracting

  • A non-equity option: no new company, no buying or selling of shares.
  • Companies realise more and more that they cannot do everything. Fast fashion companies design (colours, fabrics) and subcontract manufacturing. Car makers are really assembly companies buying from multiple suppliers; airplanes likewise (the Boeing map).

Licensing

  • You license something unique to you: brand names, proprietary technology, intellectual property, domain names, industrial designs, logos, database rights.
  • Coca-Cola: the company sends the concentrate and in each country different bottling companies produce under licence (the Olayan slide).
  • His own case: a licensing agreement with National Geographic (Washington) to produce books, clothing and other products with the National Geographic logo, brand name and colours.
  • A student asked whether such merchandising hurts an established brand. Answer: case by case. In their case it did not work: the Spanish company was not able to make money, some designs were nice but the quality was not good, and National Geographic eventually wanted to recover the licence because it was to some extent hurting the brand. National Geographic later ran product corners itself in different countries. "We were the wrong partners, I have to admit."
  • Payment problems from experience: the licence carried a minimum payment; they overspent on marketing and commercial activity while sales did not follow, so an unpaid 500,000 became one, two, three million.
  • Licensing is also a good solution where local regulation restricts foreign companies from entering directly.

Co-marketing and co-branding

  • Co-marketing: GoPro and Red Bull; Starbucks and Spotify (codes giving free or discounted access for a period, and vice versa). Two different products advertised together; the products stay separate.
  • Co-branding: a new product combining two brands. Student example accepted: Meta and Ray-Ban glasses. Others: Milka with Oreo, Philadelphia with Milka, McFlurry with M&Ms or Kit Kat.
  • Student question on who keeps the profit: it depends; often a much larger company knocks on the door of a smaller one and proposes a split such as 70 or 80 percent for itself.

Franchising

  • A student recounted the McDonald's in India case from another class: no beef, a complicated market, they needed a local joint venture partner, found one, split the country into two regions, and the relationship with one partner degraded into a public controversy with accusations that the partner was taking money from McDonald's. The professor used it as another illustration of why you check references and reputation before entering.
  • Franchising works because it combines skill centralization with operational decentralization: somebody local brings the knowledge of the market and the people. It is a fast way to get into a country, with risks on adapting to local culture.
  • His company was on both sides: the licensing contract with National Geographic Washington gave it the right to open franchise agreements with local stores in whichever country it wanted. Products were sold through shops the company owned and through franchised shops in different countries.

Strategic alliances (5 Oct)

  • The BP quote is the basis for alliances: any organization that thinks it does everything best is arrogant and foolish; someone else may know more about something.
  • Link to the readiness session: when you analyse resources and capabilities, "even if you have them, do you have enough of them?" If not, an alliance is a way to acquire or obtain them. Complementarity with the partner is crucial; the idea is to reduce risk and go hand in hand towards a mutual goal.
  • Uncertainty and ambiguity: you are dealing with another party you do not fully know; the relationship evolves.
  • Always put two things in contracts: the duration and the ways to end it. Example: "I want to work with you for two years, but the contract can be resolved with three months' notice." (Same rule he gave for agents and distributors.)
  • "Today's ally may be tomorrow's rival" comes from personal experience.
  • Non-equity alliances: no exchange of equity. As a first step, companies normally start with a non-equity alliance. "This is what we did" (General Kinematics with URBAR).

FDI (5 Oct, recording ends part way through)

  • Advantage of FDI: speed of action once you know the country. But his advice: rather than going straight to FDI, start with an agent or a distributor to get a flavour of how your products do in the country. Sometimes that is impossible (for some products or services only FDI works), but normally try a lighter alternative first.
  • FDI is the most risky alternative and the one that takes the most money, and also the one that gives you the most money, because there is no intermediary: the whole margin is yours.
  • Representative office: nothing more than a commercial office to market your products, one or two people. It does not have to be a physical shop, but you must legally create an establishment in the country; in most countries this is very easy to set up.
  • Branch: just an extension of the current company. Whatever the branch does in the new country, not only the branch but the head office is directly legally responsible. A branch can only sell exactly the same product or service as the parent company. (The recording cuts off here; the subsidiary, greenfield and M&A slides were not captured on the transcript.)

Likely exam angles

  • Know that the four entry levels in order of rising resource commitment, risk and return are indirect export, direct export, contractual agreements, FDI.
  • Know that the criteria for choosing an entry mode are resource commitment (and barriers), risk, return/benefits, and time frame or speed required.
  • Know that indirect export means selling to a cross-border intermediary (middleman) that exports for you; the four types are importer (export management company), agent/representative, distributor and trading company.
  • Know that an agent works on commission, does not buy the goods, and the customers belong to the exporter; a distributor buys the goods, usually wants territorial exclusivity, and the customers belong to the distributor; a representative is a specialized agent limited to a specific geographic area and/or goods.
  • Know that agent advantages are low entry cost, low staffing, immediate presence, intermediary overcomes entry difficulties, control over the product; disadvantages are low profitability, high dependence, no international experience gained.
  • Know that trading companies give full service but buy on behalf of foreign clients, so they have no loyalty to the exporter; Japan's sogo shoshas handle 50% of exports and 75% of imports; Mitsubishi was the largest at 42.5 billion dollars in 2019.
  • Know the four due diligence checks on an intermediary (knowledge, expertise, financial capacity and facilities; prompt payment; handling of competing products; reputation and references) and the five goal areas for the trade (volume/share/margin; financial and personnel commitments; degree of control, terms of sale and channel ownership; coverage; duration/continuity).
  • Know that direct export includes internet, wholesaler (not a sale to the final customer), branded manufacturers (Lee and Wrangler) and an export department for B2B high-technology or high-value products with complex sales.
  • Know that contractual agreements are long-term, usually non-equity, associations involving transfer of knowledge, construction or manufacturing capabilities; the five types are turn-key projects, subcontracting, licensing, franchising and strategic alliances (JV).
  • Know that a turn-key project is the complete construction of a plant or infrastructure abroad, and a concession is a right granted (for example by a municipality) to run a service like waste collection.
  • Know that licensing grants rights (patents, trademarks, brand names, technology) for specific purposes in a specific country or region; it needs little capital, works where import restrictions block other entry modes, and is key where foreign ownership is sensitive; risks are wrong partner, quality problems, payment problems, loss of marketing control.
  • Know that co-marketing is joint promotion of existing products (Starbucks and Spotify, Red Bull and GoPro) while co-branding creates a new combined product (Apple Watch Nike+, McFlurry Kit Kat, Meta Ray-Ban).
  • Know that franchising is a form of licensing; the franchiser provides products, systems and management services, the franchisee provides market knowledge, capital and personal involvement; it is the fastest expansion method of all, needs low investment and enjoys friendly regulation; risks are local taste adaptation and control.
  • Know the National Geographic chain: the Society in Washington licenses the Spanish company, which franchises store operators; licence terms were worldwide brand rights with prior approval, an annual fee and a percentage of sales.
  • Know that alliances are distinguished by three elements (mutual dependence on collaborative effort, exchange of knowledge, trust because contracts cannot foresee all risks), that complementarity is crucial, and that about 60% fail, mainly because of poor partner selection and lack of trust.
  • Know the SIA formation steps: do I need one, define form and objectives, partner selection (strategic fit = complementarity; organizational fit = chemistry, similar cultures, reputation, compatible systems, common time horizon), contract negotiation (seven questions including exit strategy and monitoring).
  • Know that an equity JV creates a separate jointly owned company (the classic alliance), while a non-equity alliance involves no equity and no new company, is limited in scope or duration, and is easier to form and dissolve.
  • Know that FDI means a physical presence abroad, is a realistic option after establishing yourself as an exporter, and its forms are representative office, branch (sales office) and subsidiary.
  • Know that a representative office does marketing and promotion only and cannot buy, sell or produce; a branch can do everything the parent does including buying and selling, but is not a separate legal entity. Know the five branch versus subsidiary rows: legal entity, taxation (double taxation agreements versus taxed where formed), activities (same versus can differ), ownership (100% versus more than 50% to 100%), liabilities (extend to parent versus limited to the subsidiary).
