What the professor added in class

How he teaches and examines

  • EXAM: "For the final exam, that will be a multiple-choice exam, I never do complicated questions." Said at the unicorn slide: "you have here the definition."
  • EXAM: He and Prof. Neira will not ask dates ("that's why we have computers"); he asks many questions in class but "this is not an exam".
  • EXAM: Sessions 10, 11, 12 and 14 with him all use Harvard cases loaded on Canvas with questions; later he said his exam questions come from the cases and nothing not reviewed in class is asked.
  • All his sessions are loaded in Canvas content; this deck is "The Shifting Wealth of Nations". The course had about 50 students last edition and 10 now, which he reads as people thinking there is no risk in 2026.
  • He recommends: use the IE library's free access to The Economist while you are a student; read Peter Bernstein, "Against the Gods: The Remarkable Story of Risk" (in the library): risk and insurance began with transport and British gambling.
  • Use Coface's free website: "country risk assessment" and "business climate assessment" per country, with population, GDP per capita, a ready-made SWOT, main indicators and main trade partners. Rating agencies (S&P, Moody's, Fitch) rate countries; Coface rates country risk and business climate.

Coface country examples

  • Colombia: rating "C" is not very good, but business climate is reasonable and the country is growing; 52 million people; commodities (coffee, oil, gas); 30 percent of exports go to the US, 26 percent of imports come from the US, 5 percent of exports go to India; the weakness is solvency and a weak Colombian peso; also infrastructure, security, unemployment. Years ago Colombians went to Venezuela, now the reverse.
  • Angola: Portuguese speaking (with Brazil and Mozambique); a very long civil war because one side had the oil and the other the diamonds; he visits Luanda 3 or 4 times a year; invest with a 5-year horizon.
  • Africa: about 1.4 billion people, like China, but in 54 countries; plenty of commodities and opportunities beyond South Africa (Tanzania, Ivory Coast, Senegal); payments are by mobile phone.
  • Italy: political instability is not necessarily bad; about 45 changes of prime minister since 1944, a PM lasts 1 to 1.5 years; one of the G8.
  • Turkey: Garanti is the biggest bank, owned by BBVA (Banco Bilbao Vizcaya Argentaria, Spain's second bank after Santander); Erdogan is his example of a strong leader; lira at a historic low, so imports (oil, gas) are dear; only Muslim NATO member, wants to join the EU.
  • Spain: huge oil, gas and electricity companies (Iberdrola the biggest utility, Naturgy) but no oil, gas or electricity of its own; what Spain does well is banking; IBEX 35 is the index of the 35 biggest companies; cars are Spain's main export (as for France and Germany).

Political risk in developed countries

  • Iberdrola (with a Danish partner) won a US tender for an 80-turbine offshore wind farm; in December 2025 the Trump administration cancelled it, costing Iberdrola a huge amount. "A very good example of political risk" from inside the US.
  • Naturgy's branch in Colombia was expropriated (around 2016).
  • Twenty-five years ago the textbook political-risk countries were Argentina, then Iran; now decisions inside the US can cost a Spanish company a lot of money.

Iran, Iraq and "the allies of today are the enemies of tomorrow"

  • Film Argo (Ben Affleck, 2012, best picture): six US diplomats escaped the 1979 Tehran embassy assault via the Canadian ambassador's house; the rest were held 444 days, released January 1981. He said 67 were held (unclear; the usual figure is 52).
  • OECD (Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development: US, UK, Germany, France, Spain, Italy, Japan, South Korea, Australia, Canada and others, the highest income per capita countries) saw Iran as risky and Iraq as the ally everyone sold weapons to in the 1980s.
  • Summer 1990 Iraq invaded Kuwait; the allies freed Kuwait in January 1991 (First Gulf War); Saddam stayed; Iraq became the bad one and Iran the good one again.
  • 2003 Second Gulf War: Saddam captured and hanged; Iraq reliable again; Iran (enriching uranium) and Afghanistan the bad ones; EU and US sanctions on Iran.
  • 2025 (around June or July): the EU lifted sanctions on Iran, the first time in 45 years that a European company could do business there; then the US attacked Iran in 2025 and again in February 2026. Iran and Iraq have oil and dollars and lack almost everything else, so they are attractive markets.
  • Today's main concern is the Strait of Hormuz and commodities: oil about USD 100 a barrel; it all traces back to 1979, but nobody remembers.
  • Defence is the sector growing most (Germany will build its biggest army in 70 years); education is the other booming sector (a bubble: US student loans of 30 to 40 years, prices rising everywhere).

Developed versus developing

  • He dislikes "rich and poor countries". Japan and China are the biggest lenders in the world, so calling China poor is absurd. The World Bank line is about USD 10,000 income per capita: above, developed; below, developing. China's income per capita went from about USD 4,000 ten years ago to about 10,000 today.

The ICC contract, letters of credit and chambers of commerce

  • Chambers of commerce are paid by your taxes, exist abroad (Chamber of Commerce of India or the US in Madrid), help companies trade with the other country and keep data on what moves between the two; visit one at least once a year.
  • Letters of credit: about 44 percent of international corporate-to-corporate transactions use one; created and ruled by the ICC; there will be a dedicated session on it. He finds it amazing that a master can run 100-something hours without mentioning it.
  • The eight points and his examples are under slide 3 above. Key sentence: "The guarantee of payment and the term of payment is not exactly the same."

The three transaction risks (ICC)

  • Transport: ever more expensive (truck, ship, plane); "the only free thing in this world is the love of your parents": Amazon Prime delivery is paid by someone (the seller's margin). Cargo India to Spain can be 10 to 15 percent of the price; margins are falling because prices rise and competition is plentiful.
  • Currency: most international business is in hard currencies (euro, US dollar, Japanese yen, British pound); Brazil, Russia, India, China, Saudi Arabia do not have one. If an Indian buyer must pay in euros, the strong euro makes it expensive. IE tuition must be paid in euros, not rupees.
  • Credit: you sell on credit at 120, 150 days or a year; what happens during those months (a Saudi client at 180 days in 2026)? Plenty of uncertainty.
  • Insurance mentality: people only buy insurance when obliged (a EUR 2 insurance refused on a EUR 45-50 ski pass; Asterix's bard is called Assurancetourix, "insurers are annoying"). If you never insure, why do you do international business as if nothing can happen?

Macro rules of thumb from Session 4

  • Inflation: 2 percent is healthy (consumption); Turkey's 30 to 40 percent is destructive; inflation squeezes corporate margins; higher-inflation countries become more expensive without being better.
  • Interest rates: raising them is the best way to fight inflation, but it hurts borrowers and the poor; about 80 percent of global loans are variable rate (study guide); a half-point rise makes a working-capital loan dearer.
  • Trade balance and currency: surplus means demand for your currency, so it appreciates, your government borrows cheaply and inflation is low. A weak currency makes exports cheap but imports (energy, travel) expensive.
  • The dollar puzzle: the US has the biggest trade deficit yet a strong dollar because China invests massively in the US so that US firms keep manufacturing in China ("you have an Apple computer made in China and you don't care").
  • Original sin: lenders give developing countries dollars or euros, never their own currency; when US rates rise everyone with dollar debt pays more. Russia's foreign-currency debt is very low, so sanctions bite less.
  • Who pays government debt: citizens and corporates, through taxes. Exports are tax free everywhere (the importer pays) except Argentina, which taxes both.
  • Every crisis since 1945 was escaped through exports; protectionism is the opposite and is now very popular.
  • Japan: debt over 220 percent of GDP, owned domestically, rates near zero for 36 years, first rise in 35 years in 2025.
  • Strong leaders: easy solutions to complicated problems; Erdogan and Putin; vicious circle.
  • Growth is moving away from Europe: Asia-Pacific about 78 percent of growth; Europe below 1 percent; China 41 percent optimistic versus France 3 percent; rising middle class means more opportunities.
  • Patents and technology: China files the most (WIPO 2023), Huawei the most of any company; "without Apple no Huawei, without Mercedes or Audi no BYD"; the Mecca-Medina train paid about 25 percent in foreign patents; productive (R&D, education) versus non-productive investment (real estate: 700,000 flats in Spain in 2007, 70,000 in 2008).
  • Three biggest exporters: China, Germany, the US.
  • Nokia and Lehman: leaders disappear fast; Lehman defaulted September 2008, Bear Stearns' funds were already in trouble in June 2007.
  • Closing summary of the unit: rising interest rates, a strong dollar and huge debt (negatives) and a rising middle class (positive) are already here. If you do international business, look for clients in developing economies.

Likely exam angles

  • Know that the ICC contract template has 8 points: parties, object, transport, terms of payment, guarantees of payment, courts, legislation, risks.
  • Know that the three risks in the ICC template are transport, currency and credit.
  • Know that a term of payment (how long the buyer has to pay, for example 10 percent in advance and the rest at 180 days) is different from a guarantee of payment (security such as a deposit or bank bond).
  • Know that Aguirre's advice is to put the courts and legislation of the country of destination in the contract, and that London arbitration is only worth it for large claims.
  • Know that letters of credit cover about 44 percent of international corporate-to-corporate trade and that the ICC created both the Incoterms and the letter of credit rules.
  • Know that Cuba's average payment term is 360 days, and that 95 percent of companies are SMEs that usually sell abroad through a distributor.
  • Know the four numbered risks on the deck: 1 emerging-market capital flows and external vulnerability (original sin), 2 commodity prices, 3 debt, 4 freight costs.
  • Know what original sin means: developing countries borrow in USD or EUR, not their own currency; Turkey had the highest foreign-currency corporate debt (about 36 percent of GDP); India and China the lowest (7 to 8).
  • Know the Hormuz numbers: about 21 percent of oil supply and 27 percent of maritime oil trade; Malacca is bigger (23 / 31); only two bypass pipelines (Saudi East-West and UAE Fujairah) carrying about 3.5 mb/d against about 19 to 20 mb/d through the strait; about 33 percent of seaborne fertiliser and about 31 percent of crude flows pass through it.
  • Know that Coface's alternative scenario (energy +50 percent) gives global growth 2.1 percent, Europe 0.5, US 1.8, inflation +1.5 points, stagflation.
  • Know that "reciprocal" tariffs were computed as bilateral deficit divided by exports to the US (EU: 235 / 606 = 38.8 percent, charged 39, discounted 20; 10 percent floor), and that the cost is about 80 percent domestic, two thirds in margins, one third in consumer prices; worst case is a crisis of confidence and collapse of the dollar.
  • Know the Japan facts: third largest economy, biggest creditor, highest public debt of any developed country (over 220 percent, held domestically), 10-year yield raised from 0.25 to 0.50 at the end of 2022, first rate rise in 35 years in 2025.
  • Know the strongmania cycle: weak growth, inequality and corruption, weak institutions, protest votes and strong leaders, bad policies, weak growth.
  • Know that Asia-Pacific is about 78.7 percent of world GDP growth 2016-2026 (slide caption), that Asia crossed 50 percent of world GDP at PPP around 2020, and that more people live inside the Asian circle than outside it.
  • Know that China files the most PCT patents (69,610 in 2023), ahead of the US and Japan, and Huawei is the top applicant; CATL grew 576 percent.
  • Know the definition: a unicorn is a privately held startup valued at over USD 1 billion (Spain: Cabify and Glovo).
  • Know the GDP identity C + I + G + net exports, the balance of payments accounts current, capital, financial, and that corporates are analysed with balance sheet and P&L while countries use balance of payments plus GDP.
  • Know Mankiw's ten principles and the examples attached (airline seats for marginal thinking, biodiesel for incentives, Germany 1921-22 for printing money) and the two-line summary: trade makes everyone better off; living standards depend on productivity.
  • Know the PESTEL contents (politics, economy, social, technology, legal, environment) and that it needs an economic and political approach.
  • Know the tourism figures: 1.52 billion arrivals in 2025 (+4 percent), Spain 96.8 million, spending forecast EUR 135.8 billion, the US the only major destination declining in early 2026.
  • Know that The Economist's World Ahead missed COVID (2020) and Ukraine (2022), that Trump tweeted "trade wars are good, and easy to win" on 2 March 2018, and that Bill Clinton called globalisation a force of nature like wind or water.
  • Know that the three biggest exporters are China, Germany and the US; that 2 percent inflation is healthy; that exports are tax free except in Argentina; and that every post-1945 crisis was resolved through exports.

Traps and look-alikes

  • Term of payment versus guarantee of payment: the term is time (120, 180, 360 days); the guarantee is security (deposit, bank bond, letter of credit). Both are separate points of the ICC template.
  • Courts versus legislation: two separate points; both should be the country of destination. London arbitration is a court choice, not a legislation choice, and is expensive.
  • ICC's three risks (transport, currency, credit) versus the deck's four risks (emerging-market capital flows, commodities, debt, freight): the first list is for a single transaction; the second is the global macro list. Political risk is a third category illustrated by Iberdrola and Naturgy.
  • Incoterms versus letters of credit: both come from the ICC; Incoterms (FOB, CIF, EXW) allocate transport cost and risk; the letter of credit is a payment guarantee.
  • Malacca versus Hormuz: Malacca carries more oil (23 percent of supply, 31 of seaborne trade); Hormuz is second (21 / 27) but has almost no bypass. Suez is the best known, not the biggest.
  • Share of total supply versus share of maritime trade: the two bars on slide 18 are different denominators (Hormuz 21 versus 27).
  • East-West pipeline (Saudi, about 3 mb/d) versus Fujairah (UAE, about 0.5): together about 3.5, far below the 19 to 20 transiting.
  • Original sin versus currency risk in a contract: original sin is sovereign and corporate borrowing in hard currency; currency risk in a deal is the exchange rate between invoice and payment.
  • Hard currencies versus the rest: EUR, USD, JPY, GBP are hard; BRL, RUB, INR, CNY, SAR are not. A strong currency is good for a country in Aguirre's view (Japan, UK), bad for a borrower who took a yen loan.
  • Developed versus developing: the dividing line is about USD 10,000 income per capita, not "rich versus poor"; China is a developing economy and one of the two biggest lenders.
  • Reciprocal tariff "charged" versus "discounted": the charged figure is deficit divided by exports (EU 39), the discounted is roughly half (EU 20); 10 percent is the floor for countries with no US deficit.
  • Who bears the tariff: about 80 percent domestic; of that, two thirds margins and one third consumer prices (so far).
  • 78.7 percent versus 62.4 percent: 78.7 is the caption for Asia-Pacific 2016-2026; 62.4 is Asia ex Japan in the ten-year chart (plus Japan 1.0 and Oceania 0.9 is about 64).
  • Patents by country versus by company: China leads countries (69,610), Huawei leads companies (6,494); Samsung is second among companies, the US second among countries.
  • Productive versus non-productive investment: R&D and education (Korea, Emirates) versus real estate (Spain 2007).
  • Trade surplus and currency: surplus leads to appreciation, cheaper borrowing and low inflation; the US is the exception (deficit, strong dollar) because of Chinese capital inflows.
  • Japan's 10-year yield move: from 0.25 to 0.50 at the end of 2022 (yield cap), not a policy rate rise; the first policy rate rise in 35 years was in 2025.
  • GDP components versus balance of payments accounts: C, I, G, NX versus current, capital, financial. Corporates: balance sheet and P&L; countries: balance of payments and GDP.
  • Mankiw's groups: principles 1 to 4 are how people decide, 5 to 7 how people interact, 8 to 10 how the economy works. The invisible hand belongs with 6 and 7, not with 5.
  • PESTEL versus PESTLE: same tool, letters reordered; Environment (weather, pollution, recycling) is not Economy (inflation, rates, costs).
  • Unicorn: privately held and over USD 1 billion; a listed company or a USD 500 million startup is not one.
  • Time versus The Economist covers: Time (Trump "Meltdown", 2016) illustrates developed-economy risk; The Economist Brazil trilogy (2009, 2013, 2016) illustrates overreaction to developing economies.
  • 1979 versus 1981 versus 1990 versus 2003: embassy seized 1979, hostages freed January 1981 after 444 days, Kuwait invaded 1990 (freed January 1991), Iraq invaded 2003. He will not ask dates, but the sequence of who was the ally may come up.
Session 10 + case · complete notes · 10712 words

Session 10. The Asian financial crisis (deck + HBS 9-708-001 "Chronology of the Asian Financial Crisis")

This unit uses the 1997-98 Asian crisis as the worked example of how a country defaults and why the standard policy response (raise interest rates, defend a dollar peg, take an IMF loan with austerity conditions) can make a debt crisis worse. The deck (Prof. Mikel Aguirre, 7 Oct 2026) lists the causes, walks through Korea, Thailand, Indonesia and Malaysia under the high-interest-rate "medicine", compares the Asian Tigers of the 1990s with the BRICs, and ends with how sovereign debt "treatments" hit companies. The HBS case is a dated diary from 5 February 1997 (Somprasong Land misses a USD 3.1 million payment) to 25 November 1998 (Camdessus says the worst is over), with five exhibits of exchange rates and stock indices. In class the professor said what matters most is: a company and a country default for the same reason (short-term debt bigger than short-term liquidity); the trigger of the Asian crisis was a loss of confidence after a wave of bad news and non-performing loans; the finance ministries answered with two measures, higher interest rates and dollar pegs, and both backfired; the single lesson is "do not raise interest rates when there is already a huge debt"; and only one country in IMF history has rejected IMF aid, Malaysia in 1997. He flagged the IMF condition of higher interest rates explicitly "for the multiple choice final exam".

Part 1. The deck slide by slide

Slide 1. Title

  • Title slide, no content.

Slide 2. Asian crisis questions to be answered and discussed during the session

  • Four discussion questions frame the session:
    • What caused the Asian financial crisis?
    • What is your opinion on the implemented high interest rate policy?
    • What do you think is happening currently between the USD and the Yuan?
    • Resemblance between the Asian Miracle at the beginning of the 1990s and the current BRICS+ situation.
  • Speaker note (in Spanish): just comment, and clarify that the banknote is only an expression of the currency (the currency is the money, the note is one physical form of it).

Slide 3. What caused the crisis? (Government)

  • Fixed exchange rates (currencies pegged to the US dollar).
  • Current account deficits.
  • Lack of effective regulatory and control measures over the economy.

Slide 4. What caused the crisis? (Companies / Market)

  • A numerous financial service sector (too many banks and finance companies).
  • Dependence on short-term foreign funds.
  • Currency speculation.
  • Overpriced assets (property and shares).

Slide 5. What caused the crisis? (External reasons)

  • Incapacity of governments to resolve their problems as a result of political uncertainty.
  • Perception of the region as a unit, not as individual countries (contagion: a problem in Thailand was read as a problem in all of Asia).
  • Currency speculation (listed again, now as an external force).
  • The measures for financial institutions that were offered by the IMF (the conditions attached to IMF money).

Slide 6. Asian Financial Crisis: high interest rates, an economic medicine?

  • Section title. The next five slides test whether raising interest rates cured or worsened the crisis, country by country.

Slide 7. Korea

  • November 1997: IMF bailout. The IMF demanded that Korean banks and the government lend at extremely high interest rates. The short-term interbank rate was raised to 30%.
  • Chain of effects of the high-rate policy:
    • More corporate bankruptcies, because companies could not keep up with their debt.
    • Confidence was further ruined.
    • Which accelerated capital outflows.
    • Which accelerated the devaluation of the currency.
  • Result: things got worse during the first six months of the IMF "rescue".
  • Finally the IMF declared a return to "the Korean way". After the IMF changed its demands (lowering the interest rates), Korea recovered dramatically.

Slide 8. Thailand

  • The interest rate hike was starving local businesses of cash and strangling economic growth.
  • For companies already hit by the declines in the currency and in share values, the rate hike became a third burden "that broke their backs".
  • The Thai stock market dropped 75%.
  • Huge numbers of workers returned to their villages in the countryside, and 600,000 foreign workers were sent back to their home countries.

Slide 9. Indonesia

  • High interest rates made it difficult for Indonesian businesses to pay their debts; many failed, which further decreased investor confidence in the economy and the currency.
  • Further depreciation of the currency caused the country's (dollar) debt to keep rising, so more defaults.
  • Inflation caused widespread unrest and political turmoil: riots and violence. Suharto out.
  • Indonesia's recovery was extremely slow.

Slide 10. Malaysia

  • Despite being badly hit, Malaysia was the only Asian country that rejected the IMF bailout.
  • Bank Negara Malaysia (the central bank) required commercial banks and finance companies to peg their deposit interest rates (maturities up to 12 months) to the deposit rate of two leading domestic banks.
  • Malaysia was less affected by the crisis than Thailand, Indonesia or the Philippines.
  • Speaker note (same note repeated on slide 11): the main problem was unhealthy domestic economies (bad private debt) and low confidence; people sold the currency; central banks tried to bail out their currencies but ran out of money; they needed IMF money, but the conditions the IMF imposed (including raising interest rates) made the situation worse.

Slide 11. General overview

  • The IMF advised countries to increase interest rates to attract investment and instil confidence.
  • The money that came was short-term, speculative, "hot" money: money growth with no growth in export production.
  • After the IMF bailout policies, the devalued currency encouraged private-sector borrowing and made the private sector more vulnerable to the outside world.
  • Because of distrust of Asian currencies, the outflow of money could not be prevented.
  • The debt of the private sector became bigger and bigger.
  • High interest rate policies and restricting government expenditure deepened the recession.
  • Conclusion: the high interest rates did not fix the crisis but made it worse, and in the end the IMF changed its policies towards the Asian countries.
  • Speaker note: same as slide 10.

Slide 12. Could this situation be repeated?

  • A YouTube video link only (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=dpxio4mItlY). The question leads into the Tigers-versus-BRICs comparison.

Slide 13. Asian Tigers vs BRICs

  • Seven comparison dimensions, one per following slide: size of the economies, growth of the economies, growth model, competitive advantage sectors, type of regime, interdependence with the US, impact of the crisis.

Slide 14. Size of the economies (GNI per capita, current USD)

  • Asian Tigers at the peak before the crisis (1993, 1994, 1995) versus BRICs around the global financial crisis (2008, 2009, 2010, 2011). The slide uses European thousand separators (19.490 = 19,490).

  • Point: the Tigers were already middle-to-high income economies (Hong Kong and Singapore above 19,000); the BRICs were far poorer per head (India around 1,000 to 1,400; China 3,000 to 5,000), with Brazil and Russia near the 10,000 line.

  • Point: the Tigers grew 6 to 11% a year at the peak of the boom; the BRICs grew 4 to 10% but with a dip in 2009 (Brazil -0.3, Russia -7.8), while China and India kept growing through the subprime crisis.

Slide 16. Growth model

  • Asian Tigers: growth model started with import substitution.
  • But the aim was an outward-looking export model after industrialisation.
  • Criticism: they did not try to become self-sufficient ("self-satisfied" on the slide).

Slide 17. Global position

  • The Four Asian Tigers managed their massive growth mainly through export-driven economies that catered to richer, industrialised nations, and focused on keeping a trade surplus with those partners.
  • They rose to global prominence as NICs (newly industrialised countries) in the 1970s and 1980s.
  • The BRICs are the key emerging economies expected to lead global growth in the next 10 years.

Slide 18. Competitive advantage sectors

EconomySector

Hong KongInternational financial centre
SingaporeInternational financial centre
TaiwanInformation technology
BrazilCars, minerals
RussiaOil and gas, mining, weapons and military machinery, electrical engineering

  • Point: the Tigers were concentrated in two sectors (IT and finance); the BRICs are diversified across commodities, manufacturing, services and arms.

Slide 19. Type of regime

  • Asian Tigers: Hong Kong, a British colony until 1997; Singapore, a republic; South Korea, a liberal democracy; Taiwan, moving from an authoritarian regime towards democracy.
  • BRICs: Brazil, a democratic republic; Russia, a democratic federation (considered "not free" by Freedom House); India, the largest democracy; China, a communist "People's Republic".

Slide 20. Interdependence with the US

  • Asian Tigers: Western countries needed to transfer their labour-intensive industries; the Tigers are relatively small countries, so they have to depend on the US.
  • BRICs: big countries, but with a large amount of trade with the US (especially China); they challenge the US at the same time; they also host labour-intensive industries.

Slide 21. Impact of the (2008) crisis: BRICs

  • BRICs' contribution to the global economy since 2007: 45%.
  • However, they are too heterogeneous to make any generalised comment.
  • FDI outflow limited in China.
  • Brazil, Russia, India: stock markets fell. Became fine from 2009.
  • Decline in short-term credit.
  • Currency appreciation (except China).

Slide 22. Impact of the (2008) crisis: Asian Tigers

  • Singapore and Taiwan: relatively unscathed.
  • South Korea: high levels of NPLs (non-performing loans) and a stock market crash.
  • Hong Kong: intense speculative attacks against its stock market and currency.

Slide 23. Any sovereign debt "treatment" is likely to impact companies

  • Three models of how a government handles its debt problem, and the knock-on for companies:
    • Argentina-Russia treatment: unilateral default. Effect on companies: credit crunch + increasing financing costs + recession shock.
    • Turkey-Brazil treatment: long-lasting deep fiscal adjustment. Effect: late payments by the public sector + anaemic growth.
    • India-Lebanon treatment: banks are "encouraged" to keep (government) debt exposure. Effect: crowding-out (banks hold sovereign paper instead of lending to companies).

Slide 24. What is country risk in 2024?

  • Closing question only; no content on the slide.

Part 2. The case: Chronology of the Asian Financial Crisis (HBS 9-708-001)

Front matter and introduction

  • HBS case 9-708-001, rev. 23 April 2009, by Laura Alfaro, Rafael Di Tella and research associate Renee Kim. Compiled from published sources; covers the beginning of 1997 to the fall of 1998.
  • In the 1990s the "Asian miracle" was the model of successful growth: Korea, Malaysia, Thailand and others attracted investors and capital from around the world.
  • Developing Asia's average real GDP growth was above 9% during 1992-95, "probably unparalleled at any time by any group of economies of comparable size" (endnote 1: Martin Feldstein, "Refocusing the IMF", Foreign Affairs, March/April 1998).
  • In July 1997 Thailand became the first Asian "tiger" to abandon its fixed exchange rate in response to speculative attacks; no one expected a domino-like effect across the region.
  • Investors fled at a record pace, forcing central banks to spend billions in failed defences of their currencies and then to seek IMF bailouts.
  • Jeffrey Sachs (Columbia): "In a matter of a few months, the Asian economies went from being the darlings of the investment community to being virtual pariahs." (endnote 2: Sachs, "The Wrong Medicine for Asia", New York Times, 3 Nov 1997)

1997, February to June: Thailand's warning signs

  • February 5. Somprasong Land Plc, a Thailand-based property developer, misses a USD 3.1 million interest payment on its foreign debt, the first Thai firm to do so.
  • March 3. To boost confidence, the Bank of Thailand orders financial institutions to raise provisions for substandard loans and cash-strapped companies to boost their capital standards. Trading of banking and financial shares is suspended that day; shares tumble the next day (Exhibit 1).
  • March 11. Thailand's government proposes a 100 billion baht bailout for troubled finance companies' bad debts from the weak property sector. IMF managing director Michel Camdessus praises the move: "They are doing exactly what you must do to avoid recurrence of a Mexico-like crisis... I don't see any reason for this crisis to develop further." (The crisis then developed.)
  • May 14. The Bank of Thailand adopts selective capital controls to defend the baht: local banks ordered not to sell baht to foreigners in the swap market, and short-sellers denied access to the domestic market.
    • Headlines: "Thais Win Currency Battle, What About the War?" (Reuters); "Thai Currency Tactics Calm SE Asian Markets" (Financial Times).
    • Amnuay Viravan, Thailand's finance minister: "We need more established measures to deal with any future attacks on the baht, something like what they have in Singapore which stops its people from speculating in its own currency. We have a free and open market but we do not open our market to let people bully us."
  • June 19. Amnuay Viravan, "a proponent of defending the currency at all costs", resigns. Replaced by Thanong Bidaya, head of the Thai Military Bank. A few days later 16 finance firms are ordered to shut down or consolidate, including the prestigious Finance One.

1997, July to September: the pegs break

  • July 2. Thailand lets the baht float freely for the first time since 1984, after speculative attacks forced the central bank to spend billions of its reserves defending it. The baht immediately falls 15%.
    • Mark Mobius, president of Templeton Emerging Market Fund: "We felt it was time for them to devalue and face the reality of what their currency was really worth... now that they've done it, it helps, I think, to clear the deck."
    • The Herald (Glasgow): "The bank finally did the right thing when it had its back to the wall."
    • Reuters: "The risk is you will see some similar weaknesses of the regional currencies such as the (Indonesian) rupiah and the (Malaysian) ringgit and the peso."
  • July 14. Malaysia joins Thailand and abandons its peg, letting the ringgit float.
  • July 15. Kia Motors, Korea's third-largest car maker, is placed under bankruptcy protection. It is the fourth of Korea's top 30 conglomerates to go under or narrowly avoid bankruptcy that year, starting with Hanbo Steel (collapsed in January under USD 6 billion of debt).
  • July 20. The IMF agrees to give the Philippines USD 1 billion in emergency loans after it fails to fend off speculative attacks on the peso.
  • July 24. Malaysia's prime minister Mahathir Mohamad accuses George Soros, American billionaire financier, of causing the ringgit's depreciation, as speculative trading drags the ringgit to a 38-month low against the dollar (Exhibit 2).
  • August 11. The IMF and other Asian countries approve a USD 16 billion loan package for Thailand in exchange for a tough reform plan: major restructuring of the financial sector and a tighter fiscal budget. (Endnote 10: a few days later China pledges USD 1 billion, bringing the Thai package to USD 17 billion.)
  • August 14. Indonesia lets the rupiah float, abandoning its managed trading band, after unsuccessfully spending USD 1 billion to defend it (Exhibit 3).
  • September 20. At the IMF/World Bank annual conference in Hong Kong, Mahathir declares that "currency trading is unnecessary, unproductive, and immoral. It should be stopped." Soros then brands him "a menace to his own country."
    • Headlines: "Mahathir comments rattle regional markets" (Agence France-Presse); "Damage Control, Can Mahathir Get Malaysia Back on Course?" (BusinessWeek).
    • Anwar Ibrahim, Malaysia's deputy prime minister: "I think Soros's remarks are incorrect because the prime minister's criticism against currency speculation and abuse of freedom in the currency trading does not mean that Dr. Mahathir is totally against currency trading."
    • Robert Rubin, US Treasury Secretary: "Currency trading is an inherent and very important function in a modern and global economy, and it is integral to global trade."

1997, October to November: contagion to Indonesia, Hong Kong, Japan and Korea

  • October 8. Indonesia seeks IMF and World Bank help after the rupiah falls more than 30% in two months, despite central bank interventions.
  • October 17. Taiwan floats the new Taiwan dollar.
  • October 17. Malaysia announces tough fiscal tightening: reducing the current account deficit and cutting public spending by 2% (endnote 17 points to the companion case "Malaysia: Capital and Control", HBS 702-040).
  • October 23-28. The Hong Kong stock market loses 25% of its value amid fears over interest rates and pressure on the Hong Kong dollar, dragging other Asian markets and the Dow Jones down. The Korean won begins to tumble.
  • October 24. Malaysia's deputy prime minister says Malaysia will not seek IMF help, nor foresees needing it.
  • October 31. The IMF announces a loan package for Indonesia of USD 23 billion, which eventually reaches USD 40 billion through pledges from other countries. In return Indonesia closes 16 insolvent banks and promises other reforms.
    • Headlines: "Reform, Not Aid, Seen Key in Indonesia IMF Package" and "Asia Stocks Rally on Indonesia's IMF Package" (Reuters).
    • Financial Times: "The IMF plan may, of course, itself weaken further Mr. Suharto's political position. But if the U.S. administration and the IMF are to avert their worst fears of financial and political instability in Asia, they know that more governments must be prepared to take some painful medicine."
  • November 3. Japan's Sanyo Securities, a top-10 brokerage, files for bankruptcy, the first Japanese securities company to do so since World War II.
  • November 19. Korea's finance minister Kang Kyong-shik is dismissed, blamed for accelerating the financial problems. New minister Lim Chang-Ryul says "There is no need for financial help from the IMF" and announces measures such as opening the bond market to foreigners.
  • November 21. Two days later Korea "swallows its pride" and announces it will seek an IMF bailout worth USD 20 billion, as the stock market keeps plunging and the central bank cannot stop the won's slide (Exhibit 4).
    • Reuters: "Southeast Asia is pretty much a tea party compared to Korea."
    • Philadelphia Inquirer: "Investors are urged to Remain Calm despite Financial Crisis in Asia. Pacific Rim Leaders Say the Turmoil can be Contained. The Issue Tops the Agenda at the APEC Summit."
    • The Economist: "If Asia's governments fail to cure their sick banks, their economies' crisis, and its implications for the rest of the world, could grow much worse."
  • November 24. Yamaichi Securities, another top-10 Japanese brokerage, collapses.

1997, December: Korea's rescue and the year-end panic

  • December 3. Korea, the world's 11th largest economy, announces a USD 55 billion bailout package led by the IMF in exchange for a tough restructuring programme. Concerns over Korea spill over, dragging the Thai baht to a record low. The previous day the Malaysian ringgit fell to its lowest level since 1973.
  • December 5. Malaysia's deputy prime minister Anwar Ibrahim announces a severe austerity programme. The 1998 growth forecast is cut to 4%-5% from 7%. Measures: (1) slash federal expenditure by at least 18%; (2) restore foreign currency reserves to at least four months of retained imports; (3) cut the current account deficit to 3% of GNP from the previous 4% target; (4) freeze bailout loans for failing corporations; (5) tighter credit policies. The Kuala Lumpur Stock Exchange surges more than 5%.
  • December 8. In an unprecedented move, Thailand permanently shuts 56 of its 58 ailing finance companies, welcomed by the IMF and investors.
  • December 16. Korea removes the daily foreign exchange band of plus or minus 10%. BusinessWeek's editorial urges "Dear IMF: Don't Make Asia's Flu Worse", arguing that "in a deflationary economic environment... typical IMF policy prescriptions can do more harm than good."
  • December 17. Japan announces a surprise 2 trillion yen tax cut; markets react positively.
  • December 22. Moody's downgrades Indonesia, Korea and Thailand to junk-bond status. Malaysia's rating is cut too but stays investment grade. Korean and Malaysian markets tumble; the Jakarta exchange rises 1.9% because the downgrade was expected.
  • December 23. The World Bank announces USD 3 billion in emergency loans to Korea, bringing the Korean package to USD 58 billion.
    • Kim Dae Jung, newly elected president of Korea, the first from an opposition party: "We don't know whether we'll default tomorrow or the day after tomorrow... Our warehouse is empty. It's a matter of surviving a day, not a month. I can't believe how the government has been so negligent."
  • December 23. Chinese premier Zhu Rongji says there will be no devaluation of the yuan despite the turmoil (endnote 29: the last major revaluation of the yuan was in 1994).
  • December 24. The IMF and other economies agree to speed up disbursement of USD 10 billion to Korea, since the initial announcement failed to calm the market or stop the won's fall.
  • December 29. The rupiah suffers as reports put Indonesia's total foreign debt at around USD 200 billion; the government says it is closer to USD 130 billion.
  • December 30. Major international banks agree to roll over Korea's short-term debt.

1998, January to February: Indonesia's panic, Korea's rollover, Thailand's renegotiation

  • (The case prints January 8 before January 5.)
  • January 8. The ringgit hits a new all-time low after a Bank for International Settlements report that Malaysia's short-term debt reached 56% of total borrowings from foreign lenders, far above earlier estimates of 30%, plus concerns over other regional currencies.
  • January 5. Thai prime minister Chuan Leekpai says Thailand will renegotiate its IMF conditions; a budget surplus of 1% of 1998 GDP cannot be met.
  • January 12. Peregrine Investments Holdings, Asia's largest private investment bank (Hong Kong), files for liquidation, citing exposure to loans in Indonesia. The Hang Seng plunges 774 points, or 8.7%.
  • January 15. Suharto signs a new IMF agreement that eliminates Indonesia's monopolies and state subsidies, amid doubts about his commitment. It does little to restore confidence. Wall Street Journal: "Indonesia Reaches IMF Pact to Speed Reforms, Tougher Accord Expected to Curb Suharto System of 'Crony Capitalism'."
  • January 23. The rupiah plunges for five consecutive days, losing more than a third of its value. Trigger: indications that Suharto could pick B.J. Habibie as vice-president (and possible successor). Habibie is known for unorthodox economic views and large-scale capital-intensive industrial projects (aerospace), and lacks the army's support.
    • Headlines: "Indonesia Faces Debt, Currency Nightmare" (Reuters); "Asian Crisis Worsens as Indonesia Panics" (Evening Standard); "Soaring Ambition: B.J. Habibie, best known for his bold aerospace plans, may be set to take the co-pilot seat as Indonesia's vice-president; Investors are taking flight" (Far Eastern Economic Review).
  • January 28. Korea agrees with its global creditors to roll over USD 24 billion of short-term debt into government-guaranteed loans. The New York Times, in hindsight: "Banks were slow to see warning signs in Asia", having stepped up lending even as trouble emerged.
  • January 30. Thailand removes the two-tier currency trading system in place since May 1997 (which had restricted foreigners' holdings of baht), making the baht truly free-floating.
  • February 17. Suharto fires Soedradjad Djiwandono, the independent-minded central bank governor and key IMF negotiator, over a disagreement about a currency board and other reforms. Most Asian currencies close slightly higher on speculation that Indonesia may not adopt the board.
  • February 18. Standard & Poor's raises Korea's rating (still junk), removes it from CreditWatch and upgrades its outlook to "stable", citing reform efforts.
  • February 20. Japan's ruling party announces its fourth economic package since October; the yen slips. The package is criticised for lacking bigger tax cuts or public spending. Other G-7 leaders urge Japan to speed up stimulus (Exhibit 5), complaining that the world's second-biggest economy is undermining the international effort by failing to stimulate itself and clean up its banks.
    • New York Times: "U.S. Sees New Villain in Asia Crisis: Japan's Government." Fortune: "The Risks Are Rising: Unless Political Leaders Move Fast, the Current Crisis Will Worsen and Shock World Markets Even Harder. The Key: a Bold Plan to Restore Confidence in the Region's Shaky Banking System."
  • February 23. Indonesia backs down from the currency board plan under pressure from the IMF and world leaders, who argued it was unsustainable given insufficient reserves. Camdessus had written to Suharto in early February saying the plan would make the IMF withdraw funding.
  • February 24. The IMF eases Thailand's conditions: a budget deficit of 2% of GDP allowed (for 1997, as printed) and interest rates reduced, a "tacit acknowledgement" that the economy was worse than predicted. The baht appreciates; the stock market closes down 4.76 points to 517.06 on news the economy could contract by as much as 3.5% that year.

1998, March to May: Indonesia unravels, Korea stabilises

  • March 10. Suharto is re-elected to a seventh five-year term.
  • March 19. Zhu Rongji reiterates no yuan devaluation and a commitment to defend the Hong Kong currency board at all costs: "...it will have a bearing not only on the development of China but also on the prosperity and stability of Asia."
  • March 23. Indonesia's central bank raises key interest rates, one as high as 45%, and abandons a proposed 5% tax on foreign currency purchases. The IMF praises it as part of the strategy to control inflation and strengthen the rupiah.
  • March 31. Korea signs an agreement with foreign creditors to roll over 97%, or USD 22 billion, of its short-term debt, removing a major threat to its banks' solvency.
  • April 1. Japan unveils its "Big Bang" deregulation of financial markets: most restraints on FX trading lifted; fixed commissions on large equity transactions deregulated.
  • April 8. Indonesia signs its third letter of intent with the IMF since the crisis began: a government-backed plan to restructure USD 68 billion of foreign corporate debt, faster banking reform, and maintaining high interest rates.
  • May 6. Riots and looting in Medan (northern Indonesia) as price increases, including a fuel price hike of up to 71%, take effect under the IMF agreement.
  • May 13-14. Riots spread through Jakarta, reportedly over a thousand injuries and deaths in two days. Armed troops with tanks patrol; Suharto faces calls to resign.
  • May 21. Suharto steps down after 32 years and names vice-president B.J. Habibie his successor.
  • May 27. Korea's unions launch a two-day nationwide strike over unemployment and layoffs; unemployment 6.7% versus 2.6% a year earlier, with about 8,000 people losing their jobs daily.
  • May 29. Habibie agrees to hold elections in 1999 after a political overhaul.

1998, June to July: Japan in recession, Malaysia turns against the IMF

  • June 13. Japan officially acknowledges its first recession in 23 years: the economy contracted 0.7% in the fiscal year (ending "March 3" as printed). Fears for Korea's recovery send Japan's leading index down 8.1%, its biggest one-day fall ever; the Nikkei 225 falls below 15,000 for the first time since 13 January, and the dollar soars to an eight-year high above 145 yen.
    • Washington Times: "Wave of Recession in Asia Washes over Japan's Economy, Downturn Steeper than Analysts Feared." Dow Jones: "Japan's Inaction on Yen Indicates It Has Run out of Policy Options."
  • June 17. The US Treasury and the Federal Reserve intervene to prop up the yen, spending about USD 2 billion buying yen, amid concerns over Japanese banks' bad loans. President Clinton and other leaders urge Japan to fix its banks.
  • June 24. Mahathir appoints Daim Zainuddin (former finance minister and loyal ally) to the Cabinet with special authority over economic recovery, seen as undermining finance minister Anwar Ibrahim, who supports high interest rates; Mahathir and Daim favour easing. Ringgit and stocks slip. The next day Mahathir attacks the IMF prescription of high rates: "We thought the IMF stance was good, so we adopted that. But we found out it has been very damaging to our economy."
  • June 25. Indonesia and the IMF announce their fourth agreement: up to USD 6 billion extra funding, and Indonesia is allowed to keep fuel and food subsidies after the May riots.
  • July 23. Malaysia unveils a national economic recovery plan (stabilise the ringgit, restore confidence, financial stability), including temporarily lifting limits on foreign equity ownership in new manufacturing projects until the end of December 1999. Markets shrug: the ringgit is unchanged and the stock index slips 1.5%.
  • July 28. The IMF eases monetary and fiscal austerity for Korea as the economy sinks into its deepest recession since 1980: Korea may lower interest rates and run a budget deficit of 4% of GDP. The IMF revises its forecast to a GDP decline of 4% in 1998, versus 1% forecast three months earlier.

1998, August to November: global spillover and the end of the acute phase

  • August 4. The Dow Jones plunges nearly 300 points, its third-biggest point loss, on Asia's weak recovery and weaker corporate earnings.
  • August 11. The yen slumps to another eight-year low, hitting regional stock indices and raising fears of another round of Asian devaluations.
  • August 27. Russia's political and economic problems hammer stock markets "from Tokyo to London to San Paulo"; investors fear spread to Europe and Latin America.
  • September 2. Mahathir fires deputy prime minister Anwar Ibrahim, one day after imposing stricter currency and capital controls: freezing Malaysian shares traded on Singapore's over-the-counter market and requiring all ringgit held offshore to be repatriated within a month. Anwar, respected abroad, favoured free-market principles against Mahathir's approach.
  • September 27. Japan Leasing Corporation, the second-biggest leasing company, files for bankruptcy under an estimated USD 16 billion of debt, the largest Japanese bankruptcy since World War II.
  • September 28. Korea's president Kim Dae Jung announces recovery measures: lower interest rates, more money supply, bigger fiscal budget; he rules out a second currency crisis.
  • October 9. The dollar suffers its biggest weekly loss against the yen since 1971, more than 10%, as hedge funds dump dollars to repay yen loans amid fears of a global meltdown. Japan's finance minister Kiichi Miyazawa sees no need for central bank intervention, which rattles investors further.
  • November 25. Camdessus praises Korea and Thailand for their reforms, predicts recovery next year, and says "...the worst of the crisis is now over."

Exhibits (all compiled by the casewriter from Global Financial Data, accessed 28 January 2008; a superscript "a" means the marker shows the next day's reaction because the market was closed on the event day)

  • Exhibit 1a. Thai baht per US dollar, Feb 1997 to Nov 1998 (scale 20 to 60). The line is flat at about 25-26 baht through 2/5, 3/3, 3/11 and 5/14 (the peg holds), then steps up at 6/19 and jumps at 7/2 (the float) to about 30, reaches about 32 at 8/11, climbs steadily through the autumn, passes 45 at 12/8 and 12/22, and peaks around 55 in early January 1998 (1/5 marker), the baht's weakest point. It recovers to about 46 by 2/24 (IMF eases conditions) and drifts down to the mid-30s by 11/25/98. Reading: a rising line means a weaker baht; the baht lost more than half its dollar value from the float to the January peak.
  • Exhibit 1b. Thailand's SET index (scale 100 to 800). Starts near 800 in February 1997, falls through 3/3 and 3/11 (about 700), 5/14 (about 600), 6/19 (about 450-500), bounces after 7/2 and 8/11 (about 550-600), falls to about 350-400 by 12/8 and 12/22, rallies to about 500-520 by 1/30 and 2/24 (517.06 close), then slides through 1998 to a low near 250-300 around September 1998 before recovering towards 350-400 at 11/25. This is the chart behind the deck's "Thai stock market dropped 75%".
  • Exhibit 2a. Malaysian ringgit per US dollar, Jul 1997 to Nov 1998 (scale 2.0 to 5.0). About 2.5 at 7/14 (the float) and 7/24 (Soros accusation), about 3.0 at 9/22 (Mahathir's "immoral" speech, next-day reaction), 3.3 to 3.5 at 10/17, 10/24 and 12/5, about 3.8 at 12/22, then a spike to about 4.7-4.9 at 1/8/98 (all-time low, the BIS short-term debt report). It fluctuates between 3.6 and 4.2 through the spring, 6/24 and 7/23 at about 4.0-4.2, then from 9/2 (capital controls) the line goes perfectly flat at about 3.8: Malaysia re-pegged the ringgit at 3.80 per dollar and the chart shows no movement afterwards.
  • Exhibit 2b. Malaysia KLSE index (scale 200 to 1,200). About 1,100 at 7/14 and 7/24, about 800 at 9/22, about 700-750 at 10/17 and 10/24, about 550 at 12/5 (the austerity plan, the "surge of more than 5%" is the small bump) and 12/22, about 450 at 1/8, a recovery to 600-700 in February-March 1998, then a long slide through 6/24 (about 450) and 7/23 (about 400) to a low near 300 at 9/2, followed by a recovery to about 500 by November 1998.
  • Exhibit 3a. Indonesian rupiah per US dollar, Jul 1997 to Nov 1998 (scale 2,000 to 16,000). About 2,400-2,600 at the start and at 8/14 (the float), about 3,600-3,800 at 10/8 and 10/31, about 5,500-6,000 at 12/22 and 12/29, about 8,000-9,000 at 1/15, then a spike to roughly 14,000-15,000 at 1/23/98 (the Habibie panic, "more than a third in five days"), back to about 9,000-10,000 at 2/17, 2/23, 3/10 and 3/23, about 8,000 at 4/8, then rising again through 5/6, 5/13, 5/21 (Suharto resigns) and 5/29 to a second peak around 14,500-16,000 at 6/25, before falling to about 7,500-8,000 by November 1998. The rupiah is the worst-hit currency in the case: at the peaks it had lost about 80% of its dollar value.
  • Exhibit 3b. Jakarta SE Composite index (scale 200 to 800). About 720-740 in July 1997, about 650 at 8/14, about 500 at 10/8 and 10/31, about 400 at 12/22 (the 1.9% rise after the expected Moody's cut) and 12/29, about 420-450 at 1/15 and 1/22 (next-day marker), about 480-500 at 2/17 and 2/23, about 500 at 3/10, 3/23 and 4/8, down to 400-450 at 5/6, 5/13, 5/22 (next-day marker) and 5/29, about 450 at 6/25, then a slide to a low near 260-300 in September 1998 and a partial recovery to about 400 by November.
  • Exhibit 4a. Korean won per US dollar, Jul 1997 to Nov 1998 (scale 500 to 2,100). Flat at about 890-900 from 7/15 (Kia) until 10/23 (about 920), then a steep climb: about 1,050 at 11/19, 1,100 at 11/21 (IMF request), 1,200 at 12/3 (USD 55 billion package), 1,500 at 12/16 (band removed), 1,700 at 12/22 (Moody's junk), peak near 1,960-2,000 at 12/23 ("our warehouse is empty"), 1,800 at 12/24, 1,500 at 12/30 (rollover). In 1998 about 1,600-1,700 at 1/28, 1,600 at 2/18, 1,400 at 3/31 and 5/27, 1,300 at 7/28, 1,380 at 9/28 and about 1,250-1,300 at 11/25. The won roughly halved in value in two months (October to December 1997) and recovered about a third of the loss once the debt was rolled over.
  • Exhibit 4b. Korea Composite Stock Price Index, KOSPI (scale 200 to 900). About 760 at 7/15, about 550 at 10/23, about 500 at 11/19, 480 at 11/21, 400 at 12/3, 420 at 12/16, a low of about 350-380 around 12/22, 12/23 and 12/24, a rally to about 550 at 1/30 (next-day marker) and 520 at 2/18, then a second decline: 480 at 3/31, 330 at 5/27 (the strike), 350 at 7/28, about 290-310 at 9/28, the lowest point of the chart, and a recovery to about 450 by 11/25.
  • Exhibit 5a. Japanese yen per US dollar, Jul 1997 to Nov 1998 (scale 100 to 150). About 114-115 in July 1997 (strongest yen of the period), about 120 at 11/3 (Sanyo), 127 at 11/24 (Yamaichi), 129 at 12/17 (tax cut), 126-127 at 2/20, 133 at 4/1 (Big Bang), about 146 at 6/15 (next-day marker for the recession announcement; the "eight-year high above 145 yen"), 136-137 at 6/17 (US-Fed intervention), about 147 at 8/11 (another eight-year low for the yen), 143 at 8/27 (Russia), 134 at 9/28 (next-day marker), then a vertical drop to about 117-118 at 10/9 (the biggest weekly dollar loss since 1971), ending around 120-125 in November 1998.
  • Exhibit 5b. Nikkei 225 index (scale 12,000 to 22,000). About 20,000 in July 1997, about 16,000 at 11/4 (next-day marker for Sanyo) and 16,500 at 11/25 (next-day marker for Yamaichi), 16,500 at 12/17, a dip below 15,000 in late December-January (the "first time since January 13" reference), 17,000 at 2/20, 16,500 at 4/1, about 15,000 at 6/15 (first close below 15,000 since January) and 6/17, 15,500 at 8/11, 14,500 at 8/27, 13,800 at 9/28 (next-day marker) and about 13,000 at 10/9 (a 13-year closing low, per endnote 47), recovering to about 14,500 by November 1998.

  • Endnote 1: Martin Feldstein, "Refocusing the IMF", Foreign Affairs 77, 2 (March/April 1998). Endnote 2: Jeffrey Sachs, "The Wrong Medicine for Asia", New York Times, 3 November 1997 (the Sachs critique of the IMF's high-rate prescription).
  • Endnote 10: China pledged USD 1 billion for Thailand, raising the package to USD 17 billion.
